extraction_notes.note: Appendices B and C are whole-section proofs without proof environments (B: a second, direct proof of Proposition 1 for OBM; C: the proof of Proposition 4). Each is one proof node with its subsections as steps; the lemmas, propositions and their proofs inside them are nested Level-1 nodes.

The proofs of Proposition 1 (OSBM) and Theorem 1 (OSBM) apply the result itself, meaning its special case (SBM, resp. OBM) proved earlier; the self-\ref gives no edge, so the dependency is drawn from the special-case proof (PP2->PP8, PP10->PP11).
Equations (C.3) and (C.8) are the same display carrying the same \label{eq:W}; one node kept, the restatement in also_stated_at.
Remark 3 has a proof environment, so it is retyped as a claim. Examples 1-2 derive results via Lemma 1 and name the associated processes used later; kept as examples with nested definition nodes.
The proof map of Proposition 4 (Figure in Appendix C) is omitted from the source; its content is not extracted.
Short prose facts without later use (0-SBM is BM, reflection as infinite sigma, outline sentences before proofs) were not made nodes.

nodes.name: Statistic $\varepsilon_{n,t}^{(r,f,X)}$ of high-frequency observations
nodes.statement: Given a stochastic process $(X_t)_{t\in [0,\infty)}$, let us consider the following statistics for high frequency observations: \begin{equation} \varepsilon_{n,t}^{(r,f,X)}:=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor n t \rfloor} f(\sqrt{n}(X_{(k-1)/n}-r),\sqrt{n}(X_{k/n}-r)) \end{equation} where $f\colon \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}$ is a measurable function satisfying suitable integrability conditions.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: Normalized sum of $f$ applied to rescaled consecutive observations around level $r$.

nodes.name: Equation (1.1): Statistic $\varepsilon_{n,t}^{(r,f,X)}$
nodes.statement: \varepsilon_{n,t}^{(r,f,X)}:=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor n t \rfloor} f(\sqrt{n}(X_{(k-1)/n}-r),\sqrt{n}(X_{k/n}-r))
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.label: eq:stat

nodes.name: Simplified statement of the main CLT (Theorem 1)
nodes.statement: Let us have a look at the following simplified statement of our key result, that is Theorem~\ref{th:gen:jacod} in Section~\ref{sec:conv:rate}: let $X$ be an OSBM and $r$ be the threshold, let $(L^r_t(X))_{t\geq 0}$ be its symmetric local time at the threshold. Then for appropriate constants $c,K\in \mathbb{R}$ it holds for all $t\in [0,\infty)$ that \begin{equation} n^{1/4} \left( \frac{ \varepsilon_{n,t}^{(r,f,X)} - c \, L^r_t(X)}{K^2 \sqrt{L^r_t(X)}}\right) \overset{n\to\infty}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0,1). \end{equation}
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
assumptions: $X$ be an OSBM and $r$ be the threshold
nodes.statement_short: For OSBM, $n^{1/4}$-normalized error of the statistic w.r.t. $c L^r_t$, divided by $K^2\sqrt{L^r_t}$, is asymptotically standard normal.

nodes.name: Equation (1.2): Simplified CLT
nodes.statement: n^{1/4} \left( \frac{ \varepsilon_{n,t}^{(r,f,X)} - c \, L^r_t(X)}{K^2 \sqrt{L^r_t(X)}}\right) \overset{n\to\infty}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0,1).
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.label: intro:th

nodes.name: Heuristics on the rate
nodes.statement: The convergence is different from what one might expect (i.e.~$n^{1/2}$), because the local time at $r$, and so its estimators, depends on the behavior of the process around $r$. Indeed, as $n\to\infty$, among $n$ observations of the process on a fixed interval, the number of those which are sufficiently close to $r$ to matter is of order $n^{1/2}$. Think of the random walk approximation of BM.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: Rate is $n^{1/4}$ not $n^{1/2}$ since only about $n^{1/2}$ of $n$ observations lie close to $r$.

nodes.name: Integral notation $\langle \mu , g \rangle$
nodes.statement: Throughout this document for every measurable functions $g\colon \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ and measure $\mu$ on the Borel space $(\mathbb{R}, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}))$ we denote by $\langle \mu , g \rangle$ the integral of $g$ with respect to the measure $\mu$: \begin{equation}\langle \mu , g \rangle := \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} g(x) \mu(\!\,\mathrm{d} x).\end{equation}
nodes.section: 1.3.1 Notation

nodes.name: Equation (1.3)
nodes.statement: \langle \mu , g \rangle := \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} g(x) \mu(\!\,\mathrm{d} x).
nodes.section: 1.3.1 Notation

nodes.name: Weighted measure $\lambda^{(\gamma)}$ and space $\mathcal{L}^1(\lambda^{(\gamma)})$
nodes.statement: For every $\gamma \in [0,\infty)$ let $\lambda^{(\gamma)}$ be the measure on $(\mathbb{R}, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}))$ absolutely continuous with respect to the Lebesgue measure satisfying ${\lambda^{(\gamma)}(\,\mathrm{d} x)} = |x|^\gamma \,\mathrm{d} x$ and let \begin{equation}( \Loneg{\gamma}, \|\cdot \|_{1,\gamma} )\end{equation} be the set of Borel measurable $\lambda^{(\gamma)}$-integrable functions and its norm.
nodes.section: 1.3.1 Notation
nodes.statement_short: $\lambda^{(\gamma)}(dx)=|x|^\gamma dx$ and the normed space of $\lambda^{(\gamma)}$-integrable functions.

nodes.name: Equation (1.4)
nodes.statement: ( \Loneg{\gamma}, \|\cdot \|_{1,\gamma} )
nodes.section: 1.3.1 Notation

nodes.name: Lebesgue space $\mathcal{L}^1$
nodes.statement: If $\gamma=0$, we simply denote by $( \mathcal{L}^1, \|\cdot \|_1):=( \Loneg{0}, \|\cdot \|_{1,0})$ the normed space of Lebesgue integrable functions.
nodes.section: 1.3.1 Notation

nodes.name: Spaces $\mathcal{L}^1_b(\lambda^{(\gamma)})$ and $\mathcal{I}_\gamma$
nodes.statement: Let $\gamma \in [0,\infty)$. We denote by $\Lgb{\gamma}$ the following subspace of $\mathcal{L}^1$: \begin{equation} \Lgb{\gamma} = \{ f \colon \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} , \text{ measurable and bounded} \text{ s.t. } f\in \Loneg{\gamma}\}. \end{equation} We denote by $\Lg{\gamma}$ the following space of bi-variate measurable functions \begin{equation} \Lg{\gamma} = \{ h \colon \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R} , \exists \, \bar h \in \Lgb{\gamma}, \exists \, a\in [0,\infty) \text{ s.t. } \forall x,y\in \mathbb{R} : |h(x,y)|\leq \bar h (x) e^{a |y-x|} \}. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 1.3.1 Notation
nodes.statement_short: Bounded $\lambda^{(\gamma)}$-integrable functions, and bivariate functions dominated by $\bar h(x)e^{a|y-x|}$ with $\bar h$ in that space.
nodes.label: def:integral:gamma

nodes.name: Equation (1.5)
nodes.statement: \Lgb{\gamma} = \{ f \colon \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} , \text{ measurable and bounded} \text{ s.t. } f\in \Loneg{\gamma}\}.
nodes.section: 1.3.1 Notation

nodes.name: Equation (1.6)
nodes.statement: \Lg{\gamma} = \{ h \colon \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R} , \exists \, \bar h \in \Lgb{\gamma}, \exists \, a\in [0,\infty) \text{ s.t. } \forall x,y\in \mathbb{R} : |h(x,y)|\leq \bar h (x) e^{a |y-x|} \}.
nodes.section: 1.3.1 Notation

nodes.name: Monotonicity of the spaces in $\gamma$
nodes.statement: If $0 \leq \gamma_1 \leq \gamma_2 < +\infty$, then $\Lgb{\gamma_2} \subseteq \Lgb{\gamma_1}$ and $\Lg{\gamma_2} \subseteq \Lg{\gamma_1}$.
nodes.section: 1.3.1 Notation
nodes.label: rem:spaces:relation

nodes.name: Symmetric local time
nodes.statement: The {\em symmetric local time at the point $x$\/} accumulated on the time interval $[0,t]$ by the semi-martingale $X$ satisfies a.s. \begin{equation} L_t^x(X)=\lim_{\epsilon\to 0}\frac{1}{2\epsilon}\int_0^t \ind{\{-\epsilon\leq X_s-x\leq \epsilon\}}d\langle X\rangle_s \end{equation} and if $x=0$ we denote $L_t^0(X)$ by $L_t(X)$.

nodes.name: Stable convergence in law
nodes.statement: Let $(D,d)$ be a metric space, $(\Omega^\prime ,\mathcal{F}^\prime,\mathbb{P}^\prime)$ be an extension of the probability space $(\Omega ,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P})$, let $X_n \colon \Omega \to D$, $n\in \mathbb{N}$, be a sequence of random variables, and let $X \colon \Omega^\prime \to D$ be a random variable. Then we say that $X_n$ converges stably in law to $X$ if for all $f\colon D \to \mathbb{R}$ continuous and bounded and all bounded random variable $Y\colon \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ it holds that \begin{equation}\lim_{n\to\infty} \mathbb{E}\!\left[ f(X_n) Y\right] = \mathbb{E}^\prime\!\left[ f(X) Y\right].\end{equation}
nodes.section: 1.3.3 Notions of convergence
nodes.statement_short: $X_n\to X$ stably if $E[f(X_n)Y]\to E'[f(X)Y]$ for all bounded continuous $f$ and bounded $Y$.

nodes.name: Equation (1.8)
nodes.statement: \lim_{n\to\infty} \mathbb{E}\!\left[ f(X_n) Y\right] = \mathbb{E}^\prime\!\left[ f(X) Y\right].

nodes.statement: Let $t \in [0,\infty)$, let $\mathbb{D}_t$, resp. $\mathbb{D}_\infty$, be the Skorokhod space of c\`adl\`ag functions from $[0,t]$, resp. $[0,\infty)$, to $\mathbb{R}$ endowed with the Skorokhod topology.

nodes.name: Notation for functional stable convergence
nodes.statement: When $D=\mathbb{D}_t$, $t\in [0,\infty]$ the functional stable convergence in law is usually denoted by \begin{equation}X_n \convsl[n\to \infty] X.\end{equation}
nodes.section: 1.3.3 Notions of convergence

nodes.statement: X_n \convsl[n\to \infty] X.

nodes.name: Uniform convergence on compacts in probability (u.c.p.)
nodes.statement: Finally we recall the notion used in the convergence results, i.e.~the {\em convergence in probability locally uniformly in time\/} or convergence {\em uniform on compacts in probability\/} (u.c.p.): let $X,X_n$, $n\in \mathbb{N}$, be random variables with values in $\mathbb{D}_\infty$, then \begin{equation}X_n \convucp X,\end{equation} if for all $t\in [0,\infty)$ it holds that $ \sup_{s\in [0,t]} \left| X_n(s) - X(s) \right| \convp[n\to\infty] 0. $

nodes.name: Stochastic basis and driving Brownian motion
nodes.statement: In the entire document let $(\Omega,\mathcal{F}, (\mathcal{F}_t)_{t\in [0,\infty)},\mathbb{P})$ be a stochastic basis (for convenience, one may assume the usual conditions: completeness and right-continuity) and $W$ be an $(\mathcal{F}_t)_{t\in [0,\infty)}$-adapted standard BM.

nodes.name: Skew Brownian motion (SBM)
nodes.statement: The SBM with skewness parameter $\beta\in [-1,1]$ at the threshold $r\in \mathbb{R}$ is the diffusion which is strong solution to the following SDE \begin{equation} X_t=X_0 + W_t+ \beta L_t^{r}(X) \end{equation} where $L_t^{r}(X)$ is the symmetric local time of the process at $r$, $X_0\in \mathbb{R}$, and $\beta X_0 \geq 0$ if $|\beta|=1$.
nodes.section: 2.1.1 Skew Brownian motion
nodes.genus: diffusion which is strong solution to the following SDE

nodes.name: Equation (2.1): SBM SDE
nodes.statement: X_t=X_0 + W_t+ \beta L_t^{r}(X)
nodes.section: 2.1.1 Skew Brownian motion
nodes.label: eq:SBM

nodes.name: Standard SBM
nodes.statement: We call {\em standard SBM\/} a SBM with threshold $r=0$ starting at $X_0=0$.
nodes.section: 2.1.1 Skew Brownian motion

nodes.name: $\beta$-SBM
nodes.statement: In this paper a SBM with skewness parameter $\beta\in (-1,1)$ is also denoted by $\beta$-SBM.

nodes.name: Speed measure $\mu_\beta$ and transition density $p_\beta$ of SBM
nodes.statement: Let us denote by $\mu_\beta$ the speed measure associated to the $\beta$-SBM with threshold $r=0$, that is \begin{equation} \mu_\beta(\!\,\mathrm{d} x) := \left( (1+\beta) \ind{(0,\infty)}(x) + (1-\beta) \ind{(-\infty,0)}(x) \right)\! \,\mathrm{d} x =( 1+\mathrm{sgn}(x) \beta ) \,\mathrm{d} x, \end{equation} and $p_\beta(t,x,y)$ denotes its transition density (first computed in \cite{walsh}): \begin{equation} p_\beta(t,x,y) =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi t}}\exp\!\left(-\frac{(x-y)^2}{2t}\right) +\beta \mathrm{sgn}(y)\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi t}}\exp\!\left(-\frac{(|{x}|+|{y}|)^2}{2t}\right). \end{equation}

nodes.name: Oscillating-skew Brownian motion (OSBM)
nodes.statement: We now consider a generalisation of SBM, the oscillating-skew BM (OSBM) with threshold $r\in \mathbb{R}$ which is solution to \begin{equation} X_t = X_0 + \int_0^t \sigma(X_s) \,\mathrm{d} W_s + \beta L^r_t(X) \quad t\geq 0 \quad \mathbb{P}\text{-a.s.} \end{equation} with $\beta \in [-1,1]$, the deterministic initial condition $X_0\beta\geq 0$ if $|\beta|=1$ and $X_0\in \mathbb{R}$ otherwise, and $\sigma$ is the positive two-valued function discontinuous at the threshold \begin{equation} \sigma := \sigma_- \ind{(-\infty,r)} + \sigma_+ \ind{[r,+\infty)} \end{equation} with $\sigma_-,\sigma_+\in (0,+\infty)$.
nodes.section: 2.1.2 Oscillating-skew Brownian motion
nodes.statement_short: OSBM: solution of $dX=\sigma(X)dW+\beta dL^r(X)$ with $\sigma$ piecewise constant, jumping at the threshold $r$.

nodes.name: Equation (2.4): OSBM SDE
nodes.statement: X_t = X_0 + \int_0^t \sigma(X_s) \,\mathrm{d} W_s + \beta L^r_t(X) \quad t\geq 0 \quad \mathbb{P}\text{-a.s.}
nodes.section: 2.1.2 Oscillating-skew Brownian motion
nodes.label: eq:OSBM

nodes.name: Equation (2.5): Two-valued diffusion coefficient
nodes.statement: \sigma := \sigma_- \ind{(-\infty,r)} + \sigma_+ \ind{[r,+\infty)}

nodes.name: $(\beta,\sigma_\pm)$-OSBM notation
nodes.statement: In this document we also denote this process by $(\beta,\sigma_\pm)$-OSBM.

nodes.name: Speed measure $\mu_X$ and transition density $p_X$ of OSBM
nodes.statement: The speed measure of the OSBM with threshold $r=0$ (standard OSBM) is \begin{equation} \mu_X(\!\,\mathrm{d} x) = \frac{1+\mathrm{sgn}(x)\beta}{(\sigma(x))^2} \,\mathrm{d} x = \left( \frac{1-\beta}{\sigma_-^2} \ind{(-\infty,0)}(x) + \frac{1+\beta}{\sigma_+^2} \ind{[0,\infty)}(x) \right)\! \,\mathrm{d} x \end{equation} and (by It\^o-Tanaka formula in Lemma~\ref{lem:Ito-Tanaka}), the transition density function satisfies \begin{equation} p_X(t,x,y)=\frac{1}{\sigma(y)} \, p_{\beta_\sigma}\Big(t, \frac{x}{\sigma(x)}, \frac{y}{\sigma(y)}\Big) \quad \text{ with } \quad {\beta_\sigma}:= \frac{(1+\beta)\sigma_- -(1-\beta)\sigma_+}{(1+\beta)\sigma_-+(1-\beta)\sigma_+} \end{equation} where $p_{\beta_\sigma}$ is the density of the SBM recalled in~\eqref{eq:SBM:density}.
nodes.section: 2.1.2 Oscillating-skew Brownian motion
nodes.statement_short: Speed measure of standard OSBM and its transition density expressed via the SBM density with skewness $\beta_\sigma$.

nodes.name: Oscillating Brownian motion (OBM)

Then \begin{equation} \varepsilon_{n,\cdot}^{(r,f,X)} \convucp[n\to\infty] \langle \mu_X , \bfF f \rangle L^r_{\cdot}(X). \end{equation}

nodes.name: Uniformity in the parameters of the convergence to the local time
nodes.statement: Actually, the convergence in Proposition~\ref{prop:lmt:2:OSBM} is uniform in the parameters $\theta:= (\beta, \sigma_-,\sigma_+) \in [-1,1] \times (0,\infty) \times (0,\infty) :=\Theta$. More precisely, let $X^{(\theta)}$ denote the solution associated to the parameter $\theta \in \Theta$, then for all $t\in (0,\infty)$ it holds for all $\varepsilon \in (0,\infty)$ that \begin{equation} \lim_{n\to\infty} \sup_{\theta \in \Theta} \mathbb{P}\left( \sup_{s\in [0,t]} \left| \varepsilon_{n,s}^{(r,f,X^{(\theta)})} - \langle \mu_X , \bfF{f} \rangle L^r_{s}(X^{(\theta)})\right| \geq \varepsilon \right) = 0. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Rate of convergence to the local time (CLT for OSBM)
nodes.statement: Let $f\in \Lg{\gamma}$, $\gamma > 3$, let $X$ be the $(\beta,\sigma_\pm)$-OSBM solution to~\eqref{eq:OSBM}. Then there exists (possibly on an extension of the probability space) a BM $B$ independent of $X$ such that \begin{equation} \begin{split} & n^{1/4} \left( \varepsilon_{n,\cdot}^{(r,f,X)} - \langle \mu_X , \bfF{f} \rangle L^r_\cdot(X)\right) \convsl[n\to\infty] \sqrt{K_f^X} B_{L^r_\cdot(X)}, \end{split} \end{equation} where $K_f^X$ is the non-negative finite constant given by \begin{equation} \begin{split} K_f^X & = \langle \mu_X , \bfF{f^2} + 2 \bfF{f,\mathcal{P}_{f}^X} \rangle + \frac{ 2 \sigma_- \sigma_+}{(1+\beta)\sigma_-+(1-\beta)\sigma_+} \frac{8}{3 \sqrt{2\pi}} (\langle \mu_X , \bfF{f} \rangle)^2 \\ & \quad - 2 \sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}} \frac{ 2 \sigma_- \sigma_+}{(1+\beta)\sigma_-+(1-\beta)\sigma_+} \langle \mu_X , \bfF{f} \rangle \\ & \qquad \cdot \int_{-\infty}^\infty \left( e^{-\frac{y^2}{2(\sigma(y))^2}} -\sqrt{2\pi} \frac{|y|}{\sigma(y)} \Phi\left(-\frac{|y|}{\sigma(y)}\right)\right) \mathcal{P}_{f}^X(y) \mu_X(\!\,\mathrm{d} y) \\ & \quad - 2 \langle \mu_X , \bfF{f} \rangle \left(\frac{ 2 \sigma_- \sigma_+}{(1+\beta)\sigma_-+(1-\beta)\sigma_+}\right)^{\!2} \\ & \qquad \cdot \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \int_0^1 \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \tfrac{|x| e^{-\frac{x^2}{2(\sigma(x))^2}} \Phi\left(-\frac{|y|}{\sigma(y)}\right)}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma(x)} \sqrt{\frac{1}t-1} f(x \sqrt{t}, y \sqrt{1-t}) \mu_X(\!\,\mathrm{d} y) \,\mathrm{d} t \mu_X(\!\,\mathrm{d} x), \end{split}\end{equation} $\Phi$ is the cumulative distribution function of a standard Gaussian random variable, \begin{equation} \mathcal{P}_{f}^X(x) = \sum_{j=0}^{\infty } \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} p_X(j,x, y)\left(\bfF{f}(y)- \langle \mu_X , \bfF{f} \rangle \bfF{g_\beta}(y)\right) \,\mathrm{d} y, \end{equation} and $ g_\beta(x,y) = \frac{1}{1+\mathrm{sgn}(y)\beta}\left(|y| - \frac{1+\mathrm{sgn}(y)\beta}{1+\mathrm{sgn}(x)\beta}|x|\right) $.

nodes.name: Reflected BM
nodes.statement: The assumptions of Proposition~\ref{prop:lmt:2:OSBM} and Theorem~\ref{th:gen:jacod} include reflected BM, i.e.~$|\beta|=1$.
nodes.section: 2.3 Rate of convergence to the local time

nodes.name: About results for drifted OSBM
nodes.statement: Let us consider a drifted OBM solution of an SDE with drift coefficient given, for instance, by a bounded function $b$ of the process itself. Then, Proposition~\ref{prop:lmt:2:OSBM} and Theorem~\ref{th:gen:jacod} hold - with the same quantities and constants - for the drifted OBM. This follows by the same arguments in~\cite[Section~2.4]{j1}; to summarize, it suffices to prove the result on bounded time intervals $[0,t]$ (see the beginning of the proof if Theorem~\ref{th:gen:jacod}) and apply Girsanov's transform to pass from the driftless case to the drifted one. Since the drift is bounded, the Radon-Nikodym derivative is integrable. Then, by a dominated convergence argument, stable convergence holds for the drifted process. The result for drifted OBM implies the one for drifted OSBM by a simple space transform as a consequence of Section~\ref{sec:interplay}.
nodes.section: 2.3 Rate of convergence to the local time
nodes.statement_short: Proposition 1 and Theorem 1 extend to bounded drift via Girsanov and dominated convergence, and to drifted OSBM by a space transform.
nodes.label: rem:drift

nodes.name: Recovering the Brownian case
nodes.statement: If $\beta=0$ and $\sigma\equiv 1$ we recover the known result for BM: e.g.~\cite{borodin86,borodin89} and a special case of the already cited \cite[Theorem~1.2]{j1}. The expression for the constant $K_f^X$ we propose is slightly more explicit.
nodes.section: 2.3 Rate of convergence to the local time
nodes.label: rem:th:BM

nodes.name: Theorem 1 implies a weaker version of Proposition 1
nodes.statement: Theorem~\ref{th:gen:jacod} implies a weaker version of Proposition~\ref{prop:lmt:2:OSBM}. Proposition~\ref{prop:lmt:2:OSBM} requires Hypothesis~\ref{hp:OSBM:1} which is satisfied if for instance $f \in \Lg{2}$ (see Lemma~\ref{lem:link:theorems}). Theorem~\ref{th:gen:jacod} instead assumes $f\in \Lg{\gamma}$, $\gamma > 3$, which is a stronger condition. Let us comment briefly on how to derive the u.c.p.~convergence from Theorem~\ref{th:gen:jacod}, although in Appendix~\ref{app:prop:lmt:2} we provide a direct proof of the weaker version of Proposition~\ref{prop:lmt:2:OSBM}. The notions of convergence in law/stably in law/in probability coincide when the limit is constant and so $ \varepsilon_{n,\cdot}^{(r,f,X)} - \langle \mu_X , \bfF{f} \rangle L^r_\cdot(X) \convp[n\to\infty] 0 $ in the Skorokhod topology. Since $L^r_\cdot(X)$ is (a.s.) continuous and increasing it can be proven (splitting into positive and negative part of $f$, and so of $\bfF{f}$) that $ \varepsilon_{n,\cdot}^{(r,f,X)} \convucp[n\to\infty] \langle \mu_X , \bfF{f} \rangle L^r_\cdot(X) $ (see e.g.~(2.2.16) in \cite{jp}).
nodes.section: 2.3 Rate of convergence to the local time
nodes.statement_short: Theorem 1 gives u.c.p. convergence under stronger assumptions via constant-limit stable convergence and monotonicity.
nodes.label: comment:convergence

nodes.name: Discrete observation grid
nodes.statement: Let $T\in (0,\infty)$, $N\in \mathbb{N}$, we observe the process on the discrete time grid $i \frac{T}{N}$.
nodes.section: 3 Applications

nodes.name: Observations $X_i$
nodes.statement: We denote by $X_i = X_{ i \frac{T}{N}}$.
nodes.section: 3 Applications

nodes.name: Functions $h_\alpha$
nodes.statement: Let $\alpha\in [0,\infty)$ and note that the function $h_\alpha$ given by $h_\alpha (x,y) = |y|^\alpha \ind{(-\infty,0)}(x y)$ is in $\Lg{\gamma}$ for all $\gamma\in [0,\infty)$.
nodes.section: 3.1 Estimating the local time via the number of crossings of the threshold

nodes.name: Number-of-crossings estimators $\mathcal{L}^r_{T,N}$ and $L^r_{T,N}$
nodes.statement: We consider two estimators obtained considering the functions proportional to $h_0$ and $h_1$: \begin{align} & \mathcal{L}^r_{T,N}(X) = \varepsilon_{\frac{N}{T},T}^{(r,h_0,X)} = \sqrt{ \frac{T}{N}}\sum_{i=0}^{N-1} \ind{\{(X_i-r)(X_{i+1}-r)<0\}} \text{ and } \\ & L^r_{T,N}(X) = \varepsilon_{\frac{N}{T},T}^{(r, 2 h_1,X)} = 2 \sum_{i=0}^{N -1} \ind{\{(X_i-r)(X_{i+1}-r)<0\}}|X_{i+1}-r|. \end{align}
nodes.section: 3.1 Estimating the local time via the number of crossings of the threshold
nodes.statement_short: Normalized number of threshold crossings, and the crossing count weighted by the distance to the threshold.

nodes.name: Equation (3.1): Crossing estimators
nodes.statement: & \mathcal{L}^r_{T,N}(X) = \varepsilon_{\frac{N}{T},T}^{(r,h_0,X)} = \sqrt{ \frac{T}{N}}\sum_{i=0}^{N-1} \ind{\{(X_i-r)(X_{i+1}-r)<0\}} \text{ and } \\ & L^r_{T,N}(X) = \varepsilon_{\frac{N}{T},T}^{(r, 2 h_1,X)} = 2 \sum_{i=0}^{N -1} \ind{\{(X_i-r)(X_{i+1}-r)<0\}}|X_{i+1}-r|.
nodes.section: 3.1 Estimating the local time via the number of crossings of the threshold
nodes.label: def:LT:discr:1

nodes.name: Threshold diffusion with drift and local-time term
nodes.statement: In this section, we consider the semi-martingale satisfying \begin{equation} X_t = X_0 + \int_0^t b_s \,\mathrm{d} s + \int_0^t \sigma(X_s) \,\mathrm{d} W_s + \beta L^r_t(X) \quad t\geq 0 \quad \mathbb{P}\text{-a.s.} \end{equation} where $L^r_t(X)$ is the symmetric local time of the process at the fixed level $r\in \mathbb{R}$, $X_0\in \mathbb{R}$, and $\beta$, $b$, and $\sigma$ satisfy Hypothesis~\ref{hyp:SDE:sigma}.
nodes.section: 3.1.1 Estimator counting the number of crossings of the threshold
nodes.statement_short: Skew threshold diffusion with drift $b$, discontinuous diffusion coefficient $\sigma$ and local-time term $\beta L^r$.

nodes.name: Equation (3.3): Threshold SDE with drift
nodes.statement: X_t = X_0 + \int_0^t b_s \,\mathrm{d} s + \int_0^t \sigma(X_s) \,\mathrm{d} W_s + \beta L^r_t(X) \quad t\geq 0 \quad \mathbb{P}\text{-a.s.}
nodes.section: 3.1.1 Estimator counting the number of crossings of the threshold
nodes.label: eq:SDE:sigma

nodes.name: Hypothesis 2 (coefficients of the threshold diffusion)
nodes.statement: Let $\beta \in [-1,1]$, $X_0 \beta \geq 0$ if $|\beta|=1$, and the diffusion coefficient and drift coefficient satisfy: $b_s=b(X_s)$, with $b$ bounded measurable function, $\sigma \in C^1(\mathbb{R}\setminus\{r\})$ admits a finite jump at a fixed {\it threshold} $r\in \mathbb{R}$, its derivative admits a finite jump at $r$ as well, $\sigma$ is bounded from below by a strictly positive constant and there exists a strictly increasing function $\Sigma$ such that $(\sigma(x)-\sigma(y))^2 \leq |\Sigma(x)-\Sigma(y)|$.
nodes.section: 3.1.1 Estimator counting the number of crossings of the threshold
nodes.statement_short: Bounded drift; $\sigma$ piecewise $C^1$ with finite jumps at $r$, bounded below, and controlled by an increasing $\Sigma$.
nodes.label: hyp:SDE:sigma

nodes.name: Hypothesis 2 is stronger than necessary
nodes.statement: Hypothesis~\ref{hyp:SDE:sigma} is stronger than necessary. For instance, there is no need of a time-homogeneous drift, and the boundedness assumption can be relaxed as well.
nodes.section: 3.1.1 Estimator counting the number of crossings of the threshold

nodes.name: Existence and uniqueness of strong solutions for threshold SDEs (Bass-Chen)
nodes.statement: Under the above assumptions there exists a unique strong solution to the SDE~\eqref{eq:SDE:sigma} (see e.g.~\cite{BassChen05}).
nodes.section: 3.1.1 Estimator counting the number of crossings of the threshold
conclusions: there exists a unique strong solution to the SDE~\eqref{eq:SDE:sigma}

nodes.name: Rate of convergence of the number of crossings
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be solution to~\eqref{eq:SDE:sigma} and let $\sigma_\pm := \lim_{x\to r^\pm} \sigma(x)$. Let \begin{equation} c_{\sigma_\pm,\beta} := \frac{2 (1-\beta^2)}{(1+\beta) \sigma_-+ (1-\beta) \sigma_+} \sqrt{\frac2\pi} \end{equation} and $K_{\sigma_\pm,\beta}:=K^Y_{h_0}$ is the non-negative finite constant given by~\eqref{eq:k:th} with $Y$ $(\beta,\sigma_\pm)$-OSBM. Then, $\mathcal{L}^r_{T,N}(X)$ in \eqref{def:LT:discr:1}, counting the number of times the process $X$ crosses its threshold $r$, satisfies \begin{equation} \mathcal{L}^r_{T,N}(X) \convp[N\to\infty] c_{\sigma_\pm,\beta} L_T^r(X) \end{equation} and, as $N$ goes to infinity, \begin{equation} (N/T)^{1/4} \left( \mathcal{L}^r_{T,N}(X) - c_{\sigma_\pm,\beta} L^r_T(X)\right) \ \text{ converges stably in law to } \ \sqrt{K_{\sigma_\pm,\beta}} \, \sqrt{L^r_{T}(X)} G \end{equation} where $G\sim \mathcal N(0,1)$ is independent from $L^r_T(X)$ (more generally from $\mathcal F_T^X$: the natural filtration).
nodes.section: 3.1.1 Estimator counting the number of crossings of the threshold
conclusions: (N/T)^{1/4} \left( \mathcal{L}^r_{T,N}(X) - c_{\sigma_\pm,\beta} L^r_T(X)\right) \ \text{ converges stably in law to } \ \sqrt{K_{\sigma_\pm,\beta}} \, \sqrt{L^r_{T}(X)} G
nodes.statement_short: For general threshold diffusions the normalized crossing count converges to $c L^r_T$ with rate $(N/T)^{1/4}$ and a mixed normal limit.
nodes.label: th:crossings

nodes.name: Equation (3.4)
nodes.statement: c_{\sigma_\pm,\beta} := \frac{2 (1-\beta^2)}{(1+\beta) \sigma_-+ (1-\beta) \sigma_+} \sqrt{\frac2\pi}
nodes.section: 3.1.1 Estimator counting the number of crossings of the threshold

nodes.name: Equation (3.5)
nodes.statement: \mathcal{L}^r_{T,N}(X) \convp[N\to\infty] c_{\sigma_\pm,\beta} L_T^r(X)
nodes.section: 3.1.1 Estimator counting the number of crossings of the threshold

nodes.name: Equation (3.6): CLT for crossings
nodes.statement: (N/T)^{1/4} \left( \mathcal{L}^r_{T,N}(X) - c_{\sigma_\pm,\beta} L^r_T(X)\right) \ \text{ converges stably in law to } \ \sqrt{K_{\sigma_\pm,\beta}} \, \sqrt{L^r_{T}(X)} G
nodes.section: 3.1.1 Estimator counting the number of crossings of the threshold
nodes.label: eq:crossings_T

nodes.name: Functional version of Theorem 2
nodes.statement: If we would not have assumed to have observations until the fixed time horizon $T$, the result could be provided as a functional limit theorem as Theorem~\ref{th:gen:jacod}: \[\varepsilon^{(r,h_0,X)} \convucp[n\to\infty] c_{\sigma_\pm,\beta} L^r_{\cdot}(X) \] and then there exists (possibly on an extension of the probability space) a BM $B$ independent of $X$ such that \[ \begin{split} & n^{1/4} \left( \varepsilon_{n,\cdot}^{(r,h_0,X)} - c_{\sigma_\pm,\beta} L^r_\cdot(X)\right) \convsl[n\to\infty] \sqrt{K_{\sigma_\pm,\beta}} B_{L^r_\cdot(X)}. \end{split} \]
nodes.section: 3.1.1 Estimator counting the number of crossings of the threshold

nodes.name: Theorem 2 depends only on the sign of the process
nodes.statement: We provide Theorem~\ref{th:crossings} for a more general class than OSBM, but an extension of the more general result is object of further research. This is related to the fact that the statistics of Theorem~\ref{th:crossings} basically depends only on the sign of the process.
nodes.section: 3.1.1 Estimator counting the number of crossings of the threshold

nodes.name: Consistency of $L^r_{T,N}$ for OBM (Lemma 1 of [lp2])
nodes.statement: For an OBM solution to \eqref{eq:OBM}, say $Y$, a proof that $L^r_{T,N}(Y) \convp[N\to\infty] L_T^r(Y)$ can be found in \cite[Lemma~1]{lp2}.
nodes.section: 3.1.2 Another estimator
assumptions: For an OBM solution to \eqref{eq:OBM}, say $Y$

nodes.name: Derivation of Proposition 2
nodes.statement: Applying Proposition~\ref{prop:lmt:2:OSBM} to $\varepsilon^{(r, 2 h_1,Y)}$ (recall that $\beta=0$) we obtain a more general result. And applying Theorem~\ref{th:gen:jacod} we obtain the convergence rate.
nodes.section: 3.1.2 Another estimator
nodes.statement_short: Apply Proposition 1 and Theorem 1 to the function $2h_1$.

nodes.name: Asymptotics of the estimator $L^r_{T,N}$ for OSBM
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be let $X$ be the $(\beta,\sigma_\pm)$-OSBM solution to~\eqref{eq:OSBM} and let ${L}^r_{T,N}(X)$ be the estimator of the local time $L^r_T(X)$ in \eqref{def:LT:discr}. Then there exists (possibly on an extension of the probability space) a Gaussian random variable $G\sim \mathcal N(0,1)$ independent of $X$ (independent from $\mathcal{F}_T^X$) such that, as $N$ tends to infinity, \begin{equation} (N/T)^{1/4} \left( L^r_{T,N}(X) - \frac{(1-\beta^2) (\sigma_-+\sigma_+)}{(1+\beta)\sigma_- + (1-\beta )\sigma_+} L^r_T(X)\right) \end{equation} converges stably in law to $\sqrt {K_{\beta, \sigma_\pm}} \sqrt{L^r_T(X)} G$ where $K_{\beta, \sigma_\pm}:=K^X_{2 h_1}$ in~\eqref{eq:k:th}. Moreover if $\beta=0$ ($X$ is an OBM) then $\frac{(1-\beta^2) (\sigma_-+\sigma_+)}{(1+\beta)\sigma_- + (1-\beta )\sigma_+}=1$ and $K_{0,\sigma_\pm}= \frac{16}{3 \sqrt{2 \pi}} \frac{\sigma_-^2 +\sigma_+^2}{\sigma_-+\sigma_+}$. And if $\sigma_-=\sigma_+ =1$ ($X$ is a SBM) then $\frac{(1-\beta^2) (\sigma_-+\sigma_+)}{(1+\beta)\sigma_- + (1-\beta )\sigma_+}=1-\beta^2$.
nodes.section: 3.1.2 Another estimator
assumptions: ${L}^r_{T,N}(X)$ be the estimator of the local time $L^r_T(X)$ in \eqref{def:LT:discr}
conclusions: converges stably in law to $\sqrt {K_{\beta, \sigma_\pm}} \sqrt{L^r_T(X)} G$
nodes.statement_short: $(N/T)^{1/4}$ times the error of $L^r_{T,N}$ against a constant multiple of the local time is asymptotically mixed normal; explicit constants for OBM and SBM.
nodes.label: prop:localtime:conv:OSBM

nodes.name: Equation (3.7)
nodes.statement: (N/T)^{1/4} \left( L^r_{T,N}(X) - \frac{(1-\beta^2) (\sigma_-+\sigma_+)}{(1+\beta)\sigma_- + (1-\beta )\sigma_+} L^r_T(X)\right)
nodes.section: 3.1.2 Another estimator

nodes.name: Function $f_1$
nodes.statement: Let us introduce the following function $f_1(x,y):=\ind{[0,1)}(x)$.
nodes.section: 3.2.1 Estimating the skewness parameter for SBM

nodes.name: $f_1$ satisfies Hypothesis 1
nodes.statement: Then both $\bfF{f_1}$ in~\eqref{eq:muX} and $f_1^2$ coincide with $f_1$ and satisfy Hypothesis~\ref{hp:OSBM:1}.
nodes.section: 3.2.1 Estimating the skewness parameter for SBM
conclusions: both $\bfF{f_1}$ in~\eqref{eq:muX} and $f_1^2$ coincide with $f_1$ and satisfy Hypothesis~\ref{hp:OSBM:1}

nodes.name: Function $|f_1|$
nodes.statement: The same holds for the function $|f_1|(x):=f_1(|x|)$.
nodes.section: 3.2.1 Estimating the skewness parameter for SBM

nodes.name: Skewness estimators $\hat\beta_N$
nodes.statement: We consider the following estimators for the parameter $\beta$: \begin{equation} \hat{\beta}_N := \frac{ \sum_{k=0}^{N -1} \mathrm{sgn}(X_{k}-r) \ind{(-1,1)} (\sqrt{N/T}(X_{k}-r)) }{ \sum_{k=0}^{N -1} \ind{(-1,1)} (\sqrt{N/T}(X_{k}-r)) } \end{equation} or \begin{equation} \hat{\beta}_N := 1- \frac{L^r_{T,N}(X)}{ \sqrt{\frac{T}{N}} \sum_{k=0}^{N -1} \ind{[0,1)} (\sqrt{N/T}(X_{k}-r)) }. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 3.2.1 Estimating the skewness parameter for SBM
nodes.statement_short: Two estimators of $\beta$: signed average of near-threshold observations, or one minus a crossing/occupation ratio.

nodes.name: Equation (3.8): Skewness estimator 1
nodes.statement: \hat{\beta}_N := \frac{ \sum_{k=0}^{N -1} \mathrm{sgn}(X_{k}-r) \ind{(-1,1)} (\sqrt{N/T}(X_{k}-r)) }{ \sum_{k=0}^{N -1} \ind{(-1,1)} (\sqrt{N/T}(X_{k}-r)) }
nodes.section: 3.2.1 Estimating the skewness parameter for SBM
nodes.label: eq:beta:estim:1

nodes.name: Equation (3.9): Skewness estimator 2
nodes.statement: \hat{\beta}_N := 1- \frac{L^r_{T,N}(X)}{ \sqrt{\frac{T}{N}} \sum_{k=0}^{N -1} \ind{[0,1)} (\sqrt{N/T}(X_{k}-r)) }.
nodes.section: 3.2.1 Estimating the skewness parameter for SBM
nodes.label: eq:beta:estim:2

nodes.name: Derivation of Theorem 3
nodes.statement: The following result is a direct application of Theorem~\ref{th:gen:jacod} and of the fact that joint stable convergence for two sequences holds if one of the sequence converges stably and the other converges in probability.
nodes.section: 3.2.1 Estimating the skewness parameter for SBM
nodes.statement_short: Apply Theorem 1 jointly with convergence in probability of the denominator.

nodes.name: Asymptotic mixed normality of skewness estimators for SBM
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be the $\beta$-SBM solution to~\eqref{eq:SBM} starting at $X_0=r$. Then $\hat{\beta}_N$ in \eqref{eq:beta:estim:1} (resp.~\eqref{eq:beta:estim:2}) is a consistent estimator of $\beta$ and as $N\to\infty$ \begin{equation} N^{1/4} \left( \hat{\beta}_N -\beta \right) \ \text{ converges stably in law to } \ K \, T^{1/4} \, \frac{G}{\sqrt{L^r_T(X)}} \end{equation} with $G\sim \mathcal N(0,1)$ is a standard Gaussian random variable independent of $X$ (of $\mathcal F_T^X$) and $K={\sqrt{K_{(1-\beta) f_1 -2 h_1}}}/{(1+\beta)}$ where $K_{(1-\beta)f_1-2 h_1}$ is provided by~\eqref{eq:k:th} (resp.~$K=\frac12 \sqrt{K_{(\mathrm{sgn}(\cdot) -\beta)|f_1|}}$).
nodes.section: 3.2.1 Estimating the skewness parameter for SBM
assumptions: $X$ be the $\beta$-SBM solution to~\eqref{eq:SBM} starting at $X_0=r$
conclusions: $\hat{\beta}_N$ in \eqref{eq:beta:estim:1} (resp.~\eqref{eq:beta:estim:2}) is a consistent estimator of $\beta$
N^{1/4} \left( \hat{\beta}_N -\beta \right) \ \text{ converges stably in law to } \ K \, T^{1/4} \, \frac{G}{\sqrt{L^r_T(X)}}
nodes.statement_short: Both skewness estimators are consistent and $N^{1/4}(\hat\beta_N-\beta)$ is asymptotically mixed normal.
nodes.label: th:skew:estim

nodes.name: Equation (3.10)
nodes.statement: N^{1/4} \left( \hat{\beta}_N -\beta \right) \ \text{ converges stably in law to } \ K \, T^{1/4} \, \frac{G}{\sqrt{L^r_T(X)}}
nodes.section: 3.2.1 Estimating the skewness parameter for SBM

nodes.name: Why the SBM starts at the threshold
nodes.statement: The assumption that the $\beta$-SBM starts from $r$ is to ensure on one side that the estimator~\eqref{eq:beta:estim:1} (resp.~\eqref{eq:beta:estim:2}) is well defined and on the other side that the local time of the process at $r$ does not vanish at time $T$.
nodes.section: 3.2.1 Estimating the skewness parameter for SBM

nodes.name: Diffusion parameter estimation for OBM
nodes.statement: Similarly, we could provide an estimator for the parameters of OBM. Let $Y$ be the solution to~\eqref{eq:OBM} starting at $X_0=r$, $f_+ \colon x \to \ind{[0,1)}(x)$ and $f_- \colon x \to \ind{(-1,0]}(x)$, and let $\pm\in \{-,+\}$. Then \begin{equation} \hat{\sigma}_\pm^2 := \frac{L^r_{T,N}(Y)}{ \sqrt{\frac{T}{N}} \sum_{k=0}^{N -1} f_\pm (\sqrt{N/T}(X_{k}-r)) } \end{equation} is a consistent estimator of $\sigma_\pm^2$ and $(N/T)^{1/4} \left( \hat{\sigma}_\pm^2 - \sigma_\pm^2 \right)$ converges stably in law to a (mixed) normal law. Since the estimator proposed relies mostly on the behavior of the process around the threshold, it is slower than the ones based on quadratic variations and occupation times of the positive and negative part of the process proposed in~\cite{lp} for OBM which exploit the entire trajectory. Therefore, we propose in Proposition~\ref{lem:estim:sigma}, in the next section, an estimator based on quadratic variation for the diffusion coefficient of OSBM.
nodes.section: 3.2.1 Estimating the skewness parameter for SBM
nodes.statement_short: Ratio of $L^r_{T,N}$ to near-threshold occupation estimates $\sigma_\pm^2$ at rate $N^{1/4}$; slower than quadratic-variation estimators.

nodes.name: Equation (3.11)
nodes.statement: \hat{\sigma}_\pm^2 := \frac{L^r_{T,N}(Y)}{ \sqrt{\frac{T}{N}} \sum_{k=0}^{N -1} f_\pm (\sqrt{N/T}(X_{k}-r)) }
nodes.section: 3.2.1 Estimating the skewness parameter for SBM

nodes.name: Quadratic-variation estimators of the diffusion coefficients of OSBM
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be the standard $(\beta,\sigma_\pm)$-OSBM solution to~\eqref{eq:OSBM}, and for any process $Z$ observed at times $j T/N$ let $[Z,X]_N$ denote $\sum_{j=0}^{N-1} (Z_{j+1}-Z_j)(X_{j+1}-X_j)$. Then, the estimator $((\widehat \sigma_+^V)^2, \ (\widehat \sigma_-^V)^2)$ of $(\sigma_+^2, \ \sigma_-^2)$ given by \[ (\widehat \sigma_+^V) ^2 := \frac{ [ \max\{0,X\}, X ]_N}{\frac{T}{N} \sum_{j=0}^{N-1} \ind{\{X_{j} \geq 0\}} } , \quad (\widehat \sigma_-^V) ^2 := \frac{ [ \max\{0, -X\}, X ]_N}{\frac{T}{N} \sum_{j=0}^{N-1} \ind{\{- X_{j} \geq 0\}} } \] satisfies the following convergence property: $\sqrt N \left( (\widehat \sigma_+^V)^2 - \sigma_+ ^2, \quad (\widehat \sigma_-^V)^2 - \sigma_- ^2\right)$ converges in law to $ \sqrt{2 T} \left( \frac{\sigma_+^2}{(1+\beta)^2} \frac{\int_0^T \ind{\{ X_s \geq 0 \}} \,\mathrm{d} B_s}{\int_0^T \ind{\{ X_s \geq 0 \}} \,\mathrm{d} s}, \quad \frac{\sigma_-^2}{(1-\beta)^2} \frac{\int_0^T \ind{\{ X_s < 0 \}} \,\mathrm{d} B_s}{\int_0^T \ind{\{ X_s < 0 \}} \,\mathrm{d} s} \right) $ where $B$ is a BM independent of $X$ (possibly, on an extension of the filtered probability space).
nodes.section: 3.2.2 Joint parameter estimation for oscillating-skew Brownian motion
nodes.statement_short: Quadratic-variation estimators of $\sigma_\pm^2$ are $\sqrt N$-consistent with a mixed normal limit.
nodes.label: lem:estim:sigma

nodes.name: Derivation of Proposition 3
nodes.statement: When $T=1$ and the process is OBM, Proposition~\ref{lem:estim:sigma} is~\cite[Theorem~3.5]{lp}. By the scaling property~\eqref{Yscaling} one can take $T\neq 1$, and the result for OSBM follows by a spatial transformation given in the proofs section, more precisely Section~\ref{sec:interplay}.
nodes.section: 3.2.2 Joint parameter estimation for oscillating-skew Brownian motion
nodes.statement_short: OBM with $T=1$ is Theorem 3.5 of [lp]; extend by scaling and the OSBM/OBM space transform.

nodes.name: Joint estimator $\widehat\theta_N$ of OSBM parameters
nodes.statement: An example is the estimator \begin{equation} \widehat \theta_N:=( \widehat \beta, (\widehat \sigma_-^V)^2,(\widehat \sigma_+^V)^2) \quad \text{of} \quad \theta:=(\beta, \sigma_-^2,\sigma_+^2) \end{equation} where \begin{equation} \widehat \beta := \frac{ (\widehat \sigma_+^V)^2 \varepsilon_{\frac{N}{T},T}^{(0,f_{1},X)} - (\widehat \sigma_-^V)^2 \varepsilon_{\frac{N}{T},T}^{(0,f_{-1},X)}}{(\widehat \sigma_+^V)^2 \varepsilon_{\frac{N}{T},T}^{(0,f_{1},X)}+ (\widehat \sigma_-^V)^2 \varepsilon_{\frac{N}{T},T}^{(0,f_{-1},X)}} \end{equation} and $f_{1}=\ind{(0,1)}$ and $f_{-1}=\ind{(-1,0)}$.
nodes.section: 3.2.2 Joint parameter estimation for oscillating-skew Brownian motion
nodes.statement_short: Joint estimator of $(\beta,\sigma_-^2,\sigma_+^2)$ combining quadratic-variation estimators and threshold statistics.

nodes.name: Equation (3.12)
nodes.statement: \widehat \theta_N:=( \widehat \beta, (\widehat \sigma_-^V)^2,(\widehat \sigma_+^V)^2) \quad \text{of} \quad \theta:=(\beta, \sigma_-^2,\sigma_+^2)

nodes.name: Equation (3.13)
nodes.statement: \widehat \beta := \frac{ (\widehat \sigma_+^V)^2 \varepsilon_{\frac{N}{T},T}^{(0,f_{1},X)} - (\widehat \sigma_-^V)^2 \varepsilon_{\frac{N}{T},T}^{(0,f_{-1},X)}}{(\widehat \sigma_+^V)^2 \varepsilon_{\frac{N}{T},T}^{(0,f_{1},X)}+ (\widehat \sigma_-^V)^2 \varepsilon_{\frac{N}{T},T}^{(0,f_{-1},X)}}

nodes.name: Interplay between SBM and OBM
nodes.statement: SBM and OBM are strongly related in the following sense: Let $\sigma$ be the function in~\eqref{sigmaOBM}, let $Y$ the solution to \eqref{eq:OBM} and $X$ be a SBM solution to \eqref{eq:SBM} with skewness parameter ${{\beta_\sigma}:=\frac{\sigma_--\sigma_+}{\sigma_-+\sigma_+}}$ and suitable initial condition: Solution to the SDE \begin{equation} X_t =\frac{Y_0}{\sigma(Y_0)}+ W_t+ \beta_\sigma L_t(X) . \end{equation} It holds that $ { X_t =\frac{Y_t}{\sigma(Y_t)} }$, and the local times satisfy \begin{equation} L(X)=\frac{\sigma_++\sigma_-}{2\sigma_+\sigma_-}L(Y). \end{equation} Furthermore, since $ { X_t = \frac{Y_t}{\sigma(Y_t)} }$ and $\sigma$ is positive, then $Y_t X_t \geq 0$. And, since $\sigma$ depends only on the sign of its argument, then $\sigma(Y_t)=\sigma(X_s)$ and so it holds also ${ Y_t=\sigma(X_t) X_t }$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1
nodes.statement: We first recall the well known symmetric It\^o-Tanaka formula. Let $ Z $ be a continuous semi-martingale and let $h$ be the difference of two convex functions. Then, for any $t\ge 0 $, \begin{equation} h(Z_t) = h(Z_0) + \int_{0}^{t} \frac{h'(Z_s+)+h'(Z_s-)}2 \,\mathrm{d} Z_s + \frac{1}{2} \int_{\mathbb R} L^y_t(Z) h''(\!\,\mathrm{d} y) \end{equation} where $h''(\!\,\mathrm{d} y)$ is a measure satisfying \[ \int_{\mathbb{R}} g(y) h''(\!\,\mathrm{d} y) = - \int_{\mathbb{R}} g'(y) \frac{h'(y+) + h'(y-)}2 \,\mathrm{d} y \] for all $g\in C^1(\mathbb{R})$ with compact support. The occupation time formula helps dealing with the integral of the part of $h''(\!\,\mathrm{d} y)$ which is absolutely continuous with respect to the Lebesgue measure. Note that $f''(\! \,\mathrm{d} y) = f''(y)\,\mathrm{d} y + \frac{f'(0+) - f'(0-)}{2} \delta_{0}(\,\mathrm{d} y)$. Hence, \eqref{eq_Ito_Tanaka_plain} applied to $f$ yields the first equation in the statement. On one hand, this and \eqref{eq_Ito_Tanaka_plain} applied to $|f|$ yield \begin{multline} |Y_t|=|f(X_t)| = |f(X_0)| + \int_0^t \mathrm{sgn}(f(X_s)) \,\mathrm{d} Y_s + \frac{f'(0+) (1+\beta) + f'(0-) (1-\beta) }{ 2 } L_t(X). \end{multline} On the other hand, Tanaka formula for continuous semi-martingales states \[ |Y_t|= |Y_0| + \int_0^t \mathrm{sgn}(Y_s) \,\mathrm{d} Y_s + L_t(Y). \] Hence the conclusion on the local times. The fact that $f$ is invertible is then used to complete the proof.

nodes.statement_short: Apply the symmetric Ito-Tanaka formula to $f$ and to $|f|$, compare with Tanaka's formula for $|Y|$ to identify the local times.

nodes.name: SBM associated to OSBM/OBM
nodes.statement: Let $Y$ a $(\beta,\sigma_\pm)$-OSBM, in particular it satisfies~\eqref{eq:OSBM}. Let $f(x):=\frac{x}{\sigma(x)}$. Note that $f$ is continuous and for all $x\neq 0$ we have $f'(x)=\frac1{\sigma(x)}$ and $f''(x)=0$. Since $\sigma(x)$ depends only on the sign of $x$, then $f'\circ f^{-1}$ coincides with $f'$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:Ito-Tanaka}, $X_t:=f(Y_t)$ satisfies ~\eqref{eq:SBM:2} with $ \beta_\sigma= \frac{(1+\beta)\sigma_--(1-\beta)\sigma_+}{(1+\beta)\sigma_-+(1-\beta)\sigma_+} $ and $L_{\cdot}(X) = \frac{(1+\beta)\sigma_-+(1-\beta)\sigma_+}{2\sigma_-\sigma_+}L_{\cdot}(Y)$ holds as well. We call $X$, the {\em $\beta_\sigma$-SBM associated to the $(\beta,\sigma_\pm)$-OSBM $Y$\/}. If $Y$ is a $\sigma_\pm$-OBM, we recognize $\beta_\sigma=\frac{\sigma_--\sigma_+}{\sigma_-+\sigma_+}$ and~\eqref{eq:local_time:eq}.

nodes.name: OBM associated to OSBM/SBM
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be the solution to~\eqref{eq:SDE:sigma}. Take $\sigma_+^{(\beta)}:=\frac{1}{1 + \beta}$, $\sigma_-^{(\beta)}:=\frac{1}{1 - \beta}\in (0,\infty]$, then $\beta=\frac{\sigma_-^{(\beta)}-\sigma_+^{(\beta)}}{\sigma_-^{(\beta)}+\sigma_+^{(\beta)}}$ and construct the diffusion coefficient ${\sigma_{\beta}}:=\sigma_-^{(\beta)} \ind{(-\infty,0)}+\sigma_+^{(\beta)} \ind{[0,+\infty)}$ in~\eqref{sigmaOBM}. By Lemma~\ref{lem:Ito-Tanaka}, $\eta_t:=\sigma^{(\beta)}(X_t)X_t$ is solution to the SDE \begin{equation} \eta_t = \sigma^{(\beta)}(X_0) (X_0) + \int_0^t \sigma^{(\beta)}(\eta_s) \sigma(\eta_s/\sigma^{(\beta)}(\eta_s)) \,\mathrm{d} W_s + \int_0^t \sigma^{(\beta)}(\eta_s) b(\eta_s/\sigma^{(\beta)}(\eta_s)) \,\mathrm{d} s . \end{equation} and $ L_t(\eta) = L_t(X). $ In particular, if $X$ is the $(\beta,\sigma_\pm)$-OSBM solution to~\eqref{eq:OSBM}, then $Y_t:=\eta_t=\sigma^{(\beta)}(X_t) X_t$ is a $\sigma_\pm^{(\beta)}\sigma_\pm$-OBM with initial condition $Y_0={\sigma_{\beta}}(X_0) X_0$ and we refer to it as the {\em OBM associated to the $(\beta,\sigma_\pm)$-OSBM $X$\/}. And if $X$ is the $\beta$-SBM solution to~\eqref{eq:SBM}, then $Y_t$ is the {\em $\sigma_\pm^{(\beta)}$-OBM associated to the $\beta$-SBM $X$\/}.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 1 for OSBM
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be the $\beta_\sigma$-SBM associated to the $(\beta,\sigma_\pm)$-OSBM $Y$ (see Example~\ref{exa:OBM-SBM} in Section~\ref{sec:interplay}) and let $f_\sigma$ be the function satisfying $f_\sigma(x,y):=f(\sigma(x)x, \sigma(y)y)$. For $\gamma=1,2$ it holds that $ \bfH {f^\gamma}(\sigma(x) x)= \bfF{(f_\sigma)^\gamma}(x) $. Hence, Remark~\ref{rem:Lgb:remarks} ensures that a function $f$ satisfies Hypothesis~\ref{hp:OSBM:1} for $Y$ (that is $\bfH{f}$, $\bfH{f^2} \in \Lgb{2}$) if and only if $f_\sigma$ satisfies Hypothesis~\ref{hp:OSBM:1} for $X$ (that is $\bfF{f_\sigma}$, $\bfF{f_\sigma^2} \in \Lgb{2}$). Moreover $\frac1{\sigma(x)}\mu_{\beta_\sigma}(\!\,\mathrm{d} x) = \frac{2\sigma_-\sigma_+}{(1+\beta)\sigma_-+(1-\beta)\sigma_+} \mu_Y (\!\,\mathrm{d} x)$. So, $ \langle \mu_{\beta_\sigma} , \bfF{(f_\sigma)^\gamma} \rangle L_{\cdot}(X) = \langle \mu_Y , \bfH {f^\gamma} \rangle L_{\cdot}(Y) $. Applying Proposition~\ref{prop:lmt:2:OSBM} for the SBM $X$ and the function $f:=f_\sigma$ and taking into account the latter equalities complete the proof.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2
nodes.statement: \emph{ We reduce to prove the statement for SBM. } Let $X$ denote the standard SBM associated to $Y$ in Example~\ref{exa:OBM-SBM}. Since $f\in \Lg{\gamma}$, Remark~\ref{rem:Lgb:remarks} ensures that $f_\sigma\in \Lg{\gamma}$. Moreover $ \bfH {f}(x)= \bfF{f_\sigma}(x/\sigma(x)). $ If the first statement holds for the SBM $X$, then $\bfF{f_\sigma} \in \Lgb{\gamma}$ and Remark~\ref{rem:Lgb:remarks} ensures that $\bfH {f} \in \Lgb{\gamma}$. We can conclude similarly for the second part of the statement, just notice that $ \bfH {f,g}(x)= \bfF{f_\sigma,g_\sigma}(x/\sigma(x)) $ and $|g_\sigma(x)|/(1+|x|)$ is bounded as well. \emph{The SBM case: $Y$ is a Standard SBM.} Let $f\in \Lg{\gamma}$. Let us recall that there exist a non-negative function $ \bar f \in \Lgb{\gamma}$ and constant $a \in [0,\infty)$ such that $|f(x,y)| \leq \bar f(x) e^{a|y-x|}$. Since there exists a constant $C\in (0,\infty)$ such that for all $x,y\in \mathbb R$: $ p_\beta (1,x,y) \leq C \frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-\frac12(y-x)^2}, $ then for all $x\in \mathbb R$ \[ |\bfH{f}(x)| \leq C \bar f(x) \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} e^{a |y-x|} \frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-\frac12(y-x)^2} \,\mathrm{d} y \leq 2 e^{a^2/2} C \bar f(x). \] Thus $ \bfH{f} \in \Lgb{\gamma}$. And $\bfH{f^2} \in \Lgb{\gamma}$ is proven in the same way, since $\bar f$ is bounded. Similarly for the second part of the statement, there exists a constant $C_2\in (0,\infty)$ such that for all $x\in \mathbb R$ \[ \begin{split} |\bfH{f,g}(x)| & \leq C_2 \bar f(x) \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} (1+|y|) e^{a |y-x|} \frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-\frac12(y-x)^2} \,\mathrm{d} y \\ & \leq C_2 \bar f(x) \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} (e^{|y-x|}+|x|) e^{a |y-x|} \frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-\frac12(y-x)^2} \,\mathrm{d} y \\ & \leq 2 e^{(a+1)^2/2} C_2 \bar f(x) + 2 e^{a^2/2} C_2 \bar f(x) |x| \leq 2 e^{(a+1)^2/2} C_2 \bar f(x) (1+|x|) \end{split} \] where we recall that $ \bar f \in \Lgb{\gamma}$. The proof is thus completed.
nodes.section: 4.2 Proof of Proposition~1
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to SBM via the associated process; bound the SBM density by a Gaussian and integrate the exponential domination.

nodes.name: Reduction to SBM
nodes.statement: \emph{ We reduce to prove the statement for SBM. } Let $X$ denote the standard SBM associated to $Y$ in Example~\ref{exa:OBM-SBM}. Since $f\in \Lg{\gamma}$, Remark~\ref{rem:Lgb:remarks} ensures that $f_\sigma\in \Lg{\gamma}$. Moreover $ \bfH {f}(x)= \bfF{f_\sigma}(x/\sigma(x)). $ If the first statement holds for the SBM $X$, then $\bfF{f_\sigma} \in \Lgb{\gamma}$ and Remark~\ref{rem:Lgb:remarks} ensures that $\bfH {f} \in \Lgb{\gamma}$. We can conclude similarly for the second part of the statement, just notice that $ \bfH {f,g}(x)= \bfF{f_\sigma,g_\sigma}(x/\sigma(x)) $ and $|g_\sigma(x)|/(1+|x|)$ is bounded as well.
nodes.section: 4.2 Proof of Proposition~1
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to SBM using the associated SBM and Remark 3.

nodes.name: SBM case
nodes.statement: \emph{The SBM case: $Y$ is a Standard SBM.} Let $f\in \Lg{\gamma}$. Let us recall that there exist a non-negative function $ \bar f \in \Lgb{\gamma}$ and constant $a \in [0,\infty)$ such that $|f(x,y)| \leq \bar f(x) e^{a|y-x|}$. Since there exists a constant $C\in (0,\infty)$ such that for all $x,y\in \mathbb R$: $ p_\beta (1,x,y) \leq C \frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-\frac12(y-x)^2}, $ then for all $x\in \mathbb R$ \[ |\bfH{f}(x)| \leq C \bar f(x) \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} e^{a |y-x|} \frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-\frac12(y-x)^2} \,\mathrm{d} y \leq 2 e^{a^2/2} C \bar f(x). \] Thus $ \bfH{f} \in \Lgb{\gamma}$. And $\bfH{f^2} \in \Lgb{\gamma}$ is proven in the same way, since $\bar f$ is bounded. Similarly for the second part of the statement, there exists a constant $C_2\in (0,\infty)$ such that for all $x\in \mathbb R$ \[ \begin{split} |\bfH{f,g}(x)| & \leq C_2 \bar f(x) \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} (1+|y|) e^{a |y-x|} \frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-\frac12(y-x)^2} \,\mathrm{d} y \\ & \leq C_2 \bar f(x) \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} (e^{|y-x|}+|x|) e^{a |y-x|} \frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-\frac12(y-x)^2} \,\mathrm{d} y \\ & \leq 2 e^{(a+1)^2/2} C_2 \bar f(x) + 2 e^{a^2/2} C_2 \bar f(x) |x| \leq 2 e^{(a+1)^2/2} C_2 \bar f(x) (1+|x|) \end{split} \] where we recall that $ \bar f \in \Lgb{\gamma}$. The proof is thus completed.

nodes.statement_short: Gaussian bound on $p_\beta$ gives $|\mathbf{E}f|\le C\bar f$ and the linear-growth variant.

nodes.name: Martingale decomposition for OBM (key proposition)
nodes.statement: Let $(Y_t)_{t\in [0,1]}$ be the OBM with threshold $r=0$ strong solution to~\eqref{eq:OBM} on a stochastic basis $(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, (\mathcal{F}_t)_{t\in [0,1]},\mathbb{P})$ (where the filtration is the natural one associated to $Y$), let $\gamma >3$, and let $h\in \Lg{\gamma}$. \\ Then constant $K_h^Y$ given by~\eqref{eq:k:th} (with $f=h$, $X=Y$, $\mu_X=\lambda_\sigma$, $\beta=0$) is a non-negative finite constant, and there exist a sequence of stochastic processes $(\mathcal{V}^n_t)_{t\in [0,1]}$, $n\in \mathbb{N}$, and a sequence $(\mathcal{M}^n_t)_{t\in [0,1]}$, $n\in \mathbb{N}$, of $(\mathcal{F}_{{\lfloor n t \rfloor}/{n}})_{t\in [0,1]}$-martingales such that for all $t\in [0,1]$, $n\in \mathbb{N}$ \begin{equation} n^{1/4}\left( \varepsilon_{n,t}^{(0,h,Y)} - \langle \lambda_\sigma , \bfH h \rangle L_t(Y)\right) = \mathcal{M}^n_t + n^{1/4} \mathcal{V}^n_t, \end{equation} $ \sup_{s\in [0,1]} m^{1/4} |\mathcal{V}^m_s| \convp[m\to\infty] 0 $, and for all $t\in [0,1]$, $n\in \mathbb{N}$ it holds that $ \mathcal{M}^n_t = \sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor n t \rfloor} \chi^n_k $ where $(\chi^n_k)_{k\in \{1, \ldots, \lfloor n t \rfloor\}}$, $n\in \mathbb{N}$, are random variables satisfying: \begin{enumerate}[i)] \item for all $k\in \{1, \ldots, \lfloor n t \rfloor\}$ $\chi^n_k$ is square integrable $\mathcal{F}_{\frac{k}{n}}$-measurable and $ \mathbb{E}\!\left[ \chi_k^n | \mathcal{F}_{(k-1)/n}\right] = 0$, \item for all $t\in [0,1]$ it holds that $ \sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor n t \rfloor} \mathbb{E}\!\left[ (\chi_k^n)^2 | \mathcal{F}_{(k-1)/n}\right] \convp[n\to\infty] K_h^Y L_t(Y), $ \item for all $t\in [0,1]$ it holds that $ \sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor n t \rfloor} \mathbb{E}\!\left[ \chi_k^n (Y_{k/n}-Y_{{(k-1)}/n})| \mathcal{F}_{(k-1)/n}\right] \convp[n\to\infty] 0 $, \item for all $\varepsilon \in (0,\infty)$ it holds that $ \sum_{k=1}^{n} \mathbb{E}\!\left[ |\chi_k^n|^2 \ind{\{|\chi_k^n|\geq \varepsilon \}}| \mathcal{F}_{(k-1)/n}\right] \convp[n\to\infty] 0 $. \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Jacod's stable limit theorem for triangular arrays
nodes.statement: Let $(Y_t)_{t\in [0,1]}$ be an $(\mathcal{F}_t)_{t\in [0,1]}$-local martingale on the stochastic basis $(\Omega,\mathcal{F}, (\mathcal{F}_t)_{t\in [0,1]},\mathbb{P})$. For $n\in \mathbb{N}$ and $k=1,\ldots, n$, let $\chi^n_k$ be square integrable $\mathcal{F}_{\frac{k}{n}}$-measurable random variables, and assume that there are $E$ and $F$ continuous processes on $(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, (\mathcal{F}_t)_{t\in [0,1]},\mathbb{P})$ such that $E$ has bounded variation and \begin{enumerate}[i)] \item $ \sup_{s\in [0,1]} \left|\sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor n s \rfloor} \mathbb{E}\!\left[ \chi_k^n | \mathcal{F}_{(k-1)/n}\right]- E_s\right| \convp[n\to\infty] 0 $, \item for all $t\in [0,1]$ it holds that $ \sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor n t \rfloor} \mathbb{E}\!\left[ \left(\chi_k^n- \mathbb{E}\!\left[ \chi_k^n | \mathcal{F}_{(k-1)/n}\right]\right)^{\!2} | \mathcal{F}_{(k-1)/n}\right] \convp[n\to\infty] F_t, $ \item for all $t\in [0,1]$ it holds that $ \sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor n t \rfloor} \mathbb{E}\!\left[ \chi_k^n (Y_{k/n}-Y_{{(k-1)}/n})| \mathcal{F}_{(k-1)/n}\right] \convp[n\to\infty] 0 $, \item for all $\varepsilon \in (0,\infty)$ it holds that $ \sum_{k=1}^{n} \mathbb{E}\!\left[ |\chi_k^n|^2 \ind{\{|\chi_k^n|\geq \varepsilon \}}| \mathcal{F}_{(k-1)/n}\right] \convp[n\to\infty] 0 $, and \item for all $t\in [0,1]$ and every $M$ bounded $(\mathcal{F}_s)_{s\in [0,1]}$-martingale such that for all $s\in [0,1]$ the cross variation $\langle M, Y\rangle_s$ is $\mathbb P$-a.s.~equal to 0, it holds that \begin{equation} \sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor n t \rfloor} \mathbb{E}\!\left[ \chi_k^n (M_{k/n}-M_{{(k-1)}/n}) | \mathcal{F}_{(k-1)/n}\right] \convp[n\to\infty] 0. \end{equation} \end{enumerate} Then there exists a BM $B$, possibly on an extension of the probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal{F},(\mathcal{F}_t)_{t\in [0,1]},\mathbb{P})$, such that $B$ and $Y$ are independent and \begin{equation} \sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor n \cdot \rfloor} \chi^n_k \convsl[n\to\infty] E_\cdot + B_{F_\cdot}.\end{equation}

conclusions: there exists a BM $B$, possibly on an extension of the probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal{F},(\mathcal{F}_t)_{t\in [0,1]},\mathbb{P})$, such that $B$ and $Y$ are independent

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1 for OBM
nodes.statement: Let $Y$ be the OBM strong solution to \eqref{eq:OBM}. Let us first assume that the filtration is the natural one associated to $Y$. Observe that \[ n^\frac14\left( \varepsilon^{(0,f,Y)}_{n,\cdot} - \langle \lambda_\sigma, \bfH{f} \rangle L_\cdot(Y)\right) \convsl[n\to\infty] \sqrt{K_f^Y} B_{L_\cdot(Y)} \] in $\mathbb{D}_\infty$ if and only if, for all $t\in [0,\infty)$, $ n^\frac14 (\varepsilon^{(0,f,Y)}_{n,\cdot} - \langle \lambda_\sigma, \bfH{f} \rangle L_\cdot(Y))|_{[0,t]} \convsl[n\to\infty] \sqrt{K_f^Y} B_{L_\cdot(Y)}|_{[0,t]} $ in $\mathbb{D}_t$ (indeed since $B_{L_\cdot(Y)}$ has (a.s.) continuous trajectories this follows, e.g.~combining~\cite[Theorem~16.2]{billingsley} and~\cite[Proposition~2.2.4]{jp}). Moreover, without loss of generality we can reduce ourselves to prove Theorem~\ref{th:gen:jacod} on the interval $[0,1]$ (on the Skorokhod space $\mathbb{D}_{[0,1]}$) for $n\in \mathbb{N}$ tending to infinity. Indeed the scaling property for the OBM and its local time (see~\eqref{Yscaling}) yields the result for all non-negative times (on the Skorokhod space $\mathbb{D}_{[0,t]}$). (The scaling property also ensures that in Theorem~\ref{th:gen:jacod} $n$ is not necessarily a natural number, but it can stay for a positive real number tending to infinity.) Proposition~\ref{th:j2:2} implies that there exists a decomposition as in \eqref{eq:decomposition} and its desired stable limit as $n\in \mathbb{N}$ goes to infinity coincides with the stable limit of the sequence $\mathcal{M}^n$ of c\`adl\`ag $(\mathcal{F}_{\frac{\lfloor n s\rfloor}n})_{s\in [0,1]}$-martingales, $n\in \mathbb{N}$. Indeed the fact that $ \sup_{s\in [0,1]} n^{1/4} |\mathcal{V}^n_s| \convp[n\to\infty] 0, $ implies that for every $h\colon \mathbb{D}_1 \to \mathbb{R}$ continuous and bounded it holds that $ |h(\mathcal{M}^n + n^\frac14 \mathcal{V}^n)-h(\mathcal{M}^n)| \convp[n\to\infty] 0$ and so for every bounded continuous function $h\colon \mathbb{D}_1 \to \mathbb{R}$ and bounded measurable random variable $Y\colon \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ it holds that \[ \lim_{n\to\infty} \mathbb{E}\!\left[|h(\mathcal{M}^n + n^\frac14 \mathcal{V}^n)-h(\mathcal{M}^n)|| Y|\right] = 0. \] Proposition~\ref{th:j2:2} also ensures that $\mathcal{M}^n$, $n\in \mathbb{N}$, satisfies all assumptions, except Item~\ref{th:j2:item5}, of Proposition~\ref{th:j2} (with $E\equiv 0$ and $ F = K_f^Y L(Y) $ where $K_f^Y$ is the constant in~equation~\eqref{eq:k:th} with $X=Y$, $\beta=0$ and $\mu_X=\lambda_\sigma$). Item~\ref{th:j2:item5} of Proposition~\ref{th:j2} is trivial because such bounded martingale $M$, measurable with respect to the natural filtration of the OBM and orthogonal to OBM, is nothing but a constant (follows from a martingale representation theorem, see Lemma~\ref{lem:trivial:OBM} in Appendix~\ref{sec:orthogonal}). Therefore, applying Proposition~\ref{th:j2} as described above, completes the proof of Theorem~\ref{th:gen:jacod} under the assumption that the filtration is the one associated to $Y$. It remains to relax this assumption on the filtration, by the same argument in~\cite[Section 2.2]{j1}. The proof of Theorem~\ref{th:gen:jacod} is thus completed.

Indeed the fact that $ \sup_{s\in [0,1]} n^{1/4} |\mathcal{V}^n_s| \convp[n\to\infty] 0, $ implies that for every $h\colon \mathbb{D}_1 \to \mathbb{R}$ continuous and bounded it holds that $ |h(\mathcal{M}^n + n^\frac14 \mathcal{V}^n)-h(\mathcal{M}^n)| \convp[n\to\infty] 0$ and so for every bounded continuous function $h\colon \mathbb{D}_1 \to \mathbb{R}$ and bounded measurable random variable $Y\colon \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ it holds that \[ \lim_{n\to\infty} \mathbb{E}\!\left[|h(\mathcal{M}^n + n^\frac14 \mathcal{V}^n)-h(\mathcal{M}^n)|| Y|\right] = 0. \]

nodes.statement: Proposition~\ref{th:j2:2} also ensures that $\mathcal{M}^n$, $n\in \mathbb{N}$, satisfies all assumptions, except Item~\ref{th:j2:item5}, of Proposition~\ref{th:j2} (with $E\equiv 0$ and $ F = K_f^Y L(Y) $ where $K_f^Y$ is the constant in~equation~\eqref{eq:k:th} with $X=Y$, $\beta=0$ and $\mu_X=\lambda_\sigma$). Item~\ref{th:j2:item5} of Proposition~\ref{th:j2} is trivial because such bounded martingale $M$, measurable with respect to the natural filtration of the OBM and orthogonal to OBM, is nothing but a constant (follows from a martingale representation theorem, see Lemma~\ref{lem:trivial:OBM} in Appendix~\ref{sec:orthogonal}).

It remains to relax this assumption on the filtration, by the same argument in~\cite[Section 2.2]{j1}. The proof of Theorem~\ref{th:gen:jacod} is thus completed.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1 for OSBM
nodes.statement: Let $\gamma >3$, $X$ the $(\beta,\sigma_\pm)$-OSBM solution to \eqref{eq:OSBM}, and $f \in \Lg{\gamma}$. Let $Y$ be the OBM associated to $X$ (in the notation of Example~\ref{exa:SBM-OBM} in Section~\ref{sec:interplay}) and let $h \colon \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}$ be the function satisfying $h(x,y) :=f(x/{\sigma^{(\beta)}}(x), y/{\sigma^{(\beta)}}(y))$. Remark~\ref{rem:Lgb:remarks} ensures that $f\in \Lg{\gamma}$ if and only if $h \in \Lg{\gamma}$. Theorem~\ref{th:gen:jacod} applied to the OBM $Y$ and the function $h$ yields \begin{equation} n^{1/4} \left( \varepsilon_{n,\cdot}^{(0,h,Y)} - \langle \lambda_{\sigma^{(\beta)}\sigma} , \bfH { h } \rangle L_\cdot(Y) \right) \convsl[n\to \infty] \sqrt{K_{h}^\beta} B_{L_\cdot(Y)} \end{equation} with $K_{h}^\beta$ given by~\eqref{eq:k:th} (taking $f=h$, $X=Y$, $\sigma_\pm=\sigma_\pm^{(\beta)}\sigma_\pm$, $\beta=0$, $\mu_X=\lambda_{\sigma^{(\beta)}\sigma}$). As in the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:lmt:2:OSBM}, the fact that $Y=\sigma^{(\beta)}(X)X$, $L_{\cdot}(X)=L_{\cdot}(Y)$, and the transition densities~\eqref{eq:densities:X}, implies that for $\gamma=1,2$ it holds $ \langle \lambda_{\sigma^{(\beta)}\sigma} , \bfH { h^\gamma } \rangle = \langle \mu_X , \bfF { f^\gamma } \rangle $ and so \begin{equation} \begin{split} &n^{1/4} \left( \varepsilon_{n,\cdot}^{(0,f,X)} - \langle \mu_X , \bfF { f } \rangle L_\cdot(X) \right) \convsl[n\to \infty] \sqrt{K_{h}^\beta} B_{L_\cdot(X)}. \end{split}\end{equation} The same arguments are used to rewrite the constant $K_{h}^\beta$ obtaining $K_f^X$: more precisely note that $\bfH{h}(x \sigma^{(\beta)}(x))=\bfF { f } (x)$, $\bfH{g_0}(x \sigma^{(\beta)}(x)) = \bfF { g_\beta } (x)$, and $\mathcal{P}_{h}^Y(x \sigma^{(\beta)}(x)) = \mathcal{P}_{f}^X(x) $.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement: Let us recall that Hypothesis~\ref{hyp:SDE:sigma} holds. In particular it holds that $\sigma \in C^1(\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\})$ is strictly positive, admits a finite jump at the threshold $0$, $\sigma_\pm:=\lim_{x\to 0^\pm} \sigma(x)\in (0,\infty)$, and its derivative admits a finite jump at $0$ as well. {\it We first prove the statement for $\beta=0$ in several steps.} {\it First step.} Note that if $X$ is a driftless $\sigma_\pm$-OBM, then the statement follows from Proposition~\ref{prop:lmt:2:OSBM} and Theorem~\ref{th:gen:jacod} taking $f=h_0$. The result holds with constants $c_{\sigma_\pm,0}$ and $K_{\sigma_\pm,0}$. {\it Second step.} Assume $\sigma$ and its derivative are bounded (the derivative is defined on ${\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}}$, one may take $\sigma'(0)=(\sigma'(0^+)+\sigma'(0^-)$). Let us consider the process $Z$ satisfying that $\mathbb{P}$-a.s.~for all $t\in [0,\infty)$ \[ Z_t= Z_0 + \int_0^t \sigma(Z_s) \,\mathrm{d} W_s + \frac12 \int_0^t \sigma(Z_s) \sigma'(Z_s) \,\mathrm{d} s. \] Let \[ S(x):= \sigma_+ \int_0^x \frac{1}{\sigma(y)}\,\mathrm{d} y \, \ind{[0,+\infty)}(x) - \sigma_- \int_x^0 \frac{1}{\sigma(y)}\,\mathrm{d} y \, \ind{(-\infty,0)}(x). \] Note that $S$ is difference of two convex functions, $S\in C^1(\mathbb{R}) \cap C^2(\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\})$, $S(0)=0$, and $S$ is strictly increasing. By Lemma~\ref{lem:Ito-Tanaka}, $Y_t:=S(Z_t)$ is an OBM starting at $S(Z_0)$. Since $x S^{-1}(x) \geq 0$ for all $x\in \mathbb{R}$, then for all $t$ it holds that $Z_t$ and $S^{-1}(Z_t)=Y_t$ have the same sign and, since $\mathcal{L}^0_{T,N}$ depends only on the observations through their sign, $\mathcal{L}^0_{T,N}(Y) =\mathcal{L}^0_{T,N}(Z)$. Therefore we proved that Theorem~\ref{th:crossings} holds for the process $Z$ with the same constants $c_{\sigma_\pm,0}$ and $K_{\sigma_\pm,0}$. {\it Third step.} Assume $\sigma$ and $\sigma'$ are bounded, as in the previous step. Combining stable converge and Girsanov's transform (see Remark~\ref{rem:drift}) ensures that the same result holds for $X$ solution to~\eqref{eq:SDE:sigma} if $\beta=0$ with the same constants $c_{\sigma_\pm,0}$ and $K_{\sigma_\pm,0}$. Let us be more precise. Let $Z$ as in the previous step and let $X$ solve~\eqref{eq:SDE:sigma} with $\beta=0$. The Dol\'eans-Dade exponential, expressing the Radon-Nikodym derivative between the law of $X$ and the one of $Z$, is $\mathcal{E}(\xi)$ with $ \xi_t := \int_0^t \frac{b(Z_s)-\frac12 \sigma(Z_s) \sigma'(Z_s)}{\sigma(Z_s)} \,\mathrm{d} W_s. $ It is an exponential martingale (see e.g.~Novikov's condition in~\cite[Corollary 3.5.14]{ks}) because $b$, $\sigma'$ are bounded and $\sigma$ is bounded from below by a strictly-positive constant. By a localization argument, the boundedness conditions for $\sigma$ and $\sigma'$ can be removed. {\it Now let us consider $\beta\neq 0$.} Consider the process $\eta_s:=\sigma^{(\beta)}(X_s) X_s$ of Example~\ref{exa:SBM-OBM} in Section~\ref{sec:interplay}. Note that $\mathcal{L}^0_{T,N}(\eta) =\mathcal{L}^0_{T,N}(X)$ because the statistics depends only on the sign of the observations of $\eta$ and $X$ and this sign is preserved by the transformation we apply. We have proved above that the process $\eta$ satisfies Theorem~\ref{th:crossings} with constants $c_{\sigma^{(\beta)}_\pm \sigma_\pm,0}$ and $K_{\sigma^{(\beta)}_\pm \sigma_\pm,0}$ hence $X$ satisfies the theorem with the same constants that we just rename in order to explicit the dependence from $\sigma^{(\beta)}$ as a dependence from $\beta$. The proof is thus completed.
nodes.section: 4.4 Proof of Theorem~2
nodes.statement_short: For $\beta=0$: OBM case, then a space transform to remove the drift-like term, then Girsanov and localization. For $\beta\neq0$: pass to the associated OBM since the statistic depends only on signs.

In particular it holds that $\sigma \in C^1(\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\})$ is strictly positive, admits a finite jump at the threshold $0$, $\sigma_\pm:=\lim_{x\to 0^\pm} \sigma(x)\in (0,\infty)$, and its derivative admits a finite jump at $0$ as well. {\it We first prove the statement for $\beta=0$ in several steps.}

Therefore we proved that Theorem~\ref{th:crossings} holds for the process $Z$ with the same constants $c_{\sigma_\pm,0}$ and $K_{\sigma_\pm,0}$.

nodes.statement_short: Transform $Z$ into an OBM by $S$; the crossing statistic depends only on signs.

nodes.name: Girsanov transform
nodes.statement: {\it Third step.} Assume $\sigma$ and $\sigma'$ are bounded, as in the previous step. Combining stable converge and Girsanov's transform (see Remark~\ref{rem:drift}) ensures that the same result holds for $X$ solution to~\eqref{eq:SDE:sigma} if $\beta=0$ with the same constants $c_{\sigma_\pm,0}$ and $K_{\sigma_\pm,0}$. Let us be more precise. Let $Z$ as in the previous step and let $X$ solve~\eqref{eq:SDE:sigma} with $\beta=0$. The Dol\'eans-Dade exponential, expressing the Radon-Nikodym derivative between the law of $X$ and the one of $Z$, is $\mathcal{E}(\xi)$ with $ \xi_t := \int_0^t \frac{b(Z_s)-\frac12 \sigma(Z_s) \sigma'(Z_s)}{\sigma(Z_s)} \,\mathrm{d} W_s. $ It is an exponential martingale (see e.g.~Novikov's condition in~\cite[Corollary 3.5.14]{ks}) because $b$, $\sigma'$ are bounded and $\sigma$ is bounded from below by a strictly-positive constant. By a localization argument, the boundedness conditions for $\sigma$ and $\sigma'$ can be removed.
nodes.section: 4.4 Proof of Theorem~2
nodes.statement_short: Girsanov (Novikov) and localization add the drift.

nodes.name: Skew case
nodes.statement: {\it Now let us consider $\beta\neq 0$.} Consider the process $\eta_s:=\sigma^{(\beta)}(X_s) X_s$ of Example~\ref{exa:SBM-OBM} in Section~\ref{sec:interplay}. Note that $\mathcal{L}^0_{T,N}(\eta) =\mathcal{L}^0_{T,N}(X)$ because the statistics depends only on the sign of the observations of $\eta$ and $X$ and this sign is preserved by the transformation we apply. We have proved above that the process $\eta$ satisfies Theorem~\ref{th:crossings} with constants $c_{\sigma^{(\beta)}_\pm \sigma_\pm,0}$ and $K_{\sigma^{(\beta)}_\pm \sigma_\pm,0}$ hence $X$ satisfies the theorem with the same constants that we just rename in order to explicit the dependence from $\sigma^{(\beta)}$ as a dependence from $\beta$. The proof is thus completed.
nodes.section: 4.4 Proof of Theorem~2
nodes.statement_short: Pass to the associated OBM $\eta$, whose crossings coincide with those of $X$.

nodes.name: Diffusive scaling property of OBM and its local time
nodes.statement: \bigg(\frac{1}{\sqrt{c}} Z_{ct} , \frac{1}{\sqrt{c}} L_{ct}(Z)\bigg)_{t\geq 0} \stackrel{\mathrm{law}}{=} \big( Y_{t}, L_t(Y) \big)_{t\geq 0}.
nodes.section: A.1 Scaling property
assumptions: $Z$ denote the OBM with threshold $r=0$ starting from $\sqrt{c} Y_0$
nodes.label: Yscaling

nodes.name: Scaling of the transition and joint densities
nodes.statement: The transition density satisfies for every $c>0$ that $q_\sigma(t,x,y)= \sqrt{c} q_\sigma(c t, \sqrt{c} x, \sqrt{c} y ).$ This and the Markov property imply that for all $k =0,1,\ldots$ \[ \begin{split} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\bfH{f,g}(\sqrt{n}Y_{k/n}) = \frac1{\sqrt n} \mathbb{E}\!\left[ f(\sqrt{n} Y_{k/n}, \sqrt{n} Y_{(k+1)/n}) g(\sqrt{n} Y_{(k+1)/n}) | Y_{k/n} \right]. \end{split} \] And $\rho^\sigma_t(y,\ell)$, the joint density of a standard OBM and its local time introduced in the next section, satisfies for every $c>0$: $\rho^\sigma_t(y,\ell) = c \rho^\sigma_{c t}(\sqrt c y, \sqrt c \ell)$.
nodes.section: A.1 Scaling property
nodes.statement_short: Scaling identities for $q_\sigma$, for $\mathbf{E}^Y_{f,g}$ along the chain, and for the joint density of OBM and its local time.

nodes.name: Joint density of OBM and its local time
nodes.statement: The joint density of a standard OBM (i.e.~$Y_0=0$) and its local time at time $t$, $\rho^\sigma_t(y,\ell)$ coincides with \begin{equation} \rho^\sigma_t(y,\ell) = \frac{1}{(\sigma(y))^2} \rho_t\left(\frac{y}{\sigma(y)}, \frac{\sigma_-+\sigma_+}{2\sigma_-\sigma_+} \ell\right) \end{equation} for $y\neq 0$, where $\rho$ is the joint density of the BM and its local time at time $t$: \begin{equation} \rho_t(y,\ell) = \frac{|y| + \ell}{\sqrt{2\pi t^3}} \exp\!\left(- \frac{(|y| + \ell)^2}{2 t}\right) \ind{(0,\infty)}(\ell). \end{equation}
nodes.section: A.2 The joint density of a standard OBM and its local time
nodes.statement_short: Joint density of standard OBM and its local time, expressed through the Brownian one.

nodes.name: Equation (A.2): Joint density of OBM and local time
nodes.statement: \rho^\sigma_t(y,\ell) = \frac{1}{(\sigma(y))^2} \rho_t\left(\frac{y}{\sigma(y)}, \frac{\sigma_-+\sigma_+}{2\sigma_-\sigma_+} \ell\right)

nodes.label: eq:OBMl

nodes.name: Equation (A.3): Joint density of BM and local time
nodes.statement: \rho_t(y,\ell) = \frac{|y| + \ell}{\sqrt{2\pi t^3}} \exp\!\left(- \frac{(|y| + \ell)^2}{2 t}\right) \ind{(0,\infty)}(\ell).

nodes.name: Rescaled function $f_\sigma$
nodes.statement: Let ${\beta_\sigma}:=\frac{\sigma_--\sigma_+}{\sigma_-+\sigma_+}$ and recall that, for every function $f\colon \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, $f_\sigma(x):=f(\sigma(x) x)$.

nodes.name: Semigroups $Q^\sigma_t$ of OBM and $P^{\beta_\sigma}_t$ of SBM
nodes.statement: For a measurable, bounded function $f\colon \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ set \begin{equation} Q^{\sigma}_t f(x) := \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} q_\sigma(t,x, y)f(y) \,\mathrm{d} y \quad { and } \quad P^{\beta_\sigma}_t f(x) := \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} p_{\beta_\sigma}(t,x, y)f(y) \,\mathrm{d} y \end{equation} for all $t\in [0,\infty)$.
nodes.section: A.3 Bounds for the semigroup

nodes.name: Equation (A.4): Semigroups of OBM and SBM
nodes.statement: Q^{\sigma}_t f(x) := \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} q_\sigma(t,x, y)f(y) \,\mathrm{d} y \quad { and } \quad P^{\beta_\sigma}_t f(x) := \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} p_{\beta_\sigma}(t,x, y)f(y) \,\mathrm{d} y
nodes.section: A.3 Bounds for the semigroup
nodes.label: eq:def:semig

nodes.name: Relations between the semigroups of OBM, SBM and BM
nodes.statement: They are respectively the semigroup of the standard OBM and of the standard $\beta_\sigma$-SBM and they satisfy $ Q^{\sigma}_t f(x) = P^{{\beta_\sigma}}_t f_\sigma (x/\sigma(x)). $ Note that $P_t:=P^0_t=Q_t^{1}$ is the semigroup of the BM and \begin{equation} Q^\sigma_t f(x) = P_t f_\sigma(x/\sigma(x))+ {\beta_\sigma} P_t (f_\sigma \ind{[0,\infty)})(-|x|/\sigma(x)) - {\beta_\sigma} P_t (f_\sigma \ind{(-\infty,0)}) (|x|/\sigma(x)). \end{equation}
nodes.section: A.3 Bounds for the semigroup
conclusions: Q^\sigma_t f(x) = P_t f_\sigma(x/\sigma(x))+ {\beta_\sigma} P_t (f_\sigma \ind{[0,\infty)})(-|x|/\sigma(x)) - {\beta_\sigma} P_t (f_\sigma \ind{(-\infty,0)}) (|x|/\sigma(x)).
nodes.statement_short: The OBM semigroup is the SBM semigroup of $f_\sigma$, hence an explicit combination of Brownian semigroups.

nodes.name: Equation (A.5): OBM semigroup via BM semigroup
nodes.statement: Q^\sigma_t f(x) = P_t f_\sigma(x/\sigma(x))+ {\beta_\sigma} P_t (f_\sigma \ind{[0,\infty)})(-|x|/\sigma(x)) - {\beta_\sigma} P_t (f_\sigma \ind{(-\infty,0)}) (|x|/\sigma(x)).

nodes.name: Bounds for the OBM semigroup
nodes.statement: Let $f\in \Lgb{2}$, and let us denote by $p(t,\cdot)$ is the density of a Gaussian random variable with variance $t$. Then there exists a positive constant $K\in (0,\infty)$ such that for all $x,y\in \mathbb{R}$, $0 \leq s\leq t$ it holds that \begin{enumerate}[i)] \item $ |Q^\sigma_t f (x)| \leq \frac1{\min\{\sigma_-, \sigma_+\}} \left(1+\frac{|\sigma_- -\sigma_+|}{\sigma_-+\sigma_+}\right) \frac1{\sqrt{2 \pi}} \frac{\|f\|_{1}}{\sqrt t}, $ \item $ \left| Q^\sigma_t f (x) - \frac{2 \sigma_-\sigma_+}{\sigma_-+\sigma_+} \langle \lambda_\sigma , f \rangle p(t,{x}/{\sigma(x)}) \right|\leq \frac{K}{\sqrt{t^3}} \left( \| f \|_{1,2} +\| f \|_{1,1} |x|\right), $ \item for all $\zeta \geq 0 $ there exists a positive constant $K_\zeta$ such that\\ $ \left| Q^\sigma_t f (x) - \frac{2 \sigma_-\sigma_+}{\sigma_-+\sigma_+} \langle \lambda_\sigma , f \rangle p(t,{x}/{\sigma(x)}) \right| \leq \frac{K_\zeta}{t} \left( \frac{\| f \|_{1,1}}{1+(|x|/(\sigma(x)\sqrt{t}))^\zeta} +\frac{\| f \|_{1,1+\zeta}}{1+(|x|/\sigma(x))^\zeta} \right), $ \item $ \left| Q^\sigma_t f (x) - Q^\sigma_t f (y) \right| \leq \frac1{\min\{\sigma_-, \sigma_+\}} \left(1+\frac{|\sigma_- -\sigma_+|}{\sigma_-+\sigma_+}\right) K \frac{|x-y|}{t} \|f\|_{1} $, and \item $ \left| Q^\sigma_t f (x) - Q^\sigma_s f (x) \right| \leq \frac1{\min\{\sigma_-, \sigma_+\}} \left(1+\frac{|\sigma_- -\sigma_+|}{\sigma_-+\sigma_+}\right) K \frac{t-s}{\sqrt{s^{3}}} \|f\|_{1}. $ \end{enumerate}

conclusions: there exists a positive constant $K\in (0,\infty)$ such that for all $x,y\in \mathbb{R}$, $0 \leq s\leq t$ it holds that
nodes.statement_short: Sup, Gaussian-approximation, decay, spatial-Lipschitz and time-Lipschitz bounds for $Q^\sigma_t f$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3
nodes.statement: Item~\ref{item1:semig:estim} is a straightforward consequence of \eqref{eq:densities:X} (with $\beta=0$) and of the fact that \begin{equation} p_{\beta_\sigma} (t,x,y) \leq (1+|{\beta_\sigma}|) p(t,x-y) \leq \frac{1+|{\beta_\sigma}|}{\sqrt{2\pi t}}. \end{equation} To prove the other items we also use the fact for all $\alpha \geq 0$ $\| f(\sigma(\cdot)\cdot) \|_{1,\alpha} \leq \frac{\| f \|_{1,\alpha}}{(\min{\{\sigma_-,\sigma_+ \}})^{1+\alpha}}$ and $\| f \ind{[0,\infty)} \|_{1,\alpha} + \| f \ind{(-\infty,0)} \|_{1,\alpha}= \| f \|_{1,\alpha}$. Item~\ref{item2:semig:estim} follows from \eqref{eq:semig} and \cite[Lemma~1]{lmt1} for SBM. Item~\ref{item2bis:semig:estim} follows from \eqref{eq:semig} and the analogous result for BM: equation (3.2) in~\cite[Lemma~3.1]{j1}. Item~\ref{item3:semig:estim} and Item~\ref{item4:semig:estim} follow from \eqref{eq:semig} and equations (3.4)-(3.5) in \cite[Lemma~3.1]{j1}.
nodes.section: A.3 Bounds for the semigroup
nodes.statement_short: Reduce each item via the OBM-BM semigroup relation to known SBM/BM estimates ([lmt1], [j1]).

nodes.name: Bounds on the aggregated semigroup $\Gamma_t$
nodes.statement: Let $f\colon \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ and $ \Gamma_t(n,f, Y_0) $ as above. There exists a positive constant $K$ (depending on $\sigma_\pm$) such that $|\Gamma_t(n,f,Y_0)| \leq K \|f\|_{1} {\sqrt{n t}}$ and if $\langle \lambda_\sigma , f \rangle=0$ then it holds that $ |\Gamma_t(n,f,Y_0)| \leq K \left( \| f \|_{1,2} + \| f \|_{1,1} |Y_0| {\sqrt{n}}\right)$ and $ |\Gamma_t(n,f.Y_0)| \leq K \| f \|_{1,1} (1+ \log(n t)). $

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4
nodes.statement: This proof is analogous to the one of \cite[Lemma~3.3]{j1}. Item~\ref{item1:semig:estim} in Lemma~\ref{lem:semig:estim} and the fact that $ \sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor n t \rfloor -1}\frac{1}{\sqrt{k}} \leq 2 \sqrt{n t}$ prove the first result. The second part of the statement, under the assumption that $\langle \lambda_\sigma , f \rangle=0$, follows from Items~\ref{item2:semig:estim}-\ref{item2bis:semig:estim} in Lemma~\ref{lem:semig:estim} and the facts that $ \sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{\sqrt{k^3}} <\infty$ and $ \sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor n t \rfloor -1} \frac1k \leq (1+\max\{0,\log(nt)\})$.

nodes.name: Holder continuity of the local time of OBM
nodes.statement: For all $q\in (2,\infty)$, $\alpha \in (0,\frac{q-2}{2 q})$ it holds that (the pathwise continuous version of) the local time $L_\cdot(Y)$ is locally $\alpha$-H\"older continuous. In particular for all $\delta \in (-\infty,\frac12)$, $T\in [0,\infty)$ it holds that \begin{equation} \sup_{t\in [0,T]} n^{\delta} \left(L_{ t +\frac1n }(Y) - L_t(Y)\right) \convas[n\to\infty] 0.\end{equation}

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5
nodes.statement: In this proof let $T\in [0,\infty)$ and $s,t \in [0,T]$ with $s\leq t$ be fixed. Let us first note that It\^o-Tanaka formula implies that \[L_t -L_s = |Y_t|-|Y_s| -\int_s^t \mathrm{sgn}(Y_u) \sigma(Y_u) \,\mathrm{d} W_u.\] The fact that for all $a,b\in \mathbb{R}$, $p\in [1,\infty)$ it holds that $(a+b)^p \leq 2^{p-1}(|a|^p + |b|^p)$ and that $||a|-|b|| \leq |a-b|$, and Burkholder-Davis-Gundy inequality ensure that for all $q\in [2,\infty)$ there exists a constant $K_q>0$ (dependent on $q,\sigma_-$ and $\sigma_+$) such that \begin{equation} \begin{split} \mathbb{E}\!\left[|L_t -L_s|^q\right] & \leq K_q \mathbb{E}\!\left[ \left| \int_s^t \sigma^2(Y_u) \,\mathrm{d} u \right|^{\frac{q}2} \right] \leq \max{\{\sigma_-,\sigma_+\}}^q K_q (t-s)^{q/2}. \end{split} \end{equation} Finally Kolmogorov continuity theorem ensures that there exists a continuous version of the local time (that we took already) and it is locally H\"older continuous as required.
nodes.section: A.4 Local time: on time continuity and moments
nodes.statement_short: Tanaka formula and BDG give moment bounds on local-time increments; conclude with Kolmogorov's continuity theorem.

Then for all $p\in \mathbb{N}$ it hold that \begin{equation} \begin{split} & \Lm{f}{p}{x} = \int_0^1 \frac{|x|}{\sigma(x)} \frac{(1-t)^\frac{p}{2}}{\sqrt{2\pi} t^\frac32} e^{-\frac{x^2}{2 (\sigma(x))^2 t}} \mathbb{E}\!\left[ \left( L_1(Y)\right)^p f(Y_1 \sqrt{1-t})\right]\! \,\mathrm{d} t \\ & = \left(\frac{2 \sigma_-\sigma_+}{\sigma_-+\sigma_+}\right)^{\!
