nodes.name: Proof of the key Proposition 4 (Appendix C)
nodes.statement: In this section we prove Proposition~\ref{th:j2:2} which was stated in Section~\ref{sec:proof:summary}. The section is organized as follows: We split the proof of Proposition~\ref{th:j2:2} into three parts. The first part, in Section~\ref{sec:decomposition}, consists in finding the decomposition~\eqref{eq:decomposition} into a sum of martingale and a vanishing term. We deal with the vanishing term in Section~\ref{sec:th:j2:vanish}. Finally, in Section~\ref{sec:th:j2:hp}, we demonstrate that the martingale part satisfies Items~\ref{th:j2:item1:2}-\ref{th:j2:item4:2} of Proposition~\ref{th:j2:2}. In Section~\ref{sec:finite:K}, we prove that the constant $K_h^Y$ defined by~\eqref{eq:k:th} is finite. Figure~\ref{ProofMapProp} show how the results of the paper intervene in the proof of Proposition~\ref{th:j2:2}. In this section, $(Y_t)_{t\in [0,1]}$ is a standard OBM. \begin{figure}[t] \begin{figure}[omitted: a diagram of this paper's results, not reproduced here]\end{figure} \captionsetup{singlelinecheck=off} \caption[Proof Prop map]{Map of the proof of Proposition~\ref{th:j2:2}.} In the appendix we introduce many auxiliary results. This map show how they intervene in the proof of Proposition~\ref{th:j2:2} and of other results of the appendix. \end{figure} Let us recall that by assumption $\gamma >3$ and $h\in \Lg{\gamma}$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:link:theorems}, $\bfH{f}$ and $\bfH{f^2}$ are well defined and belong to $\Lgb{\gamma}$. For most of the following definitions and proof steps $\gamma\geq 0$ suffices. For the sake of precision, we specify when it does not. \subsection{The decomposition into a sum of martingale and vanishing terms} In this section we determine the terms of the decomposition in equation~\eqref{eq:decomposition} into a sum of a vanishing term $n^{1/4}\mathcal{V}^n$ and a martingale $\mathcal{M}^n$. Note that for all $n\in \mathbb{N}$, $t\in [0,1]$ : \begin{equation} \begin{split} & \varepsilon_{n,t}^{(0,h,Y)} - \langle \lambda_\sigma , \bfH h \rangle L_t(Y) = M^{n,1}_t + \mathcal{G}^n_t + \langle \lambda_\sigma , \bfH h \rangle \left( L_{\lfloor n t \rfloor/n}(Y) - L_t(Y) \right) \end{split} \end{equation} where $M^{n,1}$ and $\mathcal{G}^n$ are the processes satisfying for all $t\in [0,1]$ that \begin{equation} \begin{split} M^{n,1}_t & = \varepsilon_{n,t}^{(0,h,Y)} - \varepsilon_{n,t}^{(0,\bfH h,Y)} + \langle \lambda_\sigma , \bfH h \rangle \left( \varepsilon_{n,t}^{(0,\bfH g,Y)} - L_{\frac{\lfloor n t \rfloor}n}(Y)\right) \end{split} \end{equation} and $ \mathcal{G}^n_t = \frac1{\sqrt{n}} \sum_{k=0}^{\lfloor n t \rfloor-1} \bfG{h}( \sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k}n}) $ ($\bfG{h}$ is defined in \eqref{eq:kappa} and $g(x,y) := |y| - |x| $). We used here the abuse of notation $\varepsilon_{n,t}^{(0,\bfH h,Y)}$ and $\varepsilon_{n,t}^{(0,\bfH g,Y)}$ as in Appendix~\ref{app:prop:lmt:2}. This decomposition is not the same as the one proposed in Section~\ref{app:decomp:fake}. Indeed, Lemma~\ref{lem:holderL} suggests that $L_{\lfloor n t \rfloor/n}(Y) - L_t(Y) $ will contribute to $\mathcal{V}^n_t$, so we split into two terms the quantity $ \langle \lambda_\sigma , \bfH h \rangle \Big( \varepsilon_{n,t}^{(0,\bfH g,Y)} - L_t(Y)\Big). $ Moreover, it has been shown in Section~\ref{sec:proof:details} that $\sup_{s\in [0,t]} |\mathcal{G}^n_s|\convp[n\to\infty] 0$, but the convergence speed have not been studied. In Section~\ref{sec:decomposition} we decompose $\mathcal{G}^n_t $ into two terms, one contributing to $\mathcal{M}^n_t $ and the other to $\mathcal{V}^n_t $. More precisely, $\mathcal{G}^n= (\mathcal{G}^n - M^{n,2} ) +M^{n,2}$ where \begin{equation} \begin{split} & M^{n,2}_t = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor n t \rfloor} \sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor n^\frac14\rfloor} \left(\mathbb{E}\!\left[ \bfG{h}(\sqrt{n} Y_{(j+k)/n})| \mathcal{F}_{k/n}\right]- \mathbb{E}\!\left[ \bfG{h}(\sqrt{n} Y_{(j+k)/n})| \mathcal{F}_{(k-1)/n}\right]\right). \end{split} \end{equation} And so it holds for all $n\in \mathbb{N}$, $t\in [0,1]$ that \begin{equation} \begin{split} & \varepsilon_{n,t}^{(0,h,Y)} - \langle \lambda_\sigma , \bfH h \rangle L_t(Y) = M^{n,1}_t + M^{n,2}_t + \mathcal{G}^n_t - M^{n,2}_t + \langle \lambda_\sigma , \bfH h \rangle \left( L_{\lfloor n t \rfloor/n}(Y) - L_t(Y) \right). \end{split} \end{equation} We first show, in Lemma~\ref{lem:M:mart}, that $M^{n,1}_t$ is a good candidate for contributing to the martingale part of the decomposition. \begin{lemma} $M^{n,1}$ is a martingale with respect to the filtration $(\mathcal{F}_{\lfloor n t \rfloor/n})_{t\in [0,1]}$. \end{lemma} \begin{proof} Throughout this proof let $A^n$ and $B^n$ be the processes given by \begin{equation} A^n_t = \frac1{\sqrt{n}} \sum_{k=0}^{\lfloor n t \rfloor-1} \bfH{g}(\sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k}n}) - L_{\frac{\lfloor n t \rfloor}n}(Y) \text{ and } B^n_t = M^{n,1}_t - \langle \lambda_\sigma , \bfH h \rangle A^n_t. \end{equation} So $ B^n_t = \frac1{\sqrt{n}} \sum_{k=0}^{\lfloor n t \rfloor-1} \left( h(\sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k}{n}}, \sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k+1}{n}} ) - \bfH h( \sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k}n}) \right). $ It suffices to show the martingale property for $A^n$ and $B^n$. Let $t\in [0,1]$ be fixed. The martingale property for $A^n$ is an immediate consequence of Lemma~\ref{lem:conv:hatg}. Let us explicit the case of the process $B^n$. For all $j\in \{0,\ldots, \lfloor n t \rfloor-1\}$ it can be easily shown that \begin{equation} \begin{split} \mathbb{E}\!\left[ n^{\frac12} B^{n}_t | \mathcal{F}_{\frac j n} \right] & = \sum_{k=j}^{\lfloor n t \rfloor-1} \mathbb{E}\!\left[ h(\sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k}{n}}, \sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k+1}{n}} ) - \bfH h( \sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k}n}) | \mathcal{F}_{\frac j n} \right] + B^{n}_{\frac j n} = B^{n}_{\frac j n}. \end{split} \end{equation} because for all $k \in \{j,\ldots, \lfloor n t \rfloor-1\}$ it holds that \begin{equation} \begin{split} & \mathbb{E}\!\left[ h(\sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k}{n}}, \sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k+1}{n}} ) - \bfH h( \sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k}n}) | \mathcal{F}_{\frac j n} \right] = \mathbb{E}\!\left[ \mathbb{E}\!\left[ h(\sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k}{n}}, \sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k+1}{n}} ) - \bfH h( \sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k}n}) | \mathcal{F}_{\frac k n} \right] | \mathcal{F}_{\frac j n} \right] \\ & = \mathbb{E}\!\left[ \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} h(\sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k}{n}}, \sqrt{n} y ) q_\sigma(1/n, \sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k}{n}}, y) \,\mathrm{d} y - \bfH h( \sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k}n}) | \mathcal{F}_{\frac j n} \right] = \mathbb{E}\!\left[ 0 | \mathcal{F}_{\frac j n} \right] =0. \end{split} \end{equation} The proof is thus completed. \end{proof} Definition~\eqref{eq:W} implies that $M^{n,2}$ is a martingale as well. \begin{lemma} $M^{n,2}$ is a martingale with respect to the filtration $(\mathcal{F}_{\lfloor n t \rfloor/n})_{t\in [0,1]}$. \end{lemma} \begin{proof} Using \eqref{eq:cQ} we rewrite $M^{n,2}$ in \eqref{eq:dec:m3} as \begin{equation} \begin{split} & M^{n,2}_t = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor n t \rfloor} \sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor n^\frac14\rfloor} \left(\mathbb{E}\!\left[ \bfG{h}(\sqrt{n} Y_{(j+k)/n})| \mathcal{F}_{k/n}\right]- \mathbb{E}\!\left[ \bfG{h}(\sqrt{n} Y_{(j+k)/n})| \mathcal{F}_{(k-1)/n}\right]\right) \end{split} \end{equation} which shows that $M^{n,2}$ is a martingale with respect to the filtration $(\mathcal{F}_{\lfloor n t \rfloor/n})_{t\in [0,1]}$. \end{proof} Lemma~\ref{lem:M:mart} and Lemma~\ref{lem:M:mart:2} identify the $(\mathcal{F}_{\lfloor n t \rfloor/n})_{t\geq 0}$-martingale $\mathcal{M}^n$ and also the candidate to be the vanishing term with rate of order at least $1/4$ (denoted by $\mathcal{V}^n$): \begin{equation} \begin{split} &\mathcal{M}^n_t := n^{1/4} \left( M^{n,1}_t + M^{n,2}_t \right) \ \text{and\/} \ \\ & \mathcal{V}^n_t := \mathcal{G}^n_t - M^{n,2}_t + \langle \lambda_\sigma , \bfH h \rangle \left( L_{\frac{\lfloor n t \rfloor}n}(Y) - L_t(Y) \right). \end{split} \end{equation} To prove Proposition~\ref{th:j2:2}, it remains to show that $\sup_{t\in [0,1]} n^{1/4} |\mathcal{V}^n_t| \convp[n\to\infty] 0$ and that $\mathcal{M}^n_\cdot$ satisfies Items~\ref{th:j2:item1:2}-\ref{th:j2:item4:2}. This is done in Section~\ref{sec:th:j2:vanish} and Section~\ref{sec:th:j2:hp}. \subsection{Finiteness of the variance} In this section we provide the proof of the finiteness of the constant $K_h^Y$ defined by~\eqref{eq:k:th}. The proof is actually contained in Section~\ref{sec:th:j2:hp}, but we choose to show it separately. Instead, we do not prove separately non-negativity of the constant. The expression of $K_h^Y$ depends on a function, $\mathcal{P}_h^Y$ which is here expressed with the use of some auxiliary functions. We first introduce and prove some properties of these functions that are also used to provide an alternative expression for $M^{n,2}$. For all $i,j\in \{0,1\}$, $\eta\in [0,\infty)$ let \begin{equation} \mathcal{Q}^{(\eta)}_{n, i , j} := \sum_{k=i}^{\lfloor n^{\eta}\rfloor + j } Q^\sigma_k \bfG{h} \quad \text{ and } \quad \mathcal{Q}_{n, i , j}:=\mathcal{Q}^{(\frac14)}_{n, i , j} \end{equation} where $Q^\sigma$ is the semigroup of the OBM given in~\eqref{eq:def:semig}. These quantities may be seen as the aggregated action of the semigroup on the function $\bfG{h}$ up to different times of order $n^\eta$. We reduce to consider only some precise values of $\eta$, in particular $\eta=1/4$ and $\eta=3/4$. (The results in the next sections would restrict the parameter choices, and these precise choices would respect the restrictions.) Note that the process $M^{n,2}$ satisfy for all $t\in [0,1]$ that \begin{equation} M^{n,2}_t = \frac1{\sqrt{n}} \sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor n t \rfloor} \left(\mathcal{Q}_{n,0,0}(\sqrt{n} Y_{\frac k n}) - \mathcal{Q}_{n,1,1}(\sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k-1}{n}})\right). \end{equation} The following lemma relates the sequence $(\mathcal{Q}_{m,0,0})_{m\in \mathbb{N}}$ with $\mathcal{P}_{h}^{Y} $ in~\eqref{eq:cQ:limit} (with $\beta=0$ because $Y$ is an OBM). \begin{lemma} Pointwise $\lim_{m\to\infty} \mathcal{Q}_{m,0,0} = \mathcal{P}_{h}^{Y} $. Moreover, $x\mapsto \mathcal{P}_{h}^{Y}(x)/(1+|x|) $ is bounded. \end{lemma} \begin{proof} Let $x\in \mathbb{R}$. Note that $\mathcal{P}_{h}^{Y}$ in~\eqref{eq:cQ:limit} for OBM rewrites as \[ \mathcal{P}_{h}^{Y}(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty } \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} p_X(k, x, y) \bfG{h}(y) \,\mathrm{d} y = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty } Q^\sigma_k \bfG{h}(x) . \] Hence there exists a positive constant $K\in (0,\infty)$ such that \[ \left| \mathcal{Q}_{m,0,0}(x) - \mathcal{P}_{h}^{Y}(x) \right| \leq \sum_{k=\lfloor m^{1/4}\rfloor+1}^{\infty} \left| Q^\sigma_k \bfG{h}(x) \right| \leq K (1+|x|) \sum_{k=\lfloor m^{1/4}\rfloor+1}^{\infty} k^{-3/2} \] where the last inequality follows from Item~\ref{item2:semig:estim} in Lemma~\ref{lem:semig:estim} and Lemma~\ref{lem:prop:kappa}. Indeed, Lemma~\ref{lem:prop:kappa} establishes that $\bfG{h}\in \Lgb{\gamma}$ for all $\gamma>0$ (in particular for $\gamma =1$ and $\gamma =2$). The fact that $\sum_{k=\lfloor m^{1/4}\rfloor+1}^{\infty} k^{-3/2}$ converges to $0$ as $m\to\infty$ proves the first statement. Similarly, Item~\ref{item2:semig:estim} in Lemma~\ref{lem:semig:estim} proves that there exist constants $K,K'\in (0,+\infty)$ such that $ |\mathcal{P}_{h}^{Y}(x)| \leq |\bfG{h}(x)| + K (1+|x|) \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} k^{-3/2} \leq K' (1+|x|). $ The proof is thus completed. \end{proof} We are now ready to prove the finiteness of $K_h^Y$. \begin{lemma} The quantity $K_h^Y$ defined by~\eqref{eq:k:th} is a finite constant. \end{lemma} \begin{proof} Let us recall that \begin{equation} {\scriptsize \begin{split} & K_h^Y = \langle \mu_Y , \bfH{h^2} + 2 \bfH{h,\mathcal{P}_{h}^Y} \rangle + \frac{ 2 \sigma_- \sigma_+}{\sigma_-+\sigma_+} \frac{8}{3 \sqrt{2\pi}} (\langle \mu_Y , \bfH{h} \rangle)^2 \\ & \quad - 2 \sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}} \frac{ 2 \sigma_- \sigma_+}{\sigma_-+\sigma_+} \langle \mu_Y , \bfH{h} \rangle \int_{-\infty}^\infty \left( e^{-\frac{y^2}{2(\sigma(y))^2}} -\sqrt{2\pi} \frac{|y|}{\sigma(y)} \Phi\left(-\frac{|y|}{\sigma(y)}\right)\right) \mathcal{P}_{h}^Y(y) \mu_Y(\!\,\mathrm{d} y) \\ & \quad - 2 \langle \mu_Y , \bfH{h} \rangle \left(\frac{ 2 \sigma_- \sigma_+}{\sigma_-+\sigma_+}\right)^{\!2} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \int_0^1 \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \tfrac{|x| e^{-\frac{x^2}{2(\sigma(x))^2}} \Phi\left(-\frac{|y|}{\sigma(y)}\right)}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma(x)} \sqrt{\frac{1}t-1} h(x \sqrt{t}, y \sqrt{1-t}) \mu_Y(\!\,\mathrm{d} y) \,\mathrm{d} t \mu_Y(\!\,\mathrm{d} x), \end{split} }\end{equation} where $\Phi$ is the cumulative distribution function oh a standard Gaussian random variable, and $\mathcal{P}_{h}^Y$ has been studied in Lemma~\ref{lem:cQ:conv}. Note that $\lambda$-integrability is equivalent to $\mu_Y$-integrability. Therefore if $f\in \Lgb{0}$ then $f$ is $\lambda$-integrable and $\langle \mu_Y , f \rangle$ is finite. Since $\gamma\geq 1$, Lemma~\ref{lem:link:theorems} ensures that $f=\bfH{h},\bfH{h^2}\in \Lgb{1}$ which is contained in $\Lgb{0}$ by Remark~\ref{rem:spaces:relation}. And also, in Lemma~\ref{lem:cQ:conv} it has been shown that $|\mathcal{P}_{h}^Y (y)| \leq K (1+|y|)$ for some constant $K\in (0,\infty)$, so Lemma~\ref{lem:link:theorems} ensures that $x\mapsto \bfH{h, \mathcal{P}_{h}^Y}(x)/(1+|x|)$ belongs to $\Lgb{\gamma}$. Since $\gamma\geq 1$, we deduce that $\bfH{h, \mathcal{P}_{h}^Y}$ is $\lambda$-integrable. Let us now consider the second last integral appearing in the expression of $K_h^Y$. Since $ 1- \sqrt{2\pi} \frac{|y|}{\sigma(y)} \Phi\left(-\frac{|y|}{\sigma(y)}\right) e^{\frac{y^2}{2(\sigma(y))^2}} \in [0,1]$ for all $y\in \mathbb{R}$, we reduce to check that $e^{-y^2/2} \mathcal{P}_{h}^Y(\sigma(y)y)$ is $\lambda$-integrable. And this is the case because $e^{-y^2/2} \mathcal{P}_{h}^Y(\sigma(y)y) \leq K (1+|y|) e^{-y^2/2}$. For the last integral we use that $h\in \Lg{\gamma}$ and exploit the inequality $h(x,y) \leq \bar{h}(x) e^{a|y-x|} \leq K e^{a|y-x|}$ for some constant $a,K\in (0,\infty)$. Then we deal with $\int_0^1 \sqrt{\frac1t -1} e^{a|\sqrt t x -\sqrt{1-t}y|} \,\mathrm{d} t \leq e^{a|x|+a|y|} \int_0^1 \sqrt{\frac1t -1} \,\mathrm{d} t = e^{a|x|+a|y|} \frac{\pi}2.$ By observing that $ x\mapsto e^{a|x|} \tfrac{ |x| e^{-\frac{x^2}{2(\sigma(x))^2}} }{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma(x)} $ and $y \mapsto e^{a|y|}\Phi\left(-\frac{|y|}{\sigma(y)}\right)$ are $\lambda$-integrable, we complete the proof. \end{proof} To conclude the section we study some properties of the sequences $\mathcal{Q}_{n,i,j}$ which intervene in the next sections. The following facts are consequences of Lemma~\ref{lem:prop:kappa}, Lemma~\ref{lem:semig:estim} (which requires $\gamma \geq 2$), and the fact that $\sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac1k \leq 2 \log(n)$ for $n \geq 2$. For every $\zeta\in [0,\gamma-1]$ and every $\eta \in (0,1)$, the fact that $\langle \lambda_\sigma , \bfG{h} \rangle=0$ and Item~\ref{item2bis:semig:estim} in Lemma~\ref{lem:semig:estim} imply that for all $x\in \mathbb{R}$ it holds that \begin{equation} \begin{split} |Q^\sigma_{n^{\eta}+1} \bfG{h} (x) | & \leq \left(1+\tfrac{|\sigma_-\sigma_+|}{\sigma_-+\sigma_+}\right) K_\zeta n^{-\eta} \left(\tfrac1{1+|x n^{-\eta/2}/\sigma(x)|^\zeta} + \tfrac1{1+(|x|/\sigma(x))^\zeta}\right) \end{split} \end{equation} and \begin{equation} |\mathcal{Q}^{(\eta)}_{n,1,0}(x)|+|\mathcal{Q}^{(\eta)}_{n,1,1}(x)| \leq 2 K_\zeta \log(n) \left(\tfrac1{1+|x n^{-{\eta}/2}/\sigma(x)|^\zeta} + \tfrac1{1+|x/\sigma(x)|^\zeta}\right) \end{equation} for some $K_\zeta\in (0,\infty)$ depending also on $\eta$. Hence \eqref{eq:cQ:prop2} with $\zeta=0$ and Item~\ref{item2:semig:estim} in Lemma~\ref{lem:semig:estim} imply that for all $x\in \mathbb{R}$ it holds that \begin{equation} |\mathcal{Q}^{(\eta)}_{n,1,0}(x)|+|\mathcal{Q}^{(\eta)}_{n,1,1}(x)| \leq 2 K \min{\{ \log(n) ,(1+|x|) \}}, \end{equation} for some constant $K\in (0,\infty)$ depending on $\eta \in (0,1)$. This and the fact that $\bfG{h}$ is bounded ensures that for some positive constant $K\in (0,\infty)$ it holds that $ |\mathcal{Q}^{(\eta)}_{n,0,0}(x)|+|\mathcal{Q}^{(\eta)}_{n,0,1}(x)| \leq 2 |\bfG{h}(x)| + |\mathcal{Q}^{(\eta)}_{n,1,0}(x)|+|\mathcal{Q}^{(\eta)}_{n,1,1}(x)| \leq 2 K (\log(n) +1) $ and \begin{equation} |\mathcal{Q}^{(\eta)}_{n,0,0}(x)|+|\mathcal{Q}^{(\eta)}_{n,0,1}(x)| + |\mathcal{Q}^{(\eta)}_{n,1,0}(x)|+|\mathcal{Q}^{(\eta)}_{n,1,1}(x)| \leq 2 K ( \log(n) +1). \end{equation} \subsection{Dealing with the vanishing term} We now prove that $\mathcal{V}^n$ defined in \eqref{eq:mv}, satisfies that $\sup_{t\in [0,1]} n^{1/4} |\mathcal{V}^n_t| \convp[n\to\infty] 0$. This is a consequence of~Lemma~\ref{lem:holderL} and Lemma~\ref{lem:j1:5.2}. \begin{lemma} Let $h\in \Lg{3}$. Then $\sup_{s\in [0,1]} n^{1/4} |\mathcal{G}^n_s-M^{n,2}_s| \convp[n\to\infty] 0$. \end{lemma} \begin{proof} Using \eqref{eq:cQ} we rewrite $M^{n,2}$ in~\eqref{eq:W} as~\eqref{eq:dec:m3} and also as \begin{equation} \begin{split} & M^{n,2}_t = \mathcal{G}^n_t - \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \left( \mathcal{Q}_{n,0,0}(\sqrt{n} Y_0) - \mathcal{Q}_{n,0,0}(\sqrt{n} Y_{\lfloor n t\rfloor/n}) \right) - \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor n t \rfloor -1} Q^\sigma_{\lfloor n^\frac14\rfloor +1} \bfG{h} (\sqrt n Y_{j/n}). \end{split} \end{equation} Let \begin{equation}{m^{n}_t := \mathcal{G}^n_t - \frac1{\sqrt{n}} \left( \mathcal{Q}^{(3/4)}_{n,0,0}(\sqrt{n} Y_0) - \mathcal{Q}^{(3/4)}_{n,0,0}(\sqrt{n} Y_{\lfloor n t\rfloor/n}) \right) - \frac1{\sqrt{n}} \sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor n t \rfloor -1} Q^\sigma_{\lfloor n^\frac34\rfloor +1} \bfG{h} (\sqrt n Y_{j/n}). } \end{equation} By analogy, $m^n_t$ has an expression as~\eqref{eq:W} and so it is clear that $m^n$ is a martingale with respect to the filtration $(\mathcal{F}_{\lfloor n t \rfloor/n})_{t\in [0,1]}$. Therefore $n^{1/4} (M^{n,2}_t-m^n_t)$ as well. Let us denote by $D^n_t := n^{1/4} (\mathcal{G}^n_t - M^{n,2}_t)$ and $d^n_t := n^{1/4} (\mathcal{G}^n_t - m^n_t)$. Then $D^n-d^n = n^{1/4} (m^n-M^{n,2})$ is a martingale with respect to the filtration $(\mathcal{F}_{\lfloor n t \rfloor/n})_{t\in [0,1]}$. In this notation, the goal is to prove $\sup_{s\in [0,1]} |D^n_s|\convp[n\to\infty] 0$. {\em First step:\/} For every $t\in [0,1]$, let us show that $\lim_{n\to\infty} \mathbb{E}\!\left[( D^n_t-d^n_t)^2\right]=0$ by demonstrating the stronger fact that $\lim_{n\to\infty} \mathbb{E}\!\left[(D_t^n)^2+(d_t^n)^2\right]=0$.\\ Let $t\in [0,1]$ and $\eta \in \left\{ \frac14, \frac34 \right\}$ be fixed. Inequality \eqref{eq:cQ:prop4} implies for all $\omega\in \Omega$ that \begin{equation} \sup_{s\in [0,1]} n^{-\frac14} \left( \mathcal{Q}^{(\eta)}_{n,0,0}(\sqrt{n} Y_0(\omega)) - \mathcal{Q}^{(\eta)}_{n,0,0}(\sqrt{n} Y_{\lfloor n s\rfloor/n}(\omega)) \right) \xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{} 0, \end{equation} hence it holds also that $ \lim_{n\to\infty} \mathbb{E}\!\left[n^{-1/2} \left( \mathcal{Q}^{(\eta)}_{n,0,0}(\sqrt{n} Y_0) - \mathcal{Q}^{(\eta)}_{n,0,0}(\sqrt{n} Y_{\lfloor n t\rfloor/n}) \right)^2 \right]=0. $ Next observe that, since $\lambda_\sigma$ is a stationary measure, the sequences of functions $g_n^{(\eta)} := n^{1/4} Q^\sigma_{\lfloor n^{\eta}\rfloor +1} \bfG{h} $, $\eta \in \{\tfrac14,\tfrac34\}$ satisfy that $\langle \lambda_\sigma , g_n^{(\eta)} \rangle = n^{1/4} \langle \lambda_\sigma , \bfG{h} \rangle$ which is equal to 0 by Lemma~\ref{lem:prop:kappa}. This and inequality \eqref{eq:cQ:prop1} (with $\zeta=2$ since $h\in \Lg{\zeta+1}$) ensure that \eqref{eq:j1:4.2} holds. (A sufficient condition is $\eta \geq 1/4$.)\\ Hence, Lemma~\ref{lem:j1:4.2} shows that $ \lim_{n\to\infty} \mathbb{E}\!\left[ n^{-1/2} \left(\sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor n t \rfloor -1} Q^\sigma_{\lfloor n^{\eta}\rfloor +1} \bfG{h} (\sqrt n Y_{{j}/{n}})\right)^2\right]=0. $ {\em Second step:\/} It holds that $\sup_{s\in [0,1]} |D^n_s - d_s^n|\convp[n\to\infty] 0$.\\ This follows from \cite[Proposition~1.2]{aldous89} as a consequence of the previous step and the martingale property of $D^n - d^n$. {\em Third step:\/} It holds that $\sup_{s\in [0,1]} |d_s^n| \convp[n\to\infty] 0$. This follows from~\eqref{lem:j1:5.2.eq} and from applying Proposition~\ref{prop:th4.1a:j1} to the sequence $g_n:= n^{1/4} Q^\sigma_{\lfloor n^\frac34\rfloor +1} \bfG{h} $. (Here taking $n^{1/4} Q^\sigma_{\lfloor n^{\eta} \rfloor +1} \bfG{h}$ with $\eta>1/2$ would be sufficient.) The assumptions are indeed satisfied: $\lim_{n\to\infty} \|g_n\|_{1} =0$ by Item~\ref{item1:semig:estim} in Lemma~\ref{lem:semig:estim} and in the first step we have proven that $g_n$ satisfies \eqref{eq:j1:4.2} and in particular $\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{g_n(\sqrt{n}x)}{\sqrt{n}}=0$. Combining the two last steps yields the conclusion. \end{proof} \subsection{Dealing with the martingale term} In this section we complete the proof of Proposition~\ref{th:j2:2}. The arguments are sometimes sketched because analogous to the ones in \cite[Section~6]{j1}. Let $\gamma >3$ and $h\in \Lg{\gamma}$ be fixed. By Definition~\ref{def:integral:gamma} of $\Lg{\gamma}$ there exist a non-negative function $\bar h \in \Lgb{\gamma}$ and a constant $a\in[0,\infty)$ such that $|h(x,y)| \leq \bar h(x) e^{a |y-x|}$. In this section $\bar h$ and $a$ are fixed. \\ Let us also recall some notation: let $\bfH{}$ the functional in \eqref{eq:muX}, $Q^\sigma$ the semigroup in~\eqref{eq:def:semig}, $\bfG{h}$ in~\eqref{eq:kappa}, $\mathcal{Q}$ in~\eqref{eq:cQ} and its limit $\mathcal{P}_{h}^{Y}$ in~\eqref{eq:cQ:limit} (see Lemma~\ref{lem:cQ:conv}), and $\mathbb{L}$ in~\eqref{function:G}. For all $n\in \mathbb{N}$ the $(\mathcal{F}_{\lfloor n t\rfloor /n})_{t\in [0,1]}$-martingale $\mathcal{M}^n$ in \eqref{eq:mv} rewrites as $ { \mathcal{M}^n_t = \sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor n t \rfloor} \chi^n_k} $ where \begin{equation} \begin{split} \chi^n_k := n^{-\frac14} & \left( h(\sqrt{n} Y_{(k-1)/n}, \sqrt{n} Y_{k/n} ) - \langle \lambda_\sigma , \bfH h \rangle \, \sqrt{n}(L_{k/n}(Y) - L_{(k-1)/n}(Y)) \right) \\ + \, & n^{-\frac14} \left(\mathcal{Q}_{n,0,0}(\sqrt{n} Y_{k/n}) - \mathcal{Q}_{n,0,1}(\sqrt{n} Y_{(k-1)/n}) \right)\!. \end{split} \end{equation} Now it remains to prove Items~\ref{th:j2:item1:2}-\ref{th:j2:item4:2} in Proposition~\ref{th:j2:2}. \subsubsection{Proof of Item~\ref{th:j2:item1:2} in Proposition~\ref{th:j2:2} } It follows from scaling property \eqref{Yscaling} and Lemma~\ref{lem:conv:hatg}. For all $n\in \mathbb{N}$, $k\in \{1, \ldots, \lfloor n \rfloor \}$, the scaling property \eqref{Yscaling}, Lemma~\ref{lem:conv:hatg} and \eqref{eq:cQ} ensure that \begin{equation} \begin{split} & \mathbb{E}\!\left[ \chi_k^n | \mathcal{F}_{(k-1)/n}\right] \\ & = n^{-\frac14} \left( \bfG{h}(\sqrt{n} Y_{(k-1)/n}) + \int_{-\infty}^\infty \mathcal{Q}_{n,0,0}(y) q_\sigma(1, \sqrt{n} Y_{(k-1)/n}, y) \,\mathrm{d} y - \mathcal{Q}_{n,0,1}(\sqrt{n} Y_{(k-1)/n})\right) \\ & = n^{-\frac14} \left(Q^\sigma_1 \mathcal{Q}_{n,0,0}(\sqrt{n} Y_{(k-1)/n}) - \mathcal{Q}_{n,1,1}(\sqrt{n} Y_{(k-1)/n})\right)=0. \end{split} \end{equation} \subsubsection{Proof of Item~\ref{th:j2:item2:2} in Proposition~\ref{th:j2:2}} Let $t\in [0,1]$ be fixed. {\it First step:} It can be easily shown that \begin{equation} \begin{split} & \sqrt n \mathbb{E}\!\left[ (\chi_k^n)^2 | \mathcal{F}_{(k-1)/n}\right] \\ & = f_{n}(\sqrt{n} Y_{(k-1)/n}) + (\langle \lambda_\sigma , \bfH h \rangle)^2 \Lm{1}{2}{\sqrt{n} Y_{(k-1)/n}} - 2 \langle \lambda_\sigma , \bfH h \rangle h_n(\sqrt{n} Y_{(k-1)/n}) \end{split} \end{equation} where $f_n$ and $h_n$ are given by $ f_n(x) := \bfH {h^2}(x) + 2 \bfH{h, \mathcal{Q}_{n,0,0}} (x) + g_n(x) $ and $ h_n(x):= \Lm{h(x, \cdot)}{1}{x} + \Lm{\mathcal{Q}_{n,0,0}}{1}{x}, $ with $ g_n(x):=Q^\sigma_1\left( ( \mathcal{Q}_{n,0,0} )^2 \right) (x) - \left(\mathcal{Q}_{n,0,1}(x)\right)^2 $. In fact first note that, by \eqref{function:G:equal}, for all $k =1, \ldots, {\lfloor n t \rfloor}$ it holds that \begin{equation} h_n(\sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k-1}{n}})= \sqrt{n} \mathbb{E}\Big[ (h(\sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k-1}{n}}, \sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k}{n}}) + \mathcal{Q}_{n,0,0}(\sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k}{n}}) ) (L_{\frac{k}{n}}(Y) - L_{\frac{k-1}n}(Y)) | \mathcal{F}_{\frac{k-1}n}\Big] . \end{equation} Let us now consider $f_n$. Clearly $f_n$ have to be the sum of all remaining terms and it has to have the desired form. This follows from the fact that the scaling property~\eqref{Yscaling} and equation~\eqref{eq:cQ} ensure that $\mathbb{E}\Big[ (\mathcal{Q}_{n,0,0}(\sqrt{n} Y_{k/n}))^2 | \mathcal{F}_{(k-1)/n}\Big] = Q^\sigma_1 ( (\mathcal{Q}_{n,0,0}(\sqrt{n} Y_{k/n}))^2 ). $ but also $\mathbb{E}\Big[ \mathcal{Q}_{n,0,0}(\sqrt{n} Y_{k/n}) | \mathcal{F}_{(k-1)/n}\Big] = \mathcal{Q}_{n,1,1}(\sqrt n Y_{(k-1)/n})$ which, together with the definition of $\bfG{h}$ in \eqref{eq:kappa}, \eqref{function:G:equal}, and the fact that $ \mathcal{Q}_{n,1,1}(\sqrt{n} Y_{(k-1)/n}) = \mathcal{Q}_{n,0,1}(\sqrt{n} Y_{(k-1)/n}) - \bfG{h}(\sqrt{n} Y_{(k-1)/n}) $ show that $\mathcal{Q}_{n,0,1}(\sqrt{n} Y_{(k-1)/n})$ can be rewritten as \begin{equation} \begin{split} \mathcal{Q}_{n,0,1}(\sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k-1}{n}}) = \mathbb{E}\Big[ h(\sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k-1}n}, \sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k}{n}}) + \mathcal{Q}_{n,0,0}(\sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k}n}) -\langle \lambda_\sigma , \bfH h \rangle \sqrt{n} ( L_{\frac{k}n}(Y) - L_{\frac{k-1}n}(Y) ) | \mathcal{F}_{\frac{k-1}n}\Big] . \end{split} \end{equation} The proof of the first step is thus completed. {\it Second step:} It follows from applying Proposition~\ref{prop:th4.1b:j1} to the constant sequence of functions $\Lm{1}{2}{\cdot}$ that $ \frac1{\sqrt n} \sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor n t \rfloor} \Lm{1}{2}{\sqrt{n} Y_{(k-1)/n}} \convp[n\to\infty] \frac{2 \sigma_- \sigma_+}{\sigma_-+\sigma_+} \frac{8}{3 \sqrt{2 \pi}} L_t(Y). $ The fact that the assumptions of the proposition (i.e.~$\Lm{1}{2}{\cdot} \in \Lgb{2}$) are satisfied and $\langle \lambda_\sigma , \Lm{1}{2}{\cdot} \rangle = \frac{2 \sigma_- \sigma_+}{\sigma_-+\sigma_+} \frac{8}{3 \sqrt{2 \pi}}$ follows from the fact that $\mathbb{E}\!\left[ \left( L_1(W)\right)^2\right]= 1$ and Lemma~\ref{lem:prop:G}. In the two final steps, we want to apply Proposition~\ref{prop:th4.1b:j1} to the sequences $f_n$ and $h_n$. {\em Third step:\/} We show that $ \frac1{\sqrt n} \sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor n t \rfloor} f_n (\sqrt{n} Y_{(k-1)/n}) \convp[n\to\infty] \langle \lambda_\sigma , \bfH {h^2} + 2 \bfH{h, \mathcal{P}_{h}^{Y} } \rangle L_t(Y). $ applying Proposition~\ref{prop:th4.1b:j1}. To do so we check that the sequence $f_n$ satisfies \eqref{eq:j1:4.2} and that $ \lim_{n\to\infty}\langle \lambda_\sigma , f_n \rangle=\langle \lambda_\sigma , \bfH {h^2} + 2 \bfH{h, \mathcal{P}_{h}^{Y} } \rangle $. The fact that $\lim_{n\to\infty} \langle \lambda_\sigma , g_n \rangle$=0 follows from the fact that $\lambda_\sigma$ is a stationary measure, inequality~\eqref{eq:cQ:prop1} with $\zeta=\gamma-1 >2$, and inequality~\eqref{eq:cQ:prop2}. Note that $ \bfH{h, \mathcal{Q}_{n,0,0}}= \bfH{h, \bfG{h}}+\bfH{h, \mathcal{Q}_{n,1,0}}. $ Lemma~\ref{lem:prop:kappa} (in particular the fact that $\bfG{h}$ is bounded) ensures that there exists a constant $K\in (0,\infty)$ such that $ |\bfH{h, \bfG{h}}(x)| \leq K \bar h(x) . $ By \eqref{eq:cQ:prop3} there exists constants $K_1,K_2\in (0,\infty)$ (all depending on $\sigma_\pm$ and $K_2$ depending also on the constant $a\in [0,\infty)$) such that \begin{equation} \begin{split} |\bfH{h, \mathcal{Q}_{n,1,0}}(x)| & \leq K_1 \bar h(x) \left( \int_{-\infty}^\infty (1+|x| \ind{[-x,x]}(y)+ |y| \ind{\mathbb{R}\setminus[-x,x]}(y)) e^{a |y-x|} q_\sigma (1,x,y) \,\mathrm{d} y \right) \\ & \leq K_2 \bar h(x) (1+|x|). \end{split} \end{equation} The fact that $h\in \Lg{\gamma}\subseteq \Lg{2}$ ensures that $\bar h \in \Lgb{1}$ (by Lemma~\ref{lem:link:theorems}) and so $\bfH{h, \mathcal{Q}_{n,0,0}} \in \mathcal{L}^1$. Hence, dominated convergence and Lemma~\ref{lem:cQ:conv} show that $ \lim_{n\to\infty}\langle \lambda_\sigma , f_n \rangle=\langle \lambda_\sigma , \bfH {h^2} + 2 \bfH{h, \mathcal{P}_{h}^{Y} } \rangle $. Let us now show that $f_n$ satisfies equation \eqref{eq:j1:4.2}. By~Lemma~\ref{lem:link:theorems}, $\bfH {h^2} \in \Lgb{2}$. \\ Let us explore the contribution to \eqref{eq:j1:4.2} of the other parts of $f_n$. Let us first consider $ \bfH{h, \mathcal{Q}_{n,0,0}}= \bfH{h, \bfG{h}}+\bfH{h, \mathcal{Q}_{n,1,0}}. $ Above we saw that $|\bfH{h, \bfG{h}}|\leq K\bar h$ with $K$ non negative constant. Cauchy-Schwarz inequality implies that \begin{equation} ( \bfH{h, \mathcal{Q}_{n,1,0}}(x) )^2 \leq \int_{-\infty}^\infty h(x,y)^2 q_\sigma (1,x,y) \,\mathrm{d} y \int_{-\infty}^\infty (\mathcal{Q}_{n,1,0}(y))^2 q_\sigma (1,x,y) \,\mathrm{d} y. \end{equation} It can be easily shown that the first factor is uniformly bounded by a finite constant. And by \eqref{eq:cQ:prop2} (taking $\zeta = \gamma-1>2$) there exist constants $K_1,K_2\in (0,\infty)$ such that \begin{equation} \begin{split} Q^\sigma_1 \left( (\mathcal{Q}_{n,1,0})^2 \right) & = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} (\mathcal{Q}_{n,1,0}(y))^2 q_\sigma (1,x,y) \,\mathrm{d} y \\ & \leq K_1 \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{(\log n)^2 q_\sigma (1,x,y)}{(1+|y n^{-\frac18}/\sigma(y)|^{\gamma-1})^2} \,\mathrm{d} y \leq \frac{ K_2 (\log (n))^2}{1+|x n^{-\frac18}/\sigma(x)|^{2(\gamma-1)}}. \end{split} \end{equation} The last inequality are consequences of the upper bound for the transition density of OBM $ q_\sigma(1,x,y) \leq \frac{\left(1+\left|\frac{\sigma_--\sigma_+}{\sigma_-+\sigma_+}\right|\right)}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma(y)} e^{-\frac12(\frac{y}{\sigma(y)}-\frac{x}{\sigma(x)})^2} $ and of \cite[Lemma~3.2]{j1} (or some computations). Therefore $ \bfH{h, \mathcal{Q}_{n,0,0}}(x) \leq K \left(\bar h(x) + \frac{ \log (n)}{1+|x n^{-\frac18}/\sigma(x)|^{\gamma-1}} \right)\!.$ Finally we consider the auxiliary function $g_n$: note that $ |g_n|(x) \leq Q^\sigma_1 ( 2 (\mathcal{Q}_{n,0,0})^2 + 2 (\bfG{h})^2)(x) + 2 (\mathcal{Q}_{n,1,1}(x))^2 + 2(\bfG{h}(x))^2. $ Inequality~\eqref{eq:cQ:prop2} and inequality~\eqref{eq:recicle} imply that $Q^\sigma_1 \left( (\mathcal{Q}_{n,0,0})^2 \right) (x)+ (\mathcal{Q}_{n,1,1}(x))^2 \leq \frac{ K (\log (n))^2}{1+|x n^{-\frac18}/\sigma(x)|^{2(\gamma-1)}}$ for some non negative constant $K$. Lemma~\ref{lem:prop:kappa}, the fact that $\gamma \geq 2$ and Item~\ref{item2bis:semig:estim} of Lemma~\ref{lem:semig:estim} yields $(\bfG{h})^2\leq K \bfG{h}$ and $ Q^\sigma_1 \left((\bfG{h})^2\right) (x) \leq K (e^{-x^2/2} + \frac{1}{1+({|x|}/{\sigma(x)})^\gamma}) $ for some non-negative constant $K$. Combining all terms yields that $f_n$ satisfies~\eqref{eq:j1:4.2}. (Here we used the fact that $\gamma \geq 3$ and $\eta=1/4<1/3$ in the definition of $\mathcal{Q}$.) {\em Fourth step:\/} We show that $ \frac1{\sqrt n} \sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor n t \rfloor} h_n(\sqrt{n} Y_{(k-1)/n}) \convp[n\to\infty] c_h L_t(Y) $ applying Proposition~\ref{prop:th4.1b:j1}, where $ 2 \langle \lambda_\sigma , \bfH h \rangle c_h:= - K_h + \langle \lambda_\sigma , \bfH {h^2} + 2 \bfH{h,\mathcal{P}_{h}^{Y} } \rangle + \frac{ 2 \sigma_- \sigma_+}{\sigma_-+\sigma_+} \frac{8}{3 \sqrt{2\pi}} (\langle \lambda_\sigma , \bfH h \rangle)^2 $. To do so we check that the sequence $h_n$ satisfies \eqref{eq:j1:4.2} and that $ \lim_{n\to\infty} \langle \lambda_\sigma , h_n \rangle=c_h $. Inequality~\eqref{eq:cQ:prop3}, the fact that $\bfG{h}$ is bounded (see Lemma~\ref{lem:prop:kappa}), the fact that \begin{equation} \mathbb{E}\!\left[ L_1(W) (1 + |W_1|+ e^{a \sigma(W_1) |W_1|} \ind{\{\sigma(W_1)\in \mathbb{R}\}}) \right]<\infty \end{equation} (see the joint density of BM and its local time~\eqref{eq:BMl}), boundedness of $\bar h$, and the change of variable $s= \frac{x^2}{ (\sigma(x))^2 t}$ show that there exists $K\in (0,\infty)$ such that \begin{equation} \begin{split} & |\Lm{h(x,\cdot)}{1}{x}| + |\Lm{\mathcal{Q}_{n,0,0}}{1}{x}| \leq 2 K |x| e^{-\frac{x^2}{(\sigma(x))^2}} \in \mathcal{L}^1. \end{split} \end{equation} Hence dominated convergence, and Lemma~\ref{lem:cQ:conv} demonstrates that $\lim_{n\to\infty} \langle \lambda_\sigma , \Lm{\mathcal{Q}_{n,0,0}}{1}{\cdot} \rangle = \langle \lambda_\sigma , \Lm{ \mathcal{P}_{h}^{Y} }{1}{\cdot} \rangle$. Moreover the latter inequalities ensure also that $h_n$ satisfy \eqref{eq:j1:4.2}. Lemma~\ref{lem:prop:G} allows us to rewrite $c_h:= \langle \lambda_\sigma , \Lm{ h(\cdot,) }{1}{\cdot} \rangle + \langle \lambda_\sigma , \Lm{ \mathcal{P}_{h}^{Y} }{1}{\cdot} \rangle$ as \begin{equation}\begin{split} & c_h = \sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}} \frac{(\sigma_- + \sigma_+)}{2\sigma_-\sigma_+} \int_0^1 \sqrt{\frac{1}t-1} \int_{-\infty}^\infty \int_0^\infty \rho_1^\sigma(y,\ell) \ell \mathcal{P}_{h}^{Y} (y \sqrt{1-t}) \,\mathrm{d} \ell \,\mathrm{d} y \,\mathrm{d} t \\ & \qquad + \int_{-\infty}^\infty \int_0^1 \int_{-\infty}^\infty \int_0^\infty \frac{|x| e^{-\frac{x^2}{2 (\sigma(x))^2}}}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma(x)} \sqrt{\frac{1}t-1} \rho_1^\sigma(y,\ell) \ell h(x \sqrt{t},y \sqrt{1-t}) \,\mathrm{d} \ell \,\mathrm{d} y \,\mathrm{d} t \lambda_\sigma(\!\,\mathrm{d} x) \end{split}\end{equation} where $\rho_1^\sigma$ is the joint density of a standard OBM and its local time at time $1$ (given in \eqref{eq:OBMl}). This expression can be easily checked to be the desired expression for $c_h$. \subsubsection{Proof of Item~\ref{th:j2:item3:2} in Proposition~\ref{th:j2:2}} Let $t\in [0,1]$ be fixed. {\it First step:} Let us show that \begin{equation} \begin{split} & \mathbb{E}\!\left[\chi_k^n (Y_{k/n} - Y_{(k-1)/n}) | \mathcal{F}_{(k-1)/n}\right] \\ & = \frac1{\sqrt n} \left( n^{-\frac14} f_1(\sqrt{n} Y_{(k-1)/n}) + g_{n}(\sqrt{n} Y_{(k-1)/n}) + \langle \lambda_\sigma , \bfH h \rangle n^{-\frac14} f_2(\sqrt{n} Y_{(k-1)/n})\right) \end{split} \end{equation} where $f_1,f_2,g_n$ are given by \begin{equation} \begin{split} f_1(x)& := \int_{-\infty}^\infty (h(x,y)+\bfG{h}(y)) (y-x) q_\sigma(1,x,y) \,\mathrm{d} y , \ f_2(x):= x \Lm{1}{1}{x}, \ \text{and} \\ g_n(x) & := n^{-\frac14} \int_{-\infty}^\infty \mathcal{Q}_{n,1,0}(y) (y-x) q_\sigma(1,x,y) \,\mathrm{d} y. \end{split} \end{equation} Throughout the proof of this step let $\mathbb{Id} \colon x\mapsto x$ denote the identity function. It follows from \eqref{eq:chi:nk}, the fact that $Y$ is a martingale, \eqref{function:G:equal}, and the scaling property~\eqref{Yscaling} that \begin{equation} \begin{split} & n^{\frac34} \, \mathbb{E}\!\left[\chi_k^n (Y_{k/n} - Y_{(k-1)/n}) | \mathcal{F}_{(k-1)/n}\right] \\ & = f_1(\sqrt{n} Y_{(k-1)/n}) + \langle \lambda_\sigma , \bfH h \rangle f_2(\sqrt{n} Y_{(k-1)/n}) - \Lm{ \mathbb{Id} }{1}{\sqrt{n} Y_{(k-1)/n}} ) + n^{1/4}g_n(\sqrt{n}Y_{(k-1)/n}). \end{split} \end{equation} The proof of this step is completed if $ \Lm{ \mathbb{Id} }{1}{\cdot} =0$. This equality follows from the fact that for a standard BM, say $W$, it holds that $\mathbb{E}\!\left[ L_1(W) W_1 \right]=0$ and from Lemma~\ref{lem:prop:G}. In the next steps we want to check that Proposition~\ref{prop:th4.1a:j1} can be applied to the sequences $n^{-\frac14} f_1$, $n^{-\frac14} f_2$ and $g_n$. {\it Second step:} We show that $f_1$ is bounded and integrable: $f_1\in \Lgb{0}$. The proof follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:prop:kappa}, and Item~\ref{item2bis:semig:estim} in Lemma~\ref{lem:semig:estim}. In this proof the fact that $\gamma>3$ is strongly used. The fact that $h\in \Lg{\gamma}\subseteq \Lg{3}$ and Lemma~\ref{lem:prop:kappa} ensure that $\bar h$ and $\bfG{h}$ are in $\Lgb{2}$. This, Cauchy-Schwarz, the fact that $ \left(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} (y-x)^2 q_\sigma(1,x,y) \,\mathrm{d} y\right) \leq \sigma_-^2 \ind{\{\sigma_-\in\mathbb{R}\}} +\sigma_+^2 \ind{\{\sigma_+\in\mathbb{R}\}} $, and the fact that that $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} (\bfG{h}(y))^2 q_\sigma(1,x,y) \,\mathrm{d} y = Q^\sigma_1 \bfG{h}^2 (x)$ yield \begin{equation} \begin{split} |f_1(x)| & \leq \bar h(x) \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{a |y-x|} |y-x| q_\sigma(1,x,y) \,\mathrm{d} y + \sqrt{\sigma_-^2 \ind{\{\sigma_-\in\mathbb{R}\}} +\sigma_+^2 \ind{\{\sigma_+\in\mathbb{R}\}}} \left( |Q^\sigma_1 \bfG{h}^2 (x)| \right)^{\!1/2}. \end{split} \end{equation} By Lemma~\ref{lem:prop:kappa} $\bfG{h}$ is bounded, i.e.~there exists $K\in (0,\infty)$ such that $\sup_{x\in \mathbb{R}}|\bfG{h}(x)|\leq K$ and $\langle \lambda_\sigma , \bfG{h} \rangle=0 $, and so $ | \langle \lambda_\sigma , \bfG{h}^2 \rangle | \leq K | \langle \lambda_\sigma , \bfG{h} \rangle | =0. $ And so Item~\ref{item2bis:semig:estim} in Lemma~\ref{lem:semig:estim} implies, up to increase the constant $K\in [1,\infty)$, that \begin{equation} |Q^\sigma_1 \bfG{h}^2 (x)| \leq K \frac{1}{1+|x/\sigma(x)|^{\gamma-1}} + K \frac1{\sqrt{2 \pi}} e^{-\frac{x^2}{2 (\sigma(x))^2 }} \leq 2 K^2 \frac{1}{(1+|x/\sigma(x)|^{\frac{\gamma-1}{2}})^2} . \end{equation} Since $\gamma >3 $ it holds that $\left( |Q^\sigma_1 \bfG{h}^2 (x)| \right)^{\!\frac12}\in \Lgb{0}$ and so $|f_1|\in \Lgb{0}$. {\it Third step:} The fact that $f_2$ is bounded and integrable follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:prop:G}. This and the change of variable $s \mapsto r= \frac{x^2}{(\sigma(x))^2 s}$ show that there exists a positive constant $K$ such that \begin{equation} \begin{split} f_2(x) & = \left(\frac{2 \sigma_-\sigma_+}{\sigma_-+\sigma_+}\right)^{\! 2} \frac{x |x|}{\sigma(x)} \mathbb{E}\!\left[ \frac{L_1(W)}{\sigma(W_1)} \right] \int_0^1 \frac{\sqrt{1-s}}{\sqrt{2\pi} s^\frac32} e^{-\frac{x^2}{2 (\sigma(x))^2 s}} \! \,\mathrm{d} s \\ & = \left(\frac{2 \sigma_-\sigma_+}{\sigma_-+\sigma_+}\right)^{\! 2} \frac{x |x|}{\sigma(x)} \mathbb{E}\!\left[ \frac{L_1(W)}{\sigma(W_1)} \right] \int_{\frac{x^2}{(\sigma(x))^2}}^\infty \frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}} \sqrt{\frac{(\sigma(x))^2}{x^2}-\frac1r} e^{-\frac{r}{2}} \frac1{\sqrt{r}}\! \,\mathrm{d} r \ \ind{\{\sigma(x)\in \mathbb{R}\}} \\ & \leq \left(\frac{2 \sigma_-\sigma_+}{\sigma_-+\sigma_+}\right)^{\! 2} \frac{|x| \mathbb{E}\!\left[L_1(W)\right] }{\min\{\sigma_-,\sigma_+\}} \int_{\frac{x^2}{(\sigma(x))^2}}^\infty \frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-\frac{r}{2}} \frac1{\sqrt{r}}\! \,\mathrm{d} r \ \ind{\{\sigma(x)\in \mathbb{R}\}} \leq K e^{-\frac{x^2}{4(\sigma(x))^2}} \in \Lgb{0}. \end{split} \end{equation} In the last inequality we used that $\mathbb{E}\!\left[ L_1(W) \right] \in [0,\infty)$. This step is thus completed. {\it Fourth step:} We prove that $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} |g_n(x)| \,\mathrm{d} x$ and $\frac1{\sqrt{n}} g_n(\sqrt{n} x)$ converge to 0. Cauchy-Schwarz inequality ensures \begin{equation} \begin{split} |g_n(x)|^2 & \leq n^{-1/2} \left( \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} (\mathcal{Q}_{n,1,0}(y))^2 q_\sigma (1,x,y) \,\mathrm{d} y\right) \left(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} (y-x)^2 q_\sigma(1,x,y) \,\mathrm{d} y\right). \end{split} \end{equation} Note that $ \left(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} (y-x)^2 q_\sigma(1,x,y) \,\mathrm{d} y\right) \leq \sigma_-^2 \ind{\{\sigma_-\in \mathbb{R}\}} +\sigma_+^2 \ind{\{\sigma_+\in \mathbb{R}\}} $ and inequality~\eqref{eq:recicle} yield that there exists a constant $K\in (0,\infty)$ depending on $\gamma$ and $\sigma_\pm$ such that $ |g_n(x)| \leq \frac{n^{-\frac14} K_2 \log (n)}{1+|x n^{-\frac18}/\sigma(x)|^{\gamma-1}}. $ In the last steps we proved that Proposition~\ref{prop:th4.1a:j1} can be applied and this completes the proof. \subsubsection{Proof of Item~\ref{th:j2:item4:2} in Proposition~\ref{th:j2:2}} Let $\varepsilon \in (0,\infty)$ be fixed. For every $k$, H\"older's inequality and Markov's inequality show \begin{equation} \begin{split} & \mathbb{E}\!\left[ |\chi_k^n|^2 \ind{\{|\chi_k^n|\geq \varepsilon \}}| \mathcal{F}_{(k-1)/n}\right] \leq \mathbb{E}\!\left[ |\chi_k^n|^{5} | \mathcal{F}_{(k-1)/n}\right] \varepsilon^{-3} . \end{split} \end{equation} The fact that $h\in \Lg{\gamma}\subseteq \Lg{0}$ ensures that $\bar h$ is bounded and integrable. This combined with Jensen's inequality and \eqref{eq:cQ:prop4} ensures that $\sup_{x\in \mathbb{R}} \bar h(x) + |\langle \lambda_\sigma , \bfH h \rangle| $ is bounded by a constant $K\in (0,\infty)$ and for all $n\in \mathbb{N}\setminus\{0,1,2,3\}$ it holds that \begin{equation} \begin{split} & \mathbb{E}\!\left[ |\chi_k^n|^{5} | \mathcal{F}_{(k-1)/n}\right] \leq 4^{4} n^{-\frac{5}{4}} K^{5} \Big( \mathbb{E}\!\left[ e^{5 a \sqrt n | Y_{k/n} - Y_{(k-1)/n}|} | \mathcal{F}_{(k-1)/n}\right] \\ & \quad \qquad + \mathbb{E}\!\left[ \left(\sqrt{n}|L_{k/n}(Y) - L_{(k-1)/n}(Y)| \right)^{5} | \mathcal{F}_{(k-1)/n}\right] + (\log n)^{5} \Big). \end{split} \end{equation} The fact that density of the OBM has a Gaussian behavior together with the scaling property~\eqref{Yscaling} ensure that $ \mathbb{E}\!\left[ e^{5 a \sqrt n | Y_{k/n} - Y_{(k-1)/n}|} | \mathcal{F}_{(k-1)/n}\right] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{5 a |y-x|} q_\sigma(1,x,y) \,\mathrm{d} y $ is bounded. By \eqref{function:G} and Lemma~\ref{lem:prop:G} we can show, similarly to the third step of the proof of Item~\ref{th:j2:item3}, that there exist constants $K_1,K_2 \in (0,\infty)$ such that \begin{equation} \begin{split} & \mathbb{E}\!\left[ \left(\sqrt{n}|L_{k/n}(Y) - L_{(k-1)/n}(Y)| \right)^{5} | \mathcal{F}_{(k-1)/n}\right] = \Lm {1}{5}{\sqrt{n}Y_{(k-1)/n}} \\ & \leq K_1 \int_0^1 \frac{(1-t)^{\frac52}}{\sqrt{2 \pi} t^{\frac32}} \frac{\sqrt{n}|Y_{(k-1)/n}|}{\sigma(Y_{(k-1)/n})} e^{-\frac{n (Y_{(k-1)/n})^2}{2 (\sigma(Y_{(k-1)/n})) t } } \,\mathrm{d} t \leq K_2. \end{split} \end{equation} We conclude that there exists a constant $K\in (0,\infty)$ such that \begin{equation} \begin{split} & \sum_{k=1}^n \mathbb{E}\!\left[ |\chi_k^n|^2 \ind{\{|\chi_k^n|\geq \varepsilon \}}| \mathcal{F}_{(k-1)/n}\right] \leq n K n^{-\frac54} \log(n) \varepsilon^{-3} \xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{} 0. \end{split} \end{equation}
nodes.section: C Proof of the key Proposition~4
nodes.statement_short: Build the martingale/vanishing decomposition, show the vanishing term is $o(n^{-1/4})$, and verify items (i)-(iv) for the martingale increments. Key step: semigroup aggregation $\mathcal{Q}_{n,i,j}$ of $\mathbf{G}_h$ with bounds from Lemma 3.

nodes.name: Outline and standing assumptions
nodes.statement: In this section we prove Proposition~\ref{th:j2:2} which was stated in Section~\ref{sec:proof:summary}. The section is organized as follows: We split the proof of Proposition~\ref{th:j2:2} into three parts. The first part, in Section~\ref{sec:decomposition}, consists in finding the decomposition~\eqref{eq:decomposition} into a sum of martingale and a vanishing term. We deal with the vanishing term in Section~\ref{sec:th:j2:vanish}. Finally, in Section~\ref{sec:th:j2:hp}, we demonstrate that the martingale part satisfies Items~\ref{th:j2:item1:2}-\ref{th:j2:item4:2} of Proposition~\ref{th:j2:2}. In Section~\ref{sec:finite:K}, we prove that the constant $K_h^Y$ defined by~\eqref{eq:k:th} is finite. Figure~\ref{ProofMapProp} show how the results of the paper intervene in the proof of Proposition~\ref{th:j2:2}. In this section, $(Y_t)_{t\in [0,1]}$ is a standard OBM. \begin{figure}[t] \begin{figure}[omitted: a diagram of this paper's results, not reproduced here]\end{figure} \captionsetup{singlelinecheck=off} \caption[Proof Prop map]{Map of the proof of Proposition~\ref{th:j2:2}.} In the appendix we introduce many auxiliary results. This map show how they intervene in the proof of Proposition~\ref{th:j2:2} and of other results of the appendix. \end{figure} Let us recall that by assumption $\gamma >3$ and $h\in \Lg{\gamma}$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:link:theorems}, $\bfH{f}$ and $\bfH{f^2}$ are well defined and belong to $\Lgb{\gamma}$. For most of the following definitions and proof steps $\gamma\geq 0$ suffices. For the sake of precision, we specify when it does not.
nodes.section: C Proof of the key Proposition~4
nodes.statement_short: Outline the three parts and fix $h\in\mathcal{I}_\gamma$, $\gamma>3$.

nodes.name: The decomposition (C.1)
nodes.statement: In this section we determine the terms of the decomposition in equation~\eqref{eq:decomposition} into a sum of a vanishing term $n^{1/4}\mathcal{V}^n$ and a martingale $\mathcal{M}^n$. Note that for all $n\in \mathbb{N}$, $t\in [0,1]$ : \begin{equation} \begin{split} & \varepsilon_{n,t}^{(0,h,Y)} - \langle \lambda_\sigma , \bfH h \rangle L_t(Y) = M^{n,1}_t + \mathcal{G}^n_t + \langle \lambda_\sigma , \bfH h \rangle \left( L_{\lfloor n t \rfloor/n}(Y) - L_t(Y) \right) \end{split} \end{equation} where $M^{n,1}$ and $\mathcal{G}^n$ are the processes satisfying for all $t\in [0,1]$ that \begin{equation} \begin{split} M^{n,1}_t & = \varepsilon_{n,t}^{(0,h,Y)} - \varepsilon_{n,t}^{(0,\bfH h,Y)} + \langle \lambda_\sigma , \bfH h \rangle \left( \varepsilon_{n,t}^{(0,\bfH g,Y)} - L_{\frac{\lfloor n t \rfloor}n}(Y)\right) \end{split} \end{equation} and $ \mathcal{G}^n_t = \frac1{\sqrt{n}} \sum_{k=0}^{\lfloor n t \rfloor-1} \bfG{h}( \sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k}n}) $ ($\bfG{h}$ is defined in \eqref{eq:kappa} and $g(x,y) := |y| - |x| $). We used here the abuse of notation $\varepsilon_{n,t}^{(0,\bfH h,Y)}$ and $\varepsilon_{n,t}^{(0,\bfH g,Y)}$ as in Appendix~\ref{app:prop:lmt:2}. This decomposition is not the same as the one proposed in Section~\ref{app:decomp:fake}. Indeed, Lemma~\ref{lem:holderL} suggests that $L_{\lfloor n t \rfloor/n}(Y) - L_t(Y) $ will contribute to $\mathcal{V}^n_t$, so we split into two terms the quantity $ \langle \lambda_\sigma , \bfH h \rangle \Big( \varepsilon_{n,t}^{(0,\bfH g,Y)} - L_t(Y)\Big). $ Moreover, it has been shown in Section~\ref{sec:proof:details} that $\sup_{s\in [0,t]} |\mathcal{G}^n_s|\convp[n\to\infty] 0$, but the convergence speed have not been studied. In Section~\ref{sec:decomposition} we decompose $\mathcal{G}^n_t $ into two terms, one contributing to $\mathcal{M}^n_t $ and the other to $\mathcal{V}^n_t $. More precisely, $\mathcal{G}^n= (\mathcal{G}^n - M^{n,2} ) +M^{n,2}$ where \begin{equation} \begin{split} & M^{n,2}_t = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor n t \rfloor} \sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor n^\frac14\rfloor} \left(\mathbb{E}\!\left[ \bfG{h}(\sqrt{n} Y_{(j+k)/n})| \mathcal{F}_{k/n}\right]- \mathbb{E}\!\left[ \bfG{h}(\sqrt{n} Y_{(j+k)/n})| \mathcal{F}_{(k-1)/n}\right]\right). \end{split} \end{equation} And so it holds for all $n\in \mathbb{N}$, $t\in [0,1]$ that \begin{equation} \begin{split} & \varepsilon_{n,t}^{(0,h,Y)} - \langle \lambda_\sigma , \bfH h \rangle L_t(Y) = M^{n,1}_t + M^{n,2}_t + \mathcal{G}^n_t - M^{n,2}_t + \langle \lambda_\sigma , \bfH h \rangle \left( L_{\lfloor n t \rfloor/n}(Y) - L_t(Y) \right). \end{split} \end{equation} We first show, in Lemma~\ref{lem:M:mart}, that $M^{n,1}_t$ is a good candidate for contributing to the martingale part of the decomposition. \begin{lemma} $M^{n,1}$ is a martingale with respect to the filtration $(\mathcal{F}_{\lfloor n t \rfloor/n})_{t\in [0,1]}$. \end{lemma} \begin{proof} Throughout this proof let $A^n$ and $B^n$ be the processes given by \begin{equation} A^n_t = \frac1{\sqrt{n}} \sum_{k=0}^{\lfloor n t \rfloor-1} \bfH{g}(\sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k}n}) - L_{\frac{\lfloor n t \rfloor}n}(Y) \text{ and } B^n_t = M^{n,1}_t - \langle \lambda_\sigma , \bfH h \rangle A^n_t. \end{equation} So $ B^n_t = \frac1{\sqrt{n}} \sum_{k=0}^{\lfloor n t \rfloor-1} \left( h(\sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k}{n}}, \sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k+1}{n}} ) - \bfH h( \sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k}n}) \right). $ It suffices to show the martingale property for $A^n$ and $B^n$. Let $t\in [0,1]$ be fixed. The martingale property for $A^n$ is an immediate consequence of Lemma~\ref{lem:conv:hatg}. Let us explicit the case of the process $B^n$. For all $j\in \{0,\ldots, \lfloor n t \rfloor-1\}$ it can be easily shown that \begin{equation} \begin{split} \mathbb{E}\!\left[ n^{\frac12} B^{n}_t | \mathcal{F}_{\frac j n} \right] & = \sum_{k=j}^{\lfloor n t \rfloor-1} \mathbb{E}\!\left[ h(\sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k}{n}}, \sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k+1}{n}} ) - \bfH h( \sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k}n}) | \mathcal{F}_{\frac j n} \right] + B^{n}_{\frac j n} = B^{n}_{\frac j n}. \end{split} \end{equation} because for all $k \in \{j,\ldots, \lfloor n t \rfloor-1\}$ it holds that \begin{equation} \begin{split} & \mathbb{E}\!\left[ h(\sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k}{n}}, \sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k+1}{n}} ) - \bfH h( \sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k}n}) | \mathcal{F}_{\frac j n} \right] = \mathbb{E}\!\left[ \mathbb{E}\!\left[ h(\sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k}{n}}, \sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k+1}{n}} ) - \bfH h( \sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k}n}) | \mathcal{F}_{\frac k n} \right] | \mathcal{F}_{\frac j n} \right] \\ & = \mathbb{E}\!\left[ \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} h(\sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k}{n}}, \sqrt{n} y ) q_\sigma(1/n, \sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k}{n}}, y) \,\mathrm{d} y - \bfH h( \sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k}n}) | \mathcal{F}_{\frac j n} \right] = \mathbb{E}\!\left[ 0 | \mathcal{F}_{\frac j n} \right] =0. \end{split} \end{equation} The proof is thus completed. \end{proof} Definition~\eqref{eq:W} implies that $M^{n,2}$ is a martingale as well. \begin{lemma} $M^{n,2}$ is a martingale with respect to the filtration $(\mathcal{F}_{\lfloor n t \rfloor/n})_{t\in [0,1]}$. \end{lemma} \begin{proof} Using \eqref{eq:cQ} we rewrite $M^{n,2}$ in \eqref{eq:dec:m3} as \begin{equation} \begin{split} & M^{n,2}_t = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor n t \rfloor} \sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor n^\frac14\rfloor} \left(\mathbb{E}\!\left[ \bfG{h}(\sqrt{n} Y_{(j+k)/n})| \mathcal{F}_{k/n}\right]- \mathbb{E}\!\left[ \bfG{h}(\sqrt{n} Y_{(j+k)/n})| \mathcal{F}_{(k-1)/n}\right]\right) \end{split} \end{equation} which shows that $M^{n,2}$ is a martingale with respect to the filtration $(\mathcal{F}_{\lfloor n t \rfloor/n})_{t\in [0,1]}$. \end{proof} Lemma~\ref{lem:M:mart} and Lemma~\ref{lem:M:mart:2} identify the $(\mathcal{F}_{\lfloor n t \rfloor/n})_{t\geq 0}$-martingale $\mathcal{M}^n$ and also the candidate to be the vanishing term with rate of order at least $1/4$ (denoted by $\mathcal{V}^n$): \begin{equation} \begin{split} &\mathcal{M}^n_t := n^{1/4} \left( M^{n,1}_t + M^{n,2}_t \right) \ \text{and\/} \ \\ & \mathcal{V}^n_t := \mathcal{G}^n_t - M^{n,2}_t + \langle \lambda_\sigma , \bfH h \rangle \left( L_{\frac{\lfloor n t \rfloor}n}(Y) - L_t(Y) \right). \end{split} \end{equation} To prove Proposition~\ref{th:j2:2}, it remains to show that $\sup_{t\in [0,1]} n^{1/4} |\mathcal{V}^n_t| \convp[n\to\infty] 0$ and that $\mathcal{M}^n_\cdot$ satisfies Items~\ref{th:j2:item1:2}-\ref{th:j2:item4:2}. This is done in Section~\ref{sec:th:j2:vanish} and Section~\ref{sec:th:j2:hp}.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 11
nodes.statement: Throughout this proof let $A^n$ and $B^n$ be the processes given by \begin{equation} A^n_t = \frac1{\sqrt{n}} \sum_{k=0}^{\lfloor n t \rfloor-1} \bfH{g}(\sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k}n}) - L_{\frac{\lfloor n t \rfloor}n}(Y) \text{ and } B^n_t = M^{n,1}_t - \langle \lambda_\sigma , \bfH h \rangle A^n_t. \end{equation} So $ B^n_t = \frac1{\sqrt{n}} \sum_{k=0}^{\lfloor n t \rfloor-1} \left( h(\sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k}{n}}, \sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k+1}{n}} ) - \bfH h( \sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k}n}) \right). $ It suffices to show the martingale property for $A^n$ and $B^n$. Let $t\in [0,1]$ be fixed. The martingale property for $A^n$ is an immediate consequence of Lemma~\ref{lem:conv:hatg}. Let us explicit the case of the process $B^n$. For all $j\in \{0,\ldots, \lfloor n t \rfloor-1\}$ it can be easily shown that \begin{equation} \begin{split} \mathbb{E}\!\left[ n^{\frac12} B^{n}_t | \mathcal{F}_{\frac j n} \right] & = \sum_{k=j}^{\lfloor n t \rfloor-1} \mathbb{E}\!\left[ h(\sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k}{n}}, \sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k+1}{n}} ) - \bfH h( \sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k}n}) | \mathcal{F}_{\frac j n} \right] + B^{n}_{\frac j n} = B^{n}_{\frac j n}. \end{split} \end{equation} because for all $k \in \{j,\ldots, \lfloor n t \rfloor-1\}$ it holds that \begin{equation} \begin{split} & \mathbb{E}\!\left[ h(\sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k}{n}}, \sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k+1}{n}} ) - \bfH h( \sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k}n}) | \mathcal{F}_{\frac j n} \right] = \mathbb{E}\!\left[ \mathbb{E}\!\left[ h(\sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k}{n}}, \sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k+1}{n}} ) - \bfH h( \sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k}n}) | \mathcal{F}_{\frac k n} \right] | \mathcal{F}_{\frac j n} \right] \\ & = \mathbb{E}\!\left[ \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} h(\sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k}{n}}, \sqrt{n} y ) q_\sigma(1/n, \sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k}{n}}, y) \,\mathrm{d} y - \bfH h( \sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k}n}) | \mathcal{F}_{\frac j n} \right] = \mathbb{E}\!\left[ 0 | \mathcal{F}_{\frac j n} \right] =0. \end{split} \end{equation} The proof is thus completed.

For all $j\in \{0,\ldots, \lfloor n t \rfloor-1\}$ it can be easily shown that \begin{equation} \begin{split} \mathbb{E}\!\left[ n^{\frac12} B^{n}_t | \mathcal{F}_{\frac j n} \right] & = \sum_{k=j}^{\lfloor n t \rfloor-1} \mathbb{E}\!\left[ h(\sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k}{n}}, \sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k+1}{n}} ) - \bfH h( \sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k}n}) | \mathcal{F}_{\frac j n} \right] + B^{n}_{\frac j n} = B^{n}_{\frac j n}. \end{split} \end{equation} because for all $k \in \{j,\ldots, \lfloor n t \rfloor-1\}$ it holds that \begin{equation} \begin{split} & \mathbb{E}\!\left[ h(\sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k}{n}}, \sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k+1}{n}} ) - \bfH h( \sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k}n}) | \mathcal{F}_{\frac j n} \right] = \mathbb{E}\!\left[ \mathbb{E}\!\left[ h(\sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k}{n}}, \sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k+1}{n}} ) - \bfH h( \sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k}n}) | \mathcal{F}_{\frac k n} \right] | \mathcal{F}_{\frac j n} \right] \\ & = \mathbb{E}\!\left[ \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} h(\sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k}{n}}, \sqrt{n} y ) q_\sigma(1/n, \sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k}{n}}, y) \,\mathrm{d} y - \bfH h( \sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k}n}) | \mathcal{F}_{\frac j n} \right] = \mathbb{E}\!\left[ 0 | \mathcal{F}_{\frac j n} \right] =0. \end{split} \end{equation} The proof is thus completed.

nodes.statement: Using \eqref{eq:cQ} we rewrite $M^{n,2}$ in \eqref{eq:dec:m3} as \begin{equation} \begin{split} & M^{n,2}_t = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor n t \rfloor} \sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor n^\frac14\rfloor} \left(\mathbb{E}\!\left[ \bfG{h}(\sqrt{n} Y_{(j+k)/n})| \mathcal{F}_{k/n}\right]- \mathbb{E}\!\left[ \bfG{h}(\sqrt{n} Y_{(j+k)/n})| \mathcal{F}_{(k-1)/n}\right]\right) \end{split} \end{equation} which shows that $M^{n,2}$ is a martingale with respect to the filtration $(\mathcal{F}_{\lfloor n t \rfloor/n})_{t\in [0,1]}$.
nodes.section: C.1 The decomposition into a sum of martingale and vanishing terms
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite $M^{n,2}$ as a sum of differences of conditional expectations.

nodes.name: Equation (C.9): Martingale and vanishing terms
nodes.statement: \begin{split} &\mathcal{M}^n_t := n^{1/4} \left( M^{n,1}_t + M^{n,2}_t \right) \ \text{and\/} \ \\ & \mathcal{V}^n_t := \mathcal{G}^n_t - M^{n,2}_t + \langle \lambda_\sigma , \bfH h \rangle \left( L_{\frac{\lfloor n t \rfloor}n}(Y) - L_t(Y) \right). \end{split}
nodes.section: C.1 The decomposition into a sum of martingale and vanishing terms
nodes.label: eq:mv

nodes.name: Finiteness of the variance (C.2)
nodes.statement: In this section we provide the proof of the finiteness of the constant $K_h^Y$ defined by~\eqref{eq:k:th}. The proof is actually contained in Section~\ref{sec:th:j2:hp}, but we choose to show it separately. Instead, we do not prove separately non-negativity of the constant. The expression of $K_h^Y$ depends on a function, $\mathcal{P}_h^Y$ which is here expressed with the use of some auxiliary functions. We first introduce and prove some properties of these functions that are also used to provide an alternative expression for $M^{n,2}$. For all $i,j\in \{0,1\}$, $\eta\in [0,\infty)$ let \begin{equation} \mathcal{Q}^{(\eta)}_{n, i , j} := \sum_{k=i}^{\lfloor n^{\eta}\rfloor + j } Q^\sigma_k \bfG{h} \quad \text{ and } \quad \mathcal{Q}_{n, i , j}:=\mathcal{Q}^{(\frac14)}_{n, i , j} \end{equation}
nodes.section: C.2 Finiteness of the variance
nodes.statement_short: Introduce $\mathcal{Q}^{(\eta)}_{n,i,j}$, prove Lemmas 13-14 and the bounds (C.13)-(C.16).

nodes.name: Equation (C.10): Aggregated semigroups $\mathcal{Q}$
nodes.statement: \mathcal{Q}^{(\eta)}_{n, i , j} := \sum_{k=i}^{\lfloor n^{\eta}\rfloor + j } Q^\sigma_k \bfG{h} \quad \text{ and } \quad \mathcal{Q}_{n, i , j}:=\mathcal{Q}^{(\frac14)}_{n, i , j}
nodes.section: C.2 Finiteness of the variance
nodes.label: eq:cQ

nodes.name: Equation (C.11): $M^{n,2}$ via $\mathcal{Q}$
nodes.statement: M^{n,2}_t = \frac1{\sqrt{n}} \sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor n t \rfloor} \left(\mathcal{Q}_{n,0,0}(\sqrt{n} Y_{\frac k n}) - \mathcal{Q}_{n,1,1}(\sqrt{n} Y_{\frac{k-1}{n}})\right).
nodes.section: C.2 Finiteness of the variance
nodes.label: eq:dec:m3

nodes.name: Convergence of $\mathcal{Q}_{m,0,0}$ to $\mathcal{P}_h^Y$
nodes.statement: Pointwise $\lim_{m\to\infty} \mathcal{Q}_{m,0,0} = \mathcal{P}_{h}^{Y} $. Moreover, $x\mapsto \mathcal{P}_{h}^{Y}(x)/(1+|x|) $ is bounded.
nodes.section: C.2 Finiteness of the variance
nodes.label: lem:cQ:conv

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 13
nodes.statement: Let $x\in \mathbb{R}$. Note that $\mathcal{P}_{h}^{Y}$ in~\eqref{eq:cQ:limit} for OBM rewrites as \[ \mathcal{P}_{h}^{Y}(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty } \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} p_X(k, x, y) \bfG{h}(y) \,\mathrm{d} y = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty } Q^\sigma_k \bfG{h}(x) . \] Hence there exists a positive constant $K\in (0,\infty)$ such that \[ \left| \mathcal{Q}_{m,0,0}(x) - \mathcal{P}_{h}^{Y}(x) \right| \leq \sum_{k=\lfloor m^{1/4}\rfloor+1}^{\infty} \left| Q^\sigma_k \bfG{h}(x) \right| \leq K (1+|x|) \sum_{k=\lfloor m^{1/4}\rfloor+1}^{\infty} k^{-3/2} \] where the last inequality follows from Item~\ref{item2:semig:estim} in Lemma~\ref{lem:semig:estim} and Lemma~\ref{lem:prop:kappa}. Indeed, Lemma~\ref{lem:prop:kappa} establishes that $\bfG{h}\in \Lgb{\gamma}$ for all $\gamma>0$ (in particular for $\gamma =1$ and $\gamma =2$). The fact that $\sum_{k=\lfloor m^{1/4}\rfloor+1}^{\infty} k^{-3/2}$ converges to $0$ as $m\to\infty$ proves the first statement. Similarly, Item~\ref{item2:semig:estim} in Lemma~\ref{lem:semig:estim} proves that there exist constants $K,K'\in (0,+\infty)$ such that $ |\mathcal{P}_{h}^{Y}(x)| \leq |\bfG{h}(x)| + K (1+|x|) \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} k^{-3/2} \leq K' (1+|x|). $ The proof is thus completed.
nodes.section: C.2 Finiteness of the variance
nodes.statement_short: Tail of the semigroup series is bounded by $K(1+|x|)\sum k^{-3/2}$ via Lemma 3 (ii) and Lemma 10.

nodes.name: Series form
nodes.statement: Let $x\in \mathbb{R}$. Note that $\mathcal{P}_{h}^{Y}$ in~\eqref{eq:cQ:limit} for OBM rewrites as \[ \mathcal{P}_{h}^{Y}(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty } \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} p_X(k, x, y) \bfG{h}(y) \,\mathrm{d} y = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty } Q^\sigma_k \bfG{h}(x) . \]
nodes.section: C.2 Finiteness of the variance
nodes.statement_short: Write $\mathcal{P}_h^Y$ as a series of semigroup actions on $\mathbf{G}_h$.

nodes.name: Tail bound
nodes.statement: Hence there exists a positive constant $K\in (0,\infty)$ such that \[ \left| \mathcal{Q}_{m,0,0}(x) - \mathcal{P}_{h}^{Y}(x) \right| \leq \sum_{k=\lfloor m^{1/4}\rfloor+1}^{\infty} \left| Q^\sigma_k \bfG{h}(x) \right| \leq K (1+|x|) \sum_{k=\lfloor m^{1/4}\rfloor+1}^{\infty} k^{-3/2} \] where the last inequality follows from Item~\ref{item2:semig:estim} in Lemma~\ref{lem:semig:estim} and Lemma~\ref{lem:prop:kappa}. Indeed, Lemma~\ref{lem:prop:kappa} establishes that $\bfG{h}\in \Lgb{\gamma}$ for all $\gamma>0$ (in particular for $\gamma =1$ and $\gamma =2$).
nodes.section: C.2 Finiteness of the variance
nodes.statement_short: Bound the tail by $K(1+|x|)\sum k^{-3/2}$ using Lemma 3 and Lemma 10.

nodes.name: Pointwise limit
nodes.statement: The fact that $\sum_{k=\lfloor m^{1/4}\rfloor+1}^{\infty} k^{-3/2}$ converges to $0$ as $m\to\infty$ proves the first statement.
nodes.section: C.2 Finiteness of the variance
nodes.statement_short: The tail vanishes, proving pointwise convergence.

nodes.name: Linear growth
nodes.statement: Similarly, Item~\ref{item2:semig:estim} in Lemma~\ref{lem:semig:estim} proves that there exist constants $K,K'\in (0,+\infty)$ such that $ |\mathcal{P}_{h}^{Y}(x)| \leq |\bfG{h}(x)| + K (1+|x|) \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} k^{-3/2} \leq K' (1+|x|). $ The proof is thus completed.
nodes.section: C.2 Finiteness of the variance
nodes.statement_short: Same bound gives $|\mathcal{P}_h^Y(x)|\le K'(1+|x|)$.

nodes.name: Finiteness of the variance constant $K_h^Y$
nodes.statement: The quantity $K_h^Y$ defined by~\eqref{eq:k:th} is a finite constant.
nodes.section: C.2 Finiteness of the variance
conclusions: The quantity $K_h^Y$ defined by~\eqref{eq:k:th} is a finite constant
nodes.label: lem:finite:K

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 14
nodes.statement: Let us recall that \begin{equation} {\scriptsize \begin{split} & K_h^Y = \langle \mu_Y , \bfH{h^2} + 2 \bfH{h,\mathcal{P}_{h}^Y} \rangle + \frac{ 2 \sigma_- \sigma_+}{\sigma_-+\sigma_+} \frac{8}{3 \sqrt{2\pi}} (\langle \mu_Y , \bfH{h} \rangle)^2 \\ & \quad - 2 \sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}} \frac{ 2 \sigma_- \sigma_+}{\sigma_-+\sigma_+} \langle \mu_Y , \bfH{h} \rangle \int_{-\infty}^\infty \left( e^{-\frac{y^2}{2(\sigma(y))^2}} -\sqrt{2\pi} \frac{|y|}{\sigma(y)} \Phi\left(-\frac{|y|}{\sigma(y)}\right)\right) \mathcal{P}_{h}^Y(y) \mu_Y(\!\,\mathrm{d} y) \\ & \quad - 2 \langle \mu_Y , \bfH{h} \rangle \left(\frac{ 2 \sigma_- \sigma_+}{\sigma_-+\sigma_+}\right)^{\!2} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \int_0^1 \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \tfrac{|x| e^{-\frac{x^2}{2(\sigma(x))^2}} \Phi\left(-\frac{|y|}{\sigma(y)}\right)}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma(x)} \sqrt{\frac{1}t-1} h(x \sqrt{t}, y \sqrt{1-t}) \mu_Y(\!\,\mathrm{d} y) \,\mathrm{d} t \mu_Y(\!\,\mathrm{d} x), \end{split} }\end{equation} where $\Phi$ is the cumulative distribution function oh a standard Gaussian random variable, and $\mathcal{P}_{h}^Y$ has been studied in Lemma~\ref{lem:cQ:conv}. Note that $\lambda$-integrability is equivalent to $\mu_Y$-integrability. Therefore if $f\in \Lgb{0}$ then $f$ is $\lambda$-integrable and $\langle \mu_Y , f \rangle$ is finite. Since $\gamma\geq 1$, Lemma~\ref{lem:link:theorems} ensures that $f=\bfH{h},\bfH{h^2}\in \Lgb{1}$ which is contained in $\Lgb{0}$ by Remark~\ref{rem:spaces:relation}. And also, in Lemma~\ref{lem:cQ:conv} it has been shown that $|\mathcal{P}_{h}^Y (y)| \leq K (1+|y|)$ for some constant $K\in (0,\infty)$, so Lemma~\ref{lem:link:theorems} ensures that $x\mapsto \bfH{h, \mathcal{P}_{h}^Y}(x)/(1+|x|)$ belongs to $\Lgb{\gamma}$. Since $\gamma\geq 1$, we deduce that $\bfH{h, \mathcal{P}_{h}^Y}$ is $\lambda$-integrable. Let us now consider the second last integral appearing in the expression of $K_h^Y$. Since $ 1- \sqrt{2\pi} \frac{|y|}{\sigma(y)} \Phi\left(-\frac{|y|}{\sigma(y)}\right) e^{\frac{y^2}{2(\sigma(y))^2}} \in [0,1]$ for all $y\in \mathbb{R}$, we reduce to check that $e^{-y^2/2} \mathcal{P}_{h}^Y(\sigma(y)y)$ is $\lambda$-integrable. And this is the case because $e^{-y^2/2} \mathcal{P}_{h}^Y(\sigma(y)y) \leq K (1+|y|) e^{-y^2/2}$. For the last integral we use that $h\in \Lg{\gamma}$ and exploit the inequality $h(x,y) \leq \bar{h}(x) e^{a|y-x|} \leq K e^{a|y-x|}$ for some constant $a,K\in (0,\infty)$. Then we deal with $\int_0^1 \sqrt{\frac1t -1} e^{a|\sqrt t x -\sqrt{1-t}y|} \,\mathrm{d} t \leq e^{a|x|+a|y|} \int_0^1 \sqrt{\frac1t -1} \,\mathrm{d} t = e^{a|x|+a|y|} \frac{\pi}2.$ By observing that $ x\mapsto e^{a|x|} \tfrac{ |x| e^{-\frac{x^2}{2(\sigma(x))^2}} }{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma(x)} $ and $y \mapsto e^{a|y|}\Phi\left(-\frac{|y|}{\sigma(y)}\right)$ are $\lambda$-integrable, we complete the proof.
nodes.section: C.2 Finiteness of the variance
nodes.statement_short: Check integrability of each term of $K_h^Y$ using Lemma 2, Lemma 13 and Gaussian tails.

nodes.name: Recall $K_h^Y$
nodes.statement: Let us recall that \begin{equation} {\scriptsize \begin{split} & K_h^Y = \langle \mu_Y , \bfH{h^2} + 2 \bfH{h,\mathcal{P}_{h}^Y} \rangle + \frac{ 2 \sigma_- \sigma_+}{\sigma_-+\sigma_+} \frac{8}{3 \sqrt{2\pi}} (\langle \mu_Y , \bfH{h} \rangle)^2 \\ & \quad - 2 \sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}} \frac{ 2 \sigma_- \sigma_+}{\sigma_-+\sigma_+} \langle \mu_Y , \bfH{h} \rangle \int_{-\infty}^\infty \left( e^{-\frac{y^2}{2(\sigma(y))^2}} -\sqrt{2\pi} \frac{|y|}{\sigma(y)} \Phi\left(-\frac{|y|}{\sigma(y)}\right)\right) \mathcal{P}_{h}^Y(y) \mu_Y(\!\,\mathrm{d} y) \\ & \quad - 2 \langle \mu_Y , \bfH{h} \rangle \left(\frac{ 2 \sigma_- \sigma_+}{\sigma_-+\sigma_+}\right)^{\!2} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \int_0^1 \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \tfrac{|x| e^{-\frac{x^2}{2(\sigma(x))^2}} \Phi\left(-\frac{|y|}{\sigma(y)}\right)}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma(x)} \sqrt{\frac{1}t-1} h(x \sqrt{t}, y \sqrt{1-t}) \mu_Y(\!\,\mathrm{d} y) \,\mathrm{d} t \mu_Y(\!\,\mathrm{d} x), \end{split} }\end{equation} where $\Phi$ is the cumulative distribution function oh a standard Gaussian random variable, and $\mathcal{P}_{h}^Y$ has been studied in Lemma~\ref{lem:cQ:conv}.
nodes.section: C.2 Finiteness of the variance
nodes.statement_short: Recall the expression of $K_h^Y$.

nodes.name: Equation (C.12)
nodes.statement: {\scriptsize \begin{split} & K_h^Y = \langle \mu_Y , \bfH{h^2} + 2 \bfH{h,\mathcal{P}_{h}^Y} \rangle + \frac{ 2 \sigma_- \sigma_+}{\sigma_-+\sigma_+} \frac{8}{3 \sqrt{2\pi}} (\langle \mu_Y , \bfH{h} \rangle)^2 \\ & \quad - 2 \sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}} \frac{ 2 \sigma_- \sigma_+}{\sigma_-+\sigma_+} \langle \mu_Y , \bfH{h} \rangle \int_{-\infty}^\infty \left( e^{-\frac{y^2}{2(\sigma(y))^2}} -\sqrt{2\pi} \frac{|y|}{\sigma(y)} \Phi\left(-\frac{|y|}{\sigma(y)}\right)\right) \mathcal{P}_{h}^Y(y) \mu_Y(\!\,\mathrm{d} y) \\ & \quad - 2 \langle \mu_Y , \bfH{h} \rangle \left(\frac{ 2 \sigma_- \sigma_+}{\sigma_-+\sigma_+}\right)^{\!2} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \int_0^1 \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \tfrac{|x| e^{-\frac{x^2}{2(\sigma(x))^2}} \Phi\left(-\frac{|y|}{\sigma(y)}\right)}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma(x)} \sqrt{\frac{1}t-1} h(x \sqrt{t}, y \sqrt{1-t}) \mu_Y(\!\,\mathrm{d} y) \,\mathrm{d} t \mu_Y(\!\,\mathrm{d} x), \end{split} }
nodes.section: C.2 Finiteness of the variance

nodes.name: First terms
nodes.statement: Note that $\lambda$-integrability is equivalent to $\mu_Y$-integrability. Therefore if $f\in \Lgb{0}$ then $f$ is $\lambda$-integrable and $\langle \mu_Y , f \rangle$ is finite. Since $\gamma\geq 1$, Lemma~\ref{lem:link:theorems} ensures that $f=\bfH{h},\bfH{h^2}\in \Lgb{1}$ which is contained in $\Lgb{0}$ by Remark~\ref{rem:spaces:relation}. And also, in Lemma~\ref{lem:cQ:conv} it has been shown that $|\mathcal{P}_{h}^Y (y)| \leq K (1+|y|)$ for some constant $K\in (0,\infty)$, so Lemma~\ref{lem:link:theorems} ensures that $x\mapsto \bfH{h, \mathcal{P}_{h}^Y}(x)/(1+|x|)$ belongs to $\Lgb{\gamma}$. Since $\gamma\geq 1$, we deduce that $\bfH{h, \mathcal{P}_{h}^Y}$ is $\lambda$-integrable.
nodes.section: C.2 Finiteness of the variance
nodes.statement_short: First terms finite by Lemma 2, Remark 2 and Lemma 13.

nodes.name: Second-to-last integral
nodes.statement: Let us now consider the second last integral appearing in the expression of $K_h^Y$. Since $ 1- \sqrt{2\pi} \frac{|y|}{\sigma(y)} \Phi\left(-\frac{|y|}{\sigma(y)}\right) e^{\frac{y^2}{2(\sigma(y))^2}} \in [0,1]$ for all $y\in \mathbb{R}$, we reduce to check that $e^{-y^2/2} \mathcal{P}_{h}^Y(\sigma(y)y)$ is $\lambda$-integrable. And this is the case because $e^{-y^2/2} \mathcal{P}_{h}^Y(\sigma(y)y) \leq K (1+|y|) e^{-y^2/2}$.
nodes.section: C.2 Finiteness of the variance
nodes.statement_short: Linear growth of $\mathcal{P}_h^Y$ times a Gaussian is integrable.

nodes.name: Last integral
nodes.statement: For the last integral we use that $h\in \Lg{\gamma}$ and exploit the inequality $h(x,y) \leq \bar{h}(x) e^{a|y-x|} \leq K e^{a|y-x|}$ for some constant $a,K\in (0,\infty)$. Then we deal with $\int_0^1 \sqrt{\frac1t -1} e^{a|\sqrt t x -\sqrt{1-t}y|} \,\mathrm{d} t \leq e^{a|x|+a|y|} \int_0^1 \sqrt{\frac1t -1} \,\mathrm{d} t = e^{a|x|+a|y|} \frac{\pi}2.$ By observing that $ x\mapsto e^{a|x|} \tfrac{ |x| e^{-\frac{x^2}{2(\sigma(x))^2}} }{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma(x)} $ and $y \mapsto e^{a|y|}\Phi\left(-\frac{|y|}{\sigma(y)}\right)$ are $\lambda$-integrable, we complete the proof.
nodes.section: C.2 Finiteness of the variance
nodes.statement_short: Exponential domination of $h$ and integrable weights.

nodes.name: Equation (C.13)
nodes.statement: \begin{split} |Q^\sigma_{n^{\eta}+1} \bfG{h} (x) | & \leq \left(1+\tfrac{|\sigma_-\sigma_+|}{\sigma_-+\sigma_+}\right) K_\zeta n^{-\eta} \left(\tfrac1{1+|x n^{-\eta/2}/\sigma(x)|^\zeta} + \tfrac1{1+(|x|/\sigma(x))^\zeta}\right) \end{split}
nodes.section: C.2 Finiteness of the variance
nodes.label: eq:cQ:prop1

nodes.name: Equation (C.14)
nodes.statement: |\mathcal{Q}^{(\eta)}_{n,1,0}(x)|+|\mathcal{Q}^{(\eta)}_{n,1,1}(x)| \leq 2 K_\zeta \log(n) \left(\tfrac1{1+|x n^{-{\eta}/2}/\sigma(x)|^\zeta} + \tfrac1{1+|x/\sigma(x)|^\zeta}\right)
nodes.section: C.2 Finiteness of the variance
nodes.label: eq:cQ:prop2

nodes.name: Equation (C.15)
nodes.section: C.2 Finiteness of the variance
nodes.label: eq:cQ:prop3

nodes.name: Equation (C.16)
nodes.section: C.2 Finiteness of the variance
nodes.label: eq:cQ:prop4

nodes.name: The vanishing term (C.3)
nodes.statement: We now prove that $\mathcal{V}^n$ defined in \eqref{eq:mv}, satisfies that $\sup_{t\in [0,1]} n^{1/4} |\mathcal{V}^n_t| \convp[n\to\infty] 0$. This is a consequence of~Lemma~\ref{lem:holderL} and Lemma~\ref{lem:j1:5.2}. \begin{lemma} Let $h\in \Lg{3}$. Then $\sup_{s\in [0,1]} n^{1/4} |\mathcal{G}^n_s-M^{n,2}_s| \convp[n\to\infty] 0$. \end{lemma} \begin{proof} Using \eqref{eq:cQ} we rewrite $M^{n,2}$ in~\eqref{eq:W} as~\eqref{eq:dec:m3} and also as \begin{equation} \begin{split} & M^{n,2}_t = \mathcal{G}^n_t - \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \left( \mathcal{Q}_{n,0,0}(\sqrt{n} Y_0) - \mathcal{Q}_{n,0,0}(\sqrt{n} Y_{\lfloor n t\rfloor/n}) \right) - \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor n t \rfloor -1} Q^\sigma_{\lfloor n^\frac14\rfloor +1} \bfG{h} (\sqrt n Y_{j/n}). \end{split} \end{equation} Let \begin{equation}{m^{n}_t := \mathcal{G}^n_t - \frac1{\sqrt{n}} \left( \mathcal{Q}^{(3/4)}_{n,0,0}(\sqrt{n} Y_0) - \mathcal{Q}^{(3/4)}_{n,0,0}(\sqrt{n} Y_{\lfloor n t\rfloor/n}) \right) - \frac1{\sqrt{n}} \sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor n t \rfloor -1} Q^\sigma_{\lfloor n^\frac34\rfloor +1} \bfG{h} (\sqrt n Y_{j/n}). } \end{equation} By analogy, $m^n_t$ has an expression as~\eqref{eq:W} and so it is clear that $m^n$ is a martingale with respect to the filtration $(\mathcal{F}_{\lfloor n t \rfloor/n})_{t\in [0,1]}$. Therefore $n^{1/4} (M^{n,2}_t-m^n_t)$ as well. Let us denote by $D^n_t := n^{1/4} (\mathcal{G}^n_t - M^{n,2}_t)$ and $d^n_t := n^{1/4} (\mathcal{G}^n_t - m^n_t)$. Then $D^n-d^n = n^{1/4} (m^n-M^{n,2})$ is a martingale with respect to the filtration $(\mathcal{F}_{\lfloor n t \rfloor/n})_{t\in [0,1]}$. In this notation, the goal is to prove $\sup_{s\in [0,1]} |D^n_s|\convp[n\to\infty] 0$. {\em First step:\/} For every $t\in [0,1]$, let us show that $\lim_{n\to\infty} \mathbb{E}\!\left[( D^n_t-d^n_t)^2\right]=0$ by demonstrating the stronger fact that $\lim_{n\to\infty} \mathbb{E}\!\left[(D_t^n)^2+(d_t^n)^2\right]=0$.\\ Let $t\in [0,1]$ and $\eta \in \left\{ \frac14, \frac34 \right\}$ be fixed. Inequality \eqref{eq:cQ:prop4} implies for all $\omega\in \Omega$ that \begin{equation} \sup_{s\in [0,1]} n^{-\frac14} \left( \mathcal{Q}^{(\eta)}_{n,0,0}(\sqrt{n} Y_0(\omega)) - \mathcal{Q}^{(\eta)}_{n,0,0}(\sqrt{n} Y_{\lfloor n s\rfloor/n}(\omega)) \right) \xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{} 0, \end{equation} hence it holds also that $ \lim_{n\to\infty} \mathbb{E}\!\left[n^{-1/2} \left( \mathcal{Q}^{(\eta)}_{n,0,0}(\sqrt{n} Y_0) - \mathcal{Q}^{(\eta)}_{n,0,0}(\sqrt{n} Y_{\lfloor n t\rfloor/n}) \right)^2 \right]=0. $ Next observe that, since $\lambda_\sigma$ is a stationary measure, the sequences of functions $g_n^{(\eta)} := n^{1/4} Q^\sigma_{\lfloor n^{\eta}\rfloor +1} \bfG{h} $, $\eta \in \{\tfrac14,\tfrac34\}$ satisfy that $\langle \lambda_\sigma , g_n^{(\eta)} \rangle = n^{1/4} \langle \lambda_\sigma , \bfG{h} \rangle$ which is equal to 0 by Lemma~\ref{lem:prop:kappa}. This and inequality \eqref{eq:cQ:prop1} (with $\zeta=2$ since $h\in \Lg{\zeta+1}$) ensure that \eqref{eq:j1:4.2} holds. (A sufficient condition is $\eta \geq 1/4$.)\\ Hence, Lemma~\ref{lem:j1:4.2} shows that $ \lim_{n\to\infty} \mathbb{E}\!\left[ n^{-1/2} \left(\sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor n t \rfloor -1} Q^\sigma_{\lfloor n^{\eta}\rfloor +1} \bfG{h} (\sqrt n Y_{{j}/{n}})\right)^2\right]=0. $ {\em Second step:\/} It holds that $\sup_{s\in [0,1]} |D^n_s - d_s^n|\convp[n\to\infty] 0$.\\ This follows from \cite[Proposition~1.2]{aldous89} as a consequence of the previous step and the martingale property of $D^n - d^n$. {\em Third step:\/} It holds that $\sup_{s\in [0,1]} |d_s^n| \convp[n\to\infty] 0$. This follows from~\eqref{lem:j1:5.2.eq} and from applying Proposition~\ref{prop:th4.1a:j1} to the sequence $g_n:= n^{1/4} Q^\sigma_{\lfloor n^\frac34\rfloor +1} \bfG{h} $. (Here taking $n^{1/4} Q^\sigma_{\lfloor n^{\eta} \rfloor +1} \bfG{h}$ with $\eta>1/2$ would be sufficient.) The assumptions are indeed satisfied: $\lim_{n\to\infty} \|g_n\|_{1} =0$ by Item~\ref{item1:semig:estim} in Lemma~\ref{lem:semig:estim} and in the first step we have proven that $g_n$ satisfies \eqref{eq:j1:4.2} and in particular $\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{g_n(\sqrt{n}x)}{\sqrt{n}}=0$. Combining the two last steps yields the conclusion. \end{proof}
nodes.section: C.3 Dealing with the vanishing term
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 5 and Lemma 15 show $n^{1/4}\sup|\mathcal{V}^n|\to0$.

nodes.name: The vanishing term $\mathcal{G}^n-M^{n,2}$ is $o(n^{-1/4})$
nodes.statement: Let $h\in \Lg{3}$. Then $\sup_{s\in [0,1]} n^{1/4} |\mathcal{G}^n_s-M^{n,2}_s| \convp[n\to\infty] 0$.
nodes.section: C.3 Dealing with the vanishing term
nodes.label: lem:j1:5.2

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 15
nodes.statement: Using \eqref{eq:cQ} we rewrite $M^{n,2}$ in~\eqref{eq:W} as~\eqref{eq:dec:m3} and also as \begin{equation} \begin{split} & M^{n,2}_t = \mathcal{G}^n_t - \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \left( \mathcal{Q}_{n,0,0}(\sqrt{n} Y_0) - \mathcal{Q}_{n,0,0}(\sqrt{n} Y_{\lfloor n t\rfloor/n}) \right) - \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor n t \rfloor -1} Q^\sigma_{\lfloor n^\frac14\rfloor +1} \bfG{h} (\sqrt n Y_{j/n}). \end{split} \end{equation} Let \begin{equation}{m^{n}_t := \mathcal{G}^n_t - \frac1{\sqrt{n}} \left( \mathcal{Q}^{(3/4)}_{n,0,0}(\sqrt{n} Y_0) - \mathcal{Q}^{(3/4)}_{n,0,0}(\sqrt{n} Y_{\lfloor n t\rfloor/n}) \right) - \frac1{\sqrt{n}} \sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor n t \rfloor -1} Q^\sigma_{\lfloor n^\frac34\rfloor +1} \bfG{h} (\sqrt n Y_{j/n}). } \end{equation} By analogy, $m^n_t$ has an expression as~\eqref{eq:W} and so it is clear that $m^n$ is a martingale with respect to the filtration $(\mathcal{F}_{\lfloor n t \rfloor/n})_{t\in [0,1]}$. Therefore $n^{1/4} (M^{n,2}_t-m^n_t)$ as well. Let us denote by $D^n_t := n^{1/4} (\mathcal{G}^n_t - M^{n,2}_t)$ and $d^n_t := n^{1/4} (\mathcal{G}^n_t - m^n_t)$. Then $D^n-d^n = n^{1/4} (m^n-M^{n,2})$ is a martingale with respect to the filtration $(\mathcal{F}_{\lfloor n t \rfloor/n})_{t\in [0,1]}$. In this notation, the goal is to prove $\sup_{s\in [0,1]} |D^n_s|\convp[n\to\infty] 0$. {\em First step:\/} For every $t\in [0,1]$, let us show that $\lim_{n\to\infty} \mathbb{E}\!\left[( D^n_t-d^n_t)^2\right]=0$ by demonstrating the stronger fact that $\lim_{n\to\infty} \mathbb{E}\!\left[(D_t^n)^2+(d_t^n)^2\right]=0$.\\ Let $t\in [0,1]$ and $\eta \in \left\{ \frac14, \frac34 \right\}$ be fixed. Inequality \eqref{eq:cQ:prop4} implies for all $\omega\in \Omega$ that \begin{equation} \sup_{s\in [0,1]} n^{-\frac14} \left( \mathcal{Q}^{(\eta)}_{n,0,0}(\sqrt{n} Y_0(\omega)) - \mathcal{Q}^{(\eta)}_{n,0,0}(\sqrt{n} Y_{\lfloor n s\rfloor/n}(\omega)) \right) \xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{} 0, \end{equation} hence it holds also that $ \lim_{n\to\infty} \mathbb{E}\!\left[n^{-1/2} \left( \mathcal{Q}^{(\eta)}_{n,0,0}(\sqrt{n} Y_0) - \mathcal{Q}^{(\eta)}_{n,0,0}(\sqrt{n} Y_{\lfloor n t\rfloor/n}) \right)^2 \right]=0. $ Next observe that, since $\lambda_\sigma$ is a stationary measure, the sequences of functions $g_n^{(\eta)} := n^{1/4} Q^\sigma_{\lfloor n^{\eta}\rfloor +1} \bfG{h} $, $\eta \in \{\tfrac14,\tfrac34\}$ satisfy that $\langle \lambda_\sigma , g_n^{(\eta)} \rangle = n^{1/4} \langle \lambda_\sigma , \bfG{h} \rangle$ which is equal to 0 by Lemma~\ref{lem:prop:kappa}. This and inequality \eqref{eq:cQ:prop1} (with $\zeta=2$ since $h\in \Lg{\zeta+1}$) ensure that \eqref{eq:j1:4.2} holds. (A sufficient condition is $\eta \geq 1/4$.)\\ Hence, Lemma~\ref{lem:j1:4.2} shows that $ \lim_{n\to\infty} \mathbb{E}\!\left[ n^{-1/2} \left(\sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor n t \rfloor -1} Q^\sigma_{\lfloor n^{\eta}\rfloor +1} \bfG{h} (\sqrt n Y_{{j}/{n}})\right)^2\right]=0. $ {\em Second step:\/} It holds that $\sup_{s\in [0,1]} |D^n_s - d_s^n|\convp[n\to\infty] 0$.\\ This follows from \cite[Proposition~1.2]{aldous89} as a consequence of the previous step and the martingale property of $D^n - d^n$. {\em Third step:\/} It holds that $\sup_{s\in [0,1]} |d_s^n| \convp[n\to\infty] 0$. This follows from~\eqref{lem:j1:5.2.eq} and from applying Proposition~\ref{prop:th4.1a:j1} to the sequence $g_n:= n^{1/4} Q^\sigma_{\lfloor n^\frac34\rfloor +1} \bfG{h} $. (Here taking $n^{1/4} Q^\sigma_{\lfloor n^{\eta} \rfloor +1} \bfG{h}$ with $\eta>1/2$ would be sufficient.) The assumptions are indeed satisfied: $\lim_{n\to\infty} \|g_n\|_{1} =0$ by Item~\ref{item1:semig:estim} in Lemma~\ref{lem:semig:estim} and in the first step we have proven that $g_n$ satisfies \eqref{eq:j1:4.2} and in particular $\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{g_n(\sqrt{n}x)}{\sqrt{n}}=0$. Combining the two last steps yields the conclusion.
